text: The Princess noted that a woman had developed in a remarkable manner after spending time at Cecil de la Borne's place. Forrest expressed his belief that trouble had already arrived. The Princess commented on the cowardice of men and suggested that Forrest was not the man he used to be. Forrest admitted to having bullied the Princess for many years and felt the tables were turning on him. The Princess inquired about the De la Borne money, which Forrest confirmed had been paid by his brother. The Princess mentioned that De Brensault was serious about Jeanne and would be dining that night. The Princess indicated that if Jeanne was obstinate, she would have to suffer the consequences.

Dorward was a man of unbounded courage and resource, known for his success as a war correspondent in the Russo-Japanese War. Dorward had limited experience of European countries and was somewhat contemptuous of subtler dangers. He had escaped from a hotel without serious difficulty and had remained unmolested since then. Dorward felt safe and was content while traveling in his comfortable coupe. Bellamy entered Dorward's coupe and expressed skepticism about Dorward reaching London. Bellamy informed Dorward that there were high officials of the Secret Police of Austria on the train. Dorward initially dismissed Bellamy's warning about the seriousness of his situation.

The New Tenant is a work by E. Phillips Oppenheim. The book was published in 1910 by C. H. Doscher & Co. The story is set at Thurwell Court, located by Thurwell-on-the-Sea. The narrative begins with a description of the early morning at Falcon's Nest. A breakfast table is laid for two on one of the terraces. The character Helen is introduced as waiting at the breakfast table.

The Little Anna Gold-Mine is world famous. Deane gained a room near the location where Sinclair was killed. Deane attempted to gather information from the valet de chambre about the murder. The valet confirmed that a murder occurred in the next room. The door to the murder room is locked and managed by Mr. Hartshorn. Deane offered the valet various sums of money to gain access to the murder room. The valet declined Deane's offers, valuing his character over the money.

Paul strives to keep himself without fear and without reproach. Paul is practical in his attitude towards everyday life. Paul expresses strong feelings when he speaks to Lady May. Lady May recalls a time when Paul shared his troubles with her. A tall figure, dressed as a Roman Catholic priest, appears in the avenue. The priest calms Lady May's horse after it becomes startled. Paul recognizes the priest and addresses him about being on a private road.

Mr. Alfred Burton was dressed in formal town clothes. Mr. Burton carried yellow kid gloves and a malacca cane with a gold top. Mr. Johnson was surprised to see Mr. Burton, who was formerly a friend. Mr. Burton mentioned he had returned to settle matters and take his wife out. Mr. Burton is a director of the Menatogen Company and has invested ten thousand pounds. Mr. Johnson acknowledged the Menatogen Company and mentioned a friend who made a profit from it. Mr. Burton indicated he had been busy with work and had taken chambers in town.

source.author: Edward Phillips Oppenheim
source.title: The Double Life Of Mr. Alfred Burton

text: Virginia entered the building and offered to explain a telephone message. Norris Vine recognized Virginia as Phineas Duge's niece. Virginia stated that some papers were stolen from her uncle's study and given to Vine. Virginia followed Vine to London to recover the stolen papers. Virginia overheard a plot in a café involving two men who intended to harm Vine. Virginia warned Vine about the plot and used a telephone conversation to distract an intruder. Vine acknowledged Virginia's bravery in the situation.

A carriage was waiting in the courtyard below. Ughtred expressed his intention to leave and asked Sara to wish him luck. Sara expressed a desire to bring Ughtred luck and wished she could be his mascotte. Ughtred reassured Sara that her love was the best mascotte for him. The King issued a proclamation to the Thetian Army, thanking them for their bravery. The King announced that he would take over the supreme command from General Dartnoff. The King emphasized the importance of fighting for freedom and pledged no submission to the enemy.

The narrator attempted to leave the castle unnoticed but was approached by a servant. Lady Angela was in the billiard-room waiting for the narrator to give her a lesson in billiards. The narrator mentioned that Lord Blenavon had gone out. Lady Angela expressed curiosity about the narrator's appearance and mentioned her brother's visit to a woman at Braster Grange. The narrator confirmed that Lady Angela had promised to marry Colonel Mostyn Ray. Lady Angela stated that the engagement was almost a secret and that she did not know when the marriage would take place. Lady Angela indicated that Colonel Ray was not expected to visit until the next meeting of the Council.

Lady Peggy believes that Wilhelmina views men as puppets. Deyes remarks that a woman like Wilhelmina is a mystery. Lady Peggy states that in Florence, a woman without a lover is not accepted by Society. Deyes suggests that a lover would bore Wilhelmina. Wilhelmina is described as being in a carriage, appreciating the beauty of the night. Wilhelmina feels a new light and vitality in her life, which she finds unsettling. She experiences a sense of change and fear as she is caught in a current of new emotions.

Louise expresses her feelings of fortune after her car breaks down in a wilderness. John mentions that Louise's maid, Aline, is horrified by the lack of women servants. John explains that the farm buildings are distant from the house and that they manage with Jennings and two boys. Stephen states that he has never known any good to come from the friendship or service of women. John reveals that Louise is the first woman to visit Peak Hall in six years. Louise was motoring from Edinburgh and hoped to reach Kendal for the night. John and his brother have not traveled far from their home for many years and spend their time farming and engaging in outdoor activities.

The child identified herself as Isobel de Sorrens. Isobel stated that a man she referred to as her guardian took her to a convent when she was young. Isobel mentioned that the man had a house in London. The manager's name is Huber. Mr. Greatson informed Huber that a man named Grooten shot Major Delahaye with an air-gun. Isobel claimed to have seen the shooter at Charing Cross. A doctor and a police sergeant arrived after Huber left the room.

The navy, army, post-office employees, telegraph and telephone operators, and railway men have been the main recipients of corrupt literature. Two million dollars have been spent to corrupt a class that should support France. Bernadine, Count von Hern, is identified as the leader of the organization disseminating this corrupt literature. Sogrange believes that Bernadine must die due to his actions against the Republic of France. Bernadine is guilty of treason and has fled to another country. Sogrange possesses papers that could lead to Bernadine's arrest in an English court. The discussion between Sogrange and Peter revolves around the necessity of killing Bernadine.

Josephine's husband is currently in his den having a drink. Josephine expresses fear of her husband Henry returning in a bad mood. Dredlinton enters the room and is surprised to see Wingate. Dredlinton initially displays a hostile attitude but then becomes conciliatory. Wingate declares that he loves Josephine and intends to take her from Dredlinton. Dredlinton acknowledges that Josephine has not been a wife to him for years. Wingate claims to be entirely responsible for the disappearance of Stanley Rees.

The narrator is in New York to visit their mother, who is too delicate to travel. The narrator and another person are drafting a new first act and last act of a play. They work on the draft until the first gong for dinner rings. The narrator expresses joy in collaborating with someone who understands their thoughts. Mr. Raymond Greene approaches them and invites them to join him for a cocktail. Mr. Raymond Greene mentions a wireless message about the mysterious disappearance of a young man with the same name as Philip Romilly.

Jocelyn Thew observed a little man at a cigar stall and noticed a revolver in his hip pocket. Thew suspected the little man was associated with Crawshay and was preparing a report. Thew entered a big club, left through a side entrance, and took a taxicab to a subway station. Thew arrived at a small foreign-looking restaurant near the subway station and checked for the little man. Inside the restaurant, Thew interacted with a bartender and then proceeded to a room upstairs. Thew met a girl of medium height with dark hair and grey eyes, who expressed eagerness upon his arrival. Thew informed the girl that he was being followed and planned to sail for London the next day.

source.author: Edward Phillips Oppenheim
source.title: The Box with the Broken Seals

text: Clara expresses a desire for a proposal from Sir Leslie. Mannering states he will not associate with fortune-hunters. The Duchess suggests leaving the men to make plans. Berenice and Sir Leslie discuss Lady Redford's social choices. Berenice defends Mrs. Mannering's past and social acceptance. Sir Leslie acknowledges he knows more about Mrs. Mannering than Berenice. Berenice requests Sir Leslie to inform Mr. Mannering that she wishes to speak with him.

The conversation involves a man asking a woman if he can see her again. The woman expresses indifference about seeing the man again. The woman reveals that she was married for two years and is now separated. The man is referred to as Sir Julien. The woman is known as Madame Christophor. Kendricks plans a democratic evening for Julien, emphasizing a casual atmosphere. The setting includes a large restaurant with a noisy environment and a diverse crowd.

The speaker has experience in society in Paris, Vienna, Rome, and London. The speaker has always found women agreeable companions and has never avoided them. The speaker first saw the woman in the hall at the Universal two days prior. The speaker admits to being egotistical and expresses a strong interest in the woman. The woman questions the speaker's declaration of love, suggesting it is based only on her looks. The conversation shifts to a man named Leslie Guest, whom the speaker saw the previous night. The woman expresses a lack of pity for Leslie Guest, stating that he deserves death but does not wish for him to die at present.

Lady Ruth was a self-invited guest at White Lodge. Lady Ruth asked Wingrave for advice regarding her money troubles. A struggle occurred between Wingrave and Sir William, resulting in Sir William's injuries. Sir William was driven almost twelve miles in an unconscious state without medical assistance. Wingrave's trial was notable for his self-representation and the dramatic cross-examination of Lumley. Lady Ruth testified in court, hinting at an insult and discussing the check. The court was tense during Lady Ruth's testimony and Wingrave's subsequent stand.

The narrator attempted to rob someone and was confronted by a policeman. The policeman arrested the narrator after taking a gold mouse from his pocket. The narrator was taken to Sing Sing for three years due to this incident and other offenses. Aunt Martha expressed disapproval of the Groppeltacker type of people. The burglar claimed responsibility for all the burglaries in the neighborhood. The burglar stated that he avoided entering the narrator's house due to the presence of a baby. The burglar believed that a baby is a more effective deterrent than alarms or dogs.

source.author: Frank Richard Stockton
source.title: The Stories of the Three Burglars

text: Harry's wood enterprise provided a steady income that kept Aunt Matilda comfortable. Kate worked daily on tidies for the store and knitted stockings for neighbors. Mrs. Loudon allowed Kate to work for money, believing the end justified the means. Kate visited Aunt Matilda regularly to ensure she was warm and had what she needed. Aunt Matilda decided to whitewash her cabin and the trunks of trees around her house. Kate opposed Aunt Matilda's whitewashing of trees and threatened to stop visiting if it continued. Holly Thomas, a young girl, was left in charge of Aunt Matilda's cabin while she went out.

Phedo and Alberdin lived together in a tent for several days. Alberdin expressed impatience to fight a heavy infantry man. Alberdin and Phedo traveled to the capital city of Mutjado. Alberdin sent messengers to arrange a meeting with his opponent. The messengers reported that the opponent's camp was deserted. Alberdin planned to claim the Autocracy if his opponent did not show up. Alberdin proposed to marry the late Autocrat's daughter to strengthen his claim.

source.author: Frank Richard Stockton
source.title: The Bee-Man of Orn and Other Fanciful Tales

text: Mr. Tolman plans to sell his business and leave the city. Mr. Glascow is surprised by Mr. Tolman's decision to leave. Mr. Tolman advises Mr. Glascow to propose to Miss Edwards the next day. Mr. Tolman prepares a back room for Miss Edwards' visit by arranging furniture and decorations. Mr. Tolman waits outside the shop to monitor Mr. Glascow's approach. Mr. Tolman allows Mr. Glascow twenty minutes to speak with Miss Edwards. Mr. Glascow enters the shop after the allotted time to meet Miss Edwards.

source.author: Frank Richard Stockton
source.title: The Magic Egg and Other Stories

text: The narrator presents a scheme for the brotherhood of the House of Martha to Sylvia. Sylvia expresses enthusiasm and support for the brotherhood plan. The narrator mentions knowing only one other person qualified for the brotherhood besides himself. Sylvia is visiting an old man with severe rheumatism who requires constant care. The narrator decides to accompany Sylvia to help care for the old man. They enter a house showing signs of extreme poverty, where the old man is bedridden. Sylvia encourages the old woman to rest while they take care of the old man.

The story mentioned is based on gossip from servants. Mr. Havelot is a proud and wealthy man who does not hold absurd ideas about the source of wealth. The narrator has been working on a tunnel into a glacier spur, which has reached considerable length. The ice found in the glacier is of a finer quality than the initial grayish ice. Visitors are allowed to view the ice cavern when workmen are not present. Tom Burton frequently visits with scientific parties to see the ice cavern. Aaron Boyce, a local farmer, expresses pride in the narrator's accomplishments in improving his property.

Blackbeard appointed Charter as the first officer of the Revenge. Charter was not made mate due to his lack of sailing knowledge. Dickory refused to serve under Blackbeard, expressing shame in associating with him. Black Paul warned Dickory that refusing to serve could lead to his death. Blackbeard threatened Bittern for speaking to his lieutenant. Bittern had previously aided Blackbeard in capturing Captain Bonnet's property. Dickory resolved to not leave life willingly, valuing his connections to Kate Bonnet and his mother.

Mrs. Block spent the first two days on the vessel sitting in the cabin with a dustbrush and a farmer's almanac. Mrs. Block became interested in looking out of the windows, particularly at the bow of the vessel. Captain Jim Hubbell informed Mrs. Block that sword-fish do not inhabit the cold waters they were sailing in. Captain Jim Hubbell stated that sperm-whales became scarce during his childhood and have not been seen in arctic waters since 1935. Mrs. Block expressed a mix of fear and sadness regarding the extinction of whales. Sammy Block and his companions were able to communicate with people around the world via a telegraphic wire. Roland Clewe received messages from Sammy Block indicating that the submarine voyage was proceeding satisfactorily.

The king administered justice through a method involving an arena where outcomes were uncertain. The accused could either be punished or rewarded based on their choice of door, with no prior knowledge of the outcome. The king had a daughter who was loved by a young man of lower social status. The king discovered the love affair and imprisoned the young man, scheduling a trial in the arena. The trial was of great interest to the king and the people, as it was unprecedented for a subject to love the king's daughter. The king arranged for both a fierce tiger and a suitable bride to be present for the trial. The king took pleasure in the proceedings, regardless of the outcome for the young man.

The placard in the gallery was inscribed with 'The Reversible Landscape: A New Idea in Art.' The proprietor of the gallery claimed that the painting was not the same as the previously sold pictures. The painting displayed a different morning star, identified as Jupiter instead of Venus. Uncle Pete was the elderly individual presiding over a negro church near Oxford Cross Roads in Virginia. Uncle Pete could neither read nor write but effectively expounded the Scriptures to his congregation. Uncle Pete's wife was dissatisfied with his dedication to the church over household responsibilities. During a sermon, Uncle Pete claimed that every woman was possessed by seven devils.

The Misses Thorpedyke did not enjoy cold amusement such as sleigh rides. Mrs. Cliff and Willy participated in sleigh rides with Mr. Burke a few times. Mr. Burke's opinion of his reason for living in Plainton was influenced by his experiences with Willy. Mrs. Cliff was in good health, which affected Mr. Burke's plans regarding marriage to Willy. The Buskirks were spending the winter in their country home. Mr. Burke visited the Buskirk mansion but found Mr. Buskirk was not at home. Mr. Burke perceived the furnishings of the Buskirk house to be inferior to those of Mrs. Cliff's home.

Mr. Chipperton believed that some individuals could not have survived much longer. The vessel that rescued them was a coasting schooner headed to one of the Florida Keys. Upon reaching the Florida Keys, they chartered a vessel to Fernandina and then took a steamer to Savannah. They sent a telegram upon arriving in Fernandina, proposing a stop at St. Augustine, but decided to continue to Fernandina instead. Mr. Chipperton acquired fancy clothes from a passenger on the schooner. Mrs. Chipperton expressed her gratitude by kissing the boys multiple times. Mr. Chipperton offered to be an uncle to the boys and requested they call him Uncle Chipperton.

The young lady invited the narrator to meet her mother to discuss Walford. The mother was talkative and shared information about Walford and its residents. The young lady offered to have Brownster take care of the narrator's valise and belongings. The young lady mentioned the presence of hot-houses and green-houses on the property. The young lady pointed out a mushroom-house, noting that her family does not like mushrooms. The narrator visited the orchid-house with the young lady, who explained its features. The narrator planned to stay at an inn called the 'Holly Sprig' after leaving Walford.

The Prince was accompanied by Mahbracca, who used her staff to transport him to solid ground. They arrived at the cavity of a hollow mountain with a plain floor and light coming from an opening above. The plain was populated by ghouls, demons, and herds of prong-horned Yabouks. In the center of the plain stood a tower, which Mahbracca identified as the dwelling of the Princess. The Princess appeared at a window, and the Prince expressed his love for her while she wept tears of joy. The Prince attempted to open the tower door but was unable to do so, even after using his sword. Overcome with sorrow and hunger, the Prince resolved to seek assistance to rescue the Princess.

A white house is located about a hundred feet back from the main street of a village in New Jersey. The house was built by Mr. Himes and is now owned by his widow, Mrs. Himes. There is a large chestnut tree between the house and the sidewalk. Two elderly men, Thomas Rooper and Asaph Scantle, are sitting on a bench under the chestnut tree. Thomas Rooper is described as a small man with gray side-whiskers and good clothes, smoking a meerschaum pipe. Asaph Scantle is taller, round-shouldered, and wears poorer clothing, smoking a common clay pipe. The conversation between Thomas and Asaph revolves around the idea of marrying money and the condition of Thomas's house.

The British battle-ship was prepared to defend itself against American vessels with heavy artillery and protective measures. The Syndicate completed preparations for a decisive movement in its campaign during the first week of the Adamant's involuntary cruise. A repeller and six crabs were outfitted with extraordinary powers for the British Government's planned descent on the American coast. The Adamant had been captured, leading to the abandonment of stern-jacket manufacturing, but new methods for protecting rudders and propeller-blades were adopted. The repeller, originally the Tallapoosa, was purchased from the United States government and underwent significant modifications for its new role. Repeller No. 11 was equipped with heavy steel armor and a bomb-proof canopy, making it one of the most defensively capable vessels. Repeller No. 11 departed from a Northern port of the United States, towed by crabs, on a course towards Great Britain.

The war in New Jersey involved battles and skirmishes between Tories and Whigs, often without British soldiers. The Whigs were primarily composed of militiamen defending their homes and farms. Captain Huddy of Monmouth County commanded a company of militiamen and gained a reputation as a formidable fighter. Captain Huddy was at home with only a servant, a negro girl named Lucretia Emmons, when Tories attacked his house. Huddy and Emmons defended the house against fifty or sixty Tories, leading them to believe there were more defenders inside. The Tories attempted to burn the house to force Huddy to surrender, and he eventually capitulated after wounding a Tory leader. Huddy was captured and taken away by the Tories, but his militiamen pursued them, resulting in the deaths of six Tories.

Dick spoke to the captain about Olive's troubles and provided a letter from his brother. The captain reacted negatively to the contents of the letter regarding Olive's situation. The captain felt a sense of responsibility towards Olive, believing she turned to him for help. Dick hesitated to convey Olive's message about her visit due to her concerns about the captain marrying Miss Port. The captain expressed anger at the suggestion of marrying Maria Port and was upset that Olive believed he would consider it. Old Jane inquired about the captain's plans regarding Miss Port but received no information. Dick felt dejected and uncertain about visiting Olive due to the current circumstances.

Mr. Dusante is determined to return a ginger-jar containing board money to the person responsible for overseeing its payment. Mr. Dusante traveled extensively, including across the ocean and throughout California, while carrying the ginger-jar. Mrs. Lecks received the ginger-jar from Mr. Dusante after he expressed his respect for her. Ruth and Lucille were instructed by Mrs. Lecks to take the ginger-jar and divide the money among the sailors. The sailors, including the red-bearded coxswain, expressed their loyalty and willingness to follow orders. Jim and Bill, fellow sailors, affirmed their commitment to obeying orders alongside the coxswain.

source.author: Frank Richard Stockton
source.title: The Casting Away of Mrs. Lecks and Mrs. Aleshine

text: The narrator opened a wooden shutter at the back of a shed and found a wall of snow outside. The narrator believed it would be possible to tunnel through the snow to reach voices heard nearby. The narrator used a tin pan to scoop through the snow, which took several hours of arduous labor. The narrator encountered a man near a fire and a stage-coach after tunneling through the snow. Mrs. Aleshine called out to the narrator from the other side of the snow drift, expressing concern about other people being present. The narrator's companions were alarmed upon learning about the other party snow-bound nearby. The group discussed providing food and warmth to the other party, expressing concern for their well-being.

Philip and Claire traveled south from Paris, avoiding large towns and stopping only at village inns. They traveled over two hundred miles in eight days, crossing the Loire above Orleans. Philip's retainers greeted him warmly upon their arrival at the chateau of Laville. The countess had recently returned from La Rochelle and was informed of rumors regarding violence against Huguenots. Philip introduced Claire as Mademoiselle de Valecourt, his affianced wife, to the countess. Philip recounted the details of a massacre to the countess, who expressed horror at the events. There were reports that some guests at the royal palace were murdered during the massacre.

At the end of each day's journey, camels were allowed to browse while tied with a short cord. The Arabs collected sticks to make a fire for warmth, as their food consisted of dried dates and black bread. The Arabs arranged their camels in a circle around their campfire, with one person acting as a sentry. Cuthbert planned to escape during the time between arriving at the halting place and bringing in the camels. Cuthbert pretended to be fatigued and feigned sleep to avoid suspicion from the Arabs. Cuthbert observed the direction of a specific camel and quietly shifted his robe to escape into the darkness. Cuthbert successfully mounted the camel after using commands he learned from the Arabs and rode away from the camp.

Terence was aided by prison guards to escape after receiving their help with guerillas. Terence had a conversation with the adjutant general before rejoining his regiment. Terence requested an English officer as adjutant for his battalions. Terence preferred Lieutenant Ryan for the adjutant position due to their friendship and Ryan's Portuguese skills. The adjutant general agreed to appoint Lieutenant Ryan as adjutant to the Minho Portuguese regiment with acting rank of captain. Terence had not informed Dick Ryan of his intention to request him as adjutant. Terence and Dick Ryan planned to buy horses instead of hiring a vehicle for their journey.

John was nineteen years old, strong, active, and sinewy. John carried a buckler, two light javelins, and a sword. John encountered a Roman officer while descending a valley. The Roman officer hurled a javelin at John, who avoided it. John successfully struck the Roman's horse with a javelin, causing it to fall. John engaged in combat with the Roman officer, sustaining several wounds. The Roman officer identified himself as Titus during the fight.

Archie and his guides moved cautiously to avoid detection by English horsemen surrounding the morass. The guides had to change their path due to English soldiers examining the area for tracks. Archie and his party progressed slowly, moving only a few yards at a time to find solid ground. After leaving the morass, they traveled across the country until they were beyond the English line. Archie and Ronald took refuge in a cave for a fortnight, where Ronald purchased provisions from local cottages. They lit a signal fire on Saturday nights to communicate with Duncan, who was to sail across if weather permitted. A messenger reported that Kildrummy was threatened with a siege, leading to the evacuation of the queen and ladies to St. Duthoc.

Victor opened his eyes and did not recognize Harry. Harry gave Victor a draught and spoonfuls of soup, which improved Victor's breathing. The doctor approved of Victor's condition, stating that the fever had left him. Elise reported that Martha's brother would try to help but doubted the possibility of rescuing mademoiselle. Harry received a note from Marie three days later while attending to Victor. Victor was no longer unconscious and followed movements in the room but did not fully recognize Harry. Jeanne and Virginie read Marie's letter together, which was written on a fly-leaf of a book.

Charlie is nearly twenty years old and has changed significantly since he left four years ago. Charlie's father believes that youth and strength are necessary for the business they are discussing. Charlie's father has a plan to lift the charge of assassination against him and others, which would allow them to return and reverse the Act of Confiscation of their estates. Jervoise, a former acquaintance of John Churchill, is mentioned as potentially helpful due to his favor with Anne. Charlie's father has sent a letter to Jervoise requesting an introduction to the Duke of Marlborough. Charlie is advised to stay at the Bull's Head in Fenchurch Street while in London. Charlie is warned to be careful not to kill Nicholson, as it would hinder their chance of uncovering the greater villain.

Reuben was involved in a case that generated significant interest in Sussex due to the position of Squire Ellison and the nature of the defense. The evidence presented for the prosecution was largely similar to that given during the inquiry before the magistrates. The judge presiding over Reuben's case was known to be severe and appeared biased against the prisoner from the outset. Squire Ellison was questioned about the poisoning of his dog, which was used to suggest animosity towards Reuben. Ellison expressed his belief in Reuben's innocence but struggled to provide a satisfactory reason for changing his opinion. The counsel for the prosecution suggested that Ellison's change of heart was influenced by his own goodness of heart. During cross-examination, Ellison confirmed that Reuben had no reason to be upstairs in his house while employed.

The group plans to build a wall ten feet high using shovels. The snow does not bind well in the cold, making construction difficult. Tom suggests pouring water over the snow blocks to freeze them into solid ice. A semicircular line for the wall was traced out at the top of their pathway, measuring thirty feet across. The whites will use the shovels by turns while the Indians will scout and watch at night. By dark, the wall had risen to a height of three feet and was sufficient to form a breastwork. The chief observed the area for signs of Indians and found none before resting behind the wall.

source.author: George Alfred Henty
source.title: In The Heart Of The Rockies

text: The boys rowed among anchored vessels and admired the yachts moored opposite the clubhouses. They decided to look at a fine East-Indiaman moored below Gravesend. While talking about the ship's potential voyage, they lost track of time and distance. George realized they were far from the town and needed to row back to avoid missing dinner. The boys did not know to row close to shore against the tide and ended up in the middle of the river. After rowing for half an hour, they discovered they had drifted further away from their destination. A fog rolled in, reducing visibility to ten yards.

The soldiers have been marching through difficult terrain, including hills and trees. Tim expressed a desire for a break before continuing the march. The lieutenant informed Tim that they would likely face fighting soon, with a numerical disadvantage against a hundred infantry. Percy Barclay alerted the group that they were under attack after hearing a rifle shot. Lieutenant de Maupas instructed the villagers to evacuate and prepare for the attack. The franc tireurs engaged the enemy in a skirmish, taking advantage of cover. Despite their advantageous position, the franc tireurs faced overwhelming odds against the enemy.

Her Majesty's ships Active and Tenedos were part of a military column that included 200 mounted infantry, 200 colonial mounted riflemen, and about 2000 men of the native contingent. The Tugela River was nearly 400 yards wide, making crossing difficult for the military column. A flying bridge was constructed by sailors to facilitate the crossing of the Tugela River, which was completed on the 13th. On the 18th, the leading division began its march into enemy territory, followed by the second division the next day. The first day's march ended at the Inyoni stream, ten miles north of the Tugela, and the second day was spent encamped on the Umsindusi. On the 22nd, Colonel Glyn's column was attacked by a large enemy force while halted for breakfast after crossing the Inyezane River. The attacking Zulus numbered approximately 5000, while the defending troops consisted of about 500 to 600 soldiers.

A rising in Dublin could compel the Dutch general to maintain a large force in the city. Mr. O'Brian stated that the spirit of the people has been broken and their numbers diminished. Walter visited several individuals to gather information about the sentiment throughout the country. The peasantry expressed a strong hatred towards the invaders and were in a state of sullen desperation. The peasants primarily possessed pikes and scythes, which were inadequate against larger military forces. The individuals Walter spoke with agreed that a general rising should be delayed until the Irish army achieved a significant victory. Larry reported that he suspected they were being followed by a man who appeared multiple times while Walter was visiting.

Dr. Hooper expressed interest in taking the lease of a house for three more years. Harry arranged to sell furniture and other items to Dr. Hooper at a valuation. Harry received a cheque for £500 from Dr. Hooper as part of the property settlement. The group decided to seek lodgings in Putney while looking for a permanent house. They found an address for lodgings at Putney from an old pocket-book. The group traveled to Putney by train after finishing their packing and saying goodbye. They arrived at No. 12, Charlemagne Villas, and confirmed that Mrs. Thompson still lived there.

source.author: George Alfred Henty
source.title: A Search For A Secret, a Novel, Volume 3

text: The provost of the silversmiths is a strong opponent of the butchers. There is a threat of an attack by the rabble on the house occupied by the protagonist. The count has a profession that involves intrigue and has amassed a considerable fortune. The count wishes for his daughter, Countess Katarina of Montepone, to live a life of peace and tranquility. The count believes that his daughter may have a better life in England than in France or Italy. The protagonist feels that the count could be a useful friend and ally.

Vincent and Lucy filled their cart with apples, pumpkins, and other vegetables from a farm near Mount Pleasant. The woman at the farm provided them with a letter to her sister, who lived a mile from Camden. The woman suggested that it is often awkward for farmers to stop at hotels when traveling with garden truck. Upon arriving at the sister's house, Vincent and Lucy were welcomed by the farmer and his wife. The farmer and his wife offered Vincent and Lucy a place to sleep, making arrangements for their comfort. Vincent explained that they were trying to avoid being questioned by Yankee troops while traveling. The farmer suspected that Vincent and Lucy were not farmers based on their appearance.

Leigh and his party of scouts learned that it was intended to march against Saumur. Leigh's party had doubled in strength due to the story of their previous actions. Leigh was mounted to ride with Rochejaquelein and scout with his party. Henri and Leigh decided to call each other by their first names. Leigh was requested to go forward at daybreak with his band to discover the enemy's situation. Leigonyer commanded four good regiments and occupied strong positions on the river Layon. Three spies were captured by Leigh's party while attempting to reach Leigonyer.

Edmund plans to rescue Freda from Sweyn. Edmund intends to disguise himself in Dane's clothing to approach Freda. Freda appears in the afternoon while most men are occupied. Edmund warns Freda to remain calm as they are being watched. Freda acknowledges Edmund and learns about the plan for her rescue. Sweyn is informed by his guards that a Northman spoke to Freda. Freda reveals to Sweyn that Edmund is a messenger from her father.

Dominique, Frank, and George Lechmere were the only individuals not carrying muskets. The pilot declined to carry a gun, expressing fear of firearms. The group ascended a hill and reached a cultivated area approximately three hundred feet above the water. Dominique informed Frank that he would scout the village to avoid detection. The cultivated land extended on both sides of the village, allowing for quiet passage. Dominique planned to ask questions in the next village regarding the whereabouts of a gentleman and two ladies. An old man in a hut confirmed that the group they were seeking had passed by earlier and mentioned a potential pirate threat.

Peter Lambton is identified as a royalist who joined a corps in Boston. General Montgomery ordered the seizure of Peter Lambton when he was recognized. Peter Lambton escaped into the woods before he could be captured. A Chippewa Indian pursued Peter Lambton after he fled. The Chippewa was killed by a tomahawk during the pursuit. Peter Lambton and a Seneca reached their canoe without being caught. Signals were seen from the island indicating the presence of enemies on the lake.

A wheel came off a wagon on the Clearwater Trail, causing the wagon to pitch over into a ravine. Several thousand dollars' worth of boring machines were damaged in the accident. Louis sustained a head injury and expressed anger towards the person who removed the cotter from the wheel hub. Black was transported to a station near the Washington border, where he was described as a sick employee of an American firm. Black experienced illness, including a throbbing head and dry throat, while being taken to a location surrounded by forests near Puget Sound. Black was threatened with legal consequences if he caused trouble during the transport. Black regained consciousness in a vessel's forecastle, recognizing the smell of bilge water and hearing orders from above.

The protagonist reflects on the spiritual benefits of manual labor despite its brutality. As the sobrecargo of the _Estremedura_, he observed human struggles with tolerance. He resolves to confront the challenges of his environment with determination. The protagonist aims to prove his worth and justify his existence. He assesses the water level in the hold and confirms it has not changed significantly. Jefferson expresses cautious optimism about the possibility of floating the stranded steamer. The onset of fever among the crew is noted as a developing concern.

Hetty observed a man with a rifle in the hall. Flora Schuyler suggested that Mr. Grant could escape without being seen. Hetty expressed concern about her father's potential reaction to Mr. Grant's presence. Flora Schuyler indicated that any suspicion regarding Mr. Grant would be less severe for her than for Hetty. Hetty instructed her maid to distract the cowboy in the hall. Flora Schuyler proposed that the maid could use food to divert the cowboy's attention. Hetty and Flora Schuyler assisted Mr. Grant in moving through the hall.

Leland received a packet of letters and handed some to Urmston. Leland mentioned that the implement man wants his payment, the seller in Winnipeg cannot sell the horses, and the bank requires security for further drawing. Urmston rode beside Carrie's waggon and did not open his letters. Urmston asked Carrie about Eveline Annersly and expressed concern about Custer. Urmston informed Carrie that he must leave for Edmonton soon with the men he arrived with. Carrie expressed a lack of concern about Urmston's departure and questioned his feelings. Urmston declared his love for Carrie and criticized her marriage to a ploughman.

Foster feels a thrill when Alice shows confidence in his honesty. Featherstone expresses suspicion about Foster's honesty regarding Daly. Featherstone did not give in to Daly's demands during his visit. The police have visited Featherstone again and asked questions about Foster. Featherstone received a short letter from his son, Lawrence, stating he could not come home. Foster admits that Featherstone's concerns are true but asks for specific conclusions. Alice defends Foster, suggesting he is not capable of being a dangerous plotter.

Kit is on the _Rio Negro_ and is not smoking, but is pondering his life over the last three years. Kit has lost some of his frankness and raw enthusiasm and appears thinner and older than when he left Ashness. Adam Askew, Kit's uncle, has a yellowish brown skin tone and black eyes, and he dresses in loose white clothes and a Tuxedo jacket. Adam Askew is described as having an exotic look and is known among his friends as the 'buccaneer.' Adam sent Kit to an American business school and later to Mexico and other countries to study human nature. Kit has interacted with a diverse range of people, including French and Spanish Creoles, negroes, Indians, and half-breeds. Adam Askew has suffered from malarial ague and appears haggard and thin.

Agatha wrote to Thirlwell to inform him of her readiness to begin her search for ore. Agatha is waiting for Thirlwell's reply, which may take time to arrive. The evening is calm and Agatha finds the quiet soothing. George expresses concern about Agatha's plan to find the old man's lode. Agatha receives a telegram from Thirlwell confirming the meeting and funding for her journey. Agatha plans to start her journey in three days. Agatha has prepared her outfit for the journey and arranged for it to be sent.

The skipper was unable to get up and was in a hammock under the bridge-awning. Montgomery, an African trader from a Liverpool house, seemed to have control of the situation. Barbara asked a young American doctor for help to see the captain of the African steamer. Barbara wrote an address for Wheeler to visit Don Luis Sarmiento, the best doctor in town. Barbara arranged to charter a powerful Spanish tug with the help of a junior partner from an English merchant house. The merchant engaged the crew of a Spanish fishing schooner to relieve the crew of the _Arcturus_. Barbara planned to send a check for the tug when it was ready to sail.

A chestnut horse fell after colliding with a fallen horse or man. Crestwick found Nasmyth trying to drag Lisle clear of danger. Lisle appeared to have serious injuries, including a distorted arm and shoulder. Gladwyne struggled to control the chestnut horse. Nasmyth requested Marple to fetch Irvine and a gun. Millicent expressed concern for Lisle's condition. The doctor arrived to examine Lisle after the incident.

George observed a man who appeared anxious and had a careworn woman embracing him before a steamer sailed. The man expressed concern about job opportunities and mentioned he had driven horses most of his life. George decided to hire the man at a rate of thirty dollars a month after inquiring about farm teamster wages. Edgar expressed gladness about George's decision but cautioned that teaching the man might be challenging. George reflected on the man's situation, noting the sacrifices made for passage money and the anxiety to find work. Edgar planned to stay for about twelve months before considering a return to a profession. George and Edgar left the town and explored the surrounding landscape, noting its vastness and silence.

Frank was waiting in the grass, listening for sounds that might indicate the presence of opponents. Frank understood the smuggler's hesitation to attempt to burn the barn due to the risk of being seen. Frank felt it was difficult to remain still and considered moving forward despite the risks. Harry indicated that he believed Webster fired first and that Mr. Oliver would likely hear the shots. A faint flicker of light appeared from behind the barn, indicating the smugglers had started a second fire. Frank realized that the second fire was a tactic to force Mr. Oliver into a vulnerable position. Harry urged Frank to run, indicating that any noise they made would draw the smugglers away from Mr. Oliver.

source.author: Harold Bindloss
source.title: The Boy Ranchers of Puget Sound

text: Weston spent the morning holding a drill and swinging a hammer at a mining site. The work required close attention due to the risk of injury from the heavy hammer. Weston experienced physical discomfort while working, including a stitch in his side. Grenfell spent the afternoon mending clothes, including a jacket for Weston. Weston was uncertain about how Grenfell would pay for his board. A man suggested that Grenfell could become the camp's mender and washer. The proposal to make Grenfell the camp's mender received a positive response from the group.

Whitney accidentally struck a bottle with his elbow, causing it to roll across the table and fall on the floor. Williamson suggested that Dick study some good professionals and mentioned an interesting semi-private match next Thursday. Staffer advised that Dick should stay at home due to being warned to keep regular hours. Andrew reminded Dick about their arrangement to go snipe-shooting on Wednesday. Whitney expressed his enthusiasm for snipe and mentioned they were going down the coast at the end of the week. Staffer informed Andrew that Marshall, the salmon fisher, mentioned the Burnfoot boats had been run up that afternoon. Andrew felt a sense of duty to look after Dick, believing he was not good enough for Elsie.

The speaker discussed the importance of sowing plenteously and being faithful in minor tasks. He emphasized the pioneers' duty to prepare the land for future settlers and to practice good husbandry. The speaker urged the congregation to share their surplus to help the poor in the Old Country. Hester showed Harding a dollar while the closing hymn began. Harding gave Hester three bits of paper, which she found surprising. The clergyman mentioned he needed to leave for Poplar that night due to a bad trail. Mowbray asked Beatrice to count a large amount of money collected, which was more than usual.

Dampier and Wyllard were in Kamtchatka and discussed their project. Dampier instructed the helmsman, Charly, to adjust the course of the boat. Dampier indicated that they would not return to Vancouver that year. The crew of the _Selache_ felt relieved as they made progress across the Pacific. The _Selache_ anchored in a sheltered arm of Southern Alaska with no signs of life nearby. Dampier went ashore to find a log for a mast, but the temperature fell and the boat became frozen in. In winter, Alaska was cut off from communication with the south due to severe conditions.

Dom Clemente received information that made him thoughtful. Dom Clemente observed his daughter in the patio while she was reading a book. Dom Clemente felt a sense of responsibility regarding his motherless daughter. Dom Clemente dispatched a message to Lieutenant Frequillo regarding urgent matters. The captain of a British steamer reported that a white steam yacht ignored his signals. Dom Clemente noted the unusual characteristics of the yacht and its fast speed heading south. Benicia expressed uncertainty about the interest of Señor Desmond in the situation.

Mrs. Chudleigh is coming to Hazlehurst again. Mrs. Chudleigh has no pressing invitation for her visit. Blake believes Mrs. Chudleigh's visit may be related to her uncle. Blake plans to meet Mrs. Chudleigh to prevent her from seeing his uncle. The Colonel is going to the Croxleigh meet. Challoner and Blake are well mounted for the ride to Croxleigh gorse. The meet at Croxleigh was arranged late due to difficult access.

Jimmy thought it was awkward to get down the slope. Deering brought a rope and suggested that Stannard lead while he tied on at the top. Bob got on his knees by the sheep and received the head from Stannard. Bob pushed the headless sheep over the edge before the party began to climb the slope. The group pitched camp after reaching the top of the slope. Bob calculated that the game warden was located at the other end of the range. Deering suggested they should give up the heads and take Bob to the police.

Colonel Barrington is the founder and ruler of the English community of Silverdale. Colonel Barrington was waiting for his niece, Maud Barrington, who arrived an hour late. Maud Barrington expressed a preference to stay with Colonel Barrington on the prairie rather than in Montreal. Colonel Barrington planned to see the horses put in and get the mail upon arriving at the hotel. Colonel Barrington founded the Silverdale settlement ten years earlier. He gathered men with grievances and younger sons of English gentlemen to settle on the land and farm. Colonel Barrington noted that there is less prospect for making money than he previously thought.

Brooke and Jimmy were working on a log jam that was unstable and could break apart at any moment. They bored holes into the logs and embedded several sticks of explosive. Brooke instructed Jimmy to light the fuse and prepare to escape the gully. Jimmy struggled to ignite a damp match before successfully lighting the fuse. As Jimmy attempted to climb out of the gully, he witnessed a dangerous situation involving Brooke. A warning was shouted to Jimmy as he realized the fuses would soon reach the powder. Jimmy managed to locate Brooke and attempted to pull him to safety despite the challenging conditions.

The boys were engaged in securing posts and gathering materials while Ellen kept watch. Mark decided to drive a flock of fourteen sheep into the stockade for protection. The loss of the sheep would be detrimental to the settlers due to their importance for clothing materials. Ellen alerted the boys to the sighting of a vessel approaching the harbor island. The boys observed a small schooner heading towards the harbor island, which they believed could help them. Mistress Pemberton expressed concern that the crew of the schooner might be attacked by the Abenakis. Susan noted that the schooner appeared to have a large crew, leading Mark to question its identity.

The temple entrance was formed of twenty slender shafts of white stone. Each column upheld a grotesque figure that appeared to be made of silver. Jake expressed a desire to take one of the images from the temple. Poyor insisted that the group must leave to avoid danger. A loud crash was heard from the temple, indicating that Jake had toppled one of the columns. Poyor engaged in a struggle with a man who appeared in their path. Cummings and the others were pursued through the city after the commotion at the temple.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Search for the Silver City

text: Plums expresses disbelief at his friend's statement regarding having things his way. Plums refuses to carry a message to aunt Dorcas about the paper. Master Fernald follows Plums to the cottage with a plan in mind. Plums prevents Dan Fernald from leaving the cottage by standing in front of the door. Dan Fernald states he will not give up the paper unless aunt Dorcas agrees to let him live there. Joe reacts violently to Dan's statement and forces him against the wall. Joe shakes Dan until he agrees to give up the newspaper, after which Dan is thrown out of the kitchen.

Toby was called by Mr. Job Lord to begin his first day's work. Mr. Job Lord was angry with Toby for not being present to help him. Toby attempted to explain his absence but Mr. Lord became more furious. Mr. Lord physically punished Toby with a rubber cane. Toby endured the punishment without making a sound. Ben intervened to stop Mr. Lord from continuing to punish Toby. Ben warned Mr. Lord against physically harming Toby in the future.

Mr. Crow is the president of the club. Jimmy Hedgehog spoke out in a meeting, which upset other members. The narrator felt concerned for Jimmy Hedgehog after Mr. Crow's remarks. Mrs. Bunny expressed anger about the narrator's involvement in the club. Sonny Bunny was found injured and frightened after an encounter with Jimmy Hedgehog. Jimmy Hedgehog rolled over Sonny Bunny multiple times, causing him harm. Jimmy Hedgehog threatened the narrator regarding his family.

Jet is instructed to tell a man that his number is one hundred and ten. Jet carries a traveling-bag that is light despite appearing full. Jet meets a man with red hair who takes the bag and gives Jet a heavy paper parcel. The bartender informs Jet that the gentlemen he is looking for have left. Jet is directed to a small hotel on the Bowery by the bartender. At the hotel, Jet encounters the tall man who questions him about his time. The tall man gives Jet half a dollar and instructs him to say he was at the Stock Exchange.

Mr. Harvey asked Sam if he could show the stolen goods and the location of the other burglar. Sam confirmed that he could show the stolen goods and the location of the other burglar. Mr. Hargreaves promised to pay fifty dollars for the return of his property. Uncle Nathan expressed concern about paying the reward until he was certain Sam was not involved in the theft. The 'Squire stated that Sam would receive the reward if his story was true. Hazelton expressed gratitude to Teddy for his assistance. Teddy calculated that he made two hundred and fifty-two dollars and fifty cents during the week.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Adventures of a Country Boy at a Country Fair

text: The bully decided to leave the neighborhood to avoid confrontation. Teddy reported the events of the previous twenty-four hours to a policeman. The policeman advised Teddy to enter a complaint against the bully for stealing money. Teddy expressed reluctance to file a complaint unless necessary. Teddy planned to defend himself if the bully attacked him. Carrots admired Teddy's approach of seeking protection from the authorities. Teddy and Carrots worked vigorously to avoid losing business to the bully and his gang.

Two scouts approached a fort while escorting six prisoners taken from an encampment of seventeen hundred men. The prisoners made no effort to defend themselves during their capture. The sergeant expressed amusement at the situation and considered it a story worth telling in the future. The prisoners initially believed they were being taken to a guard-tent until they realized the truth of their situation. The sergeant threatened the prisoners to keep them moving towards the fort. The scouts believed that the enemy's forces were incapacitated due to excessive drinking. The scouts communicated their arrival and the presence of prisoners to the sentinels at the fort.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of the Mohawk Valley

text: On July 1, 1898, Major-General W. R. Shafter reported a heavy engagement near Siboney that lasted from eight A.M. until sundown. Shafter's forces captured the outer works of the enemy and were positioned three-quarters of a mile from the city of Santiago. General Lawton's division and General Bates's brigade were engaged in the battle for El Caney, which was captured at four P.M. Shafter reported over four hundred casualties, with not many killed. The attack on El Caney was planned due to its strategic importance in controlling the Guantanamo road and protecting against enemy flanking maneuvers. The battle at El Caney began early on July 1st, with Lawton's forces positioned across the Guantanamo road. The battle continued until El Caney was taken by assault around 4:30 P.M.

Toby was excited about seeing Mr. and Mrs. Treat, old Ben, and little Ella at dinner in Uncle Daniel's home. Circus operations were suspended by the would-be managers due to the arrival of a real circus. The band and acrobat had time to practice and improve their skills before the circus arrived. Mr. Douglass allowed Joe to train his horse in Uncle Daniel's pasture, but there were issues with Chandler Merrill's pony. The boys attempted to drive the pony home, but it resisted and drove them away instead. Aunt Olive prepared a variety of food for the guests, including apple pies, cake, doughnuts, and custards. Toby and Abner were both unable to sleep the night before the circus due to excitement.

Pip Smith's depiction of city life is questioned for its truthfulness. Teddy expresses confidence that Seth will find success and return to share his experiences. Seth, carrying his dog Snip, prepares to leave the ferry-boat as it docks. Tim advises Seth to keep moving to avoid being caught by law enforcement. Seth feels anxious and looks over his shoulder while fleeing the city. Snip remains calm in Seth's arms despite the heat and lack of water. Seth stops at a shop after an hour of running, feeling hungry and tired.

Sam will need all the money available to spend. Fred had to attend to his duties at the store after returning from Blacktown. The news of the alleged robbery spread quickly, leading many miners to believe Sam was guilty. The cashier questioned Fred about the prisoner's intentions regarding land, but Fred refused to share information. Fred's mother reassured him that the accusation against him was false. Bill claimed to have discovered the owner of the land and expressed frustration over being called a thief. Bill decided to leave his job at the mine to investigate the robbery further.

Dick is traveling to Antelope Spring to find a doctor for his father, who shot himself in the leg. Dick left his camp at Buffalo Meadows without informing anyone. The distance from Buffalo Meadows to Antelope Spring is approximately forty-five miles. Dick's party consists of his father, mother, and sister Margie. Dick is willing to sell his rifle to pay for medical supplies for his father. Parsons and another man express concern about Dick's journey and the condition of his father. Dick is perplexed by the private conversation between Parsons and his companion.

Horace Sampson and his son Paul came from Maryland to locate a homestead. They traveled for three weeks searching for a suitable location before encountering danger. Sampson and Paul were captured by savages and bound near a cabin. Simon Kenton advised them to go to Corn Island for safety and support. Mr. Sampson expressed reluctance to accept help from strangers. Paul showed interest in the wilderness and sought to ask questions about living there.

A town meeting is scheduled at Faneuil Hall at eleven o'clock. Master Samuel Adams is expected to address the people at the town meeting. Chris Gore and another boy remain at Chris Gore's home until noon. A formal town meeting is appointed for three o'clock in the afternoon. Faneuil Hall was too small for the assembled citizens, necessitating a move to the Old South Meeting-house. Master Samuel Adams argued that it is illegal to quarter troops in the city during peacetime. Lieutenant-Governor Hutchinson stated that one regiment must remain in the city.

The old soldier received permission to camp with his recruit as long as they remained in ranks during the command's advance. The captain warned the corporal that separating from the main group could be unsafe due to the presence of Tories and Indians. Corporal 'Lige expressed confidence in his ability to care for himself and his recruit. The rations provided to the volunteers were not generous, and those who delayed in applying for them often went without food. Corporal 'Lige quickly drew rations for himself and Isaac before the main body of troops had fully halted. The corporal selected a camping place at the edge of a small brook, about fifty yards from the main road. Isaac expressed concern about their safety at the campsite, to which the corporal reassured him.

Ned and Joe left a room with heavy baggage. They were stopped by a ticket collector at the gangway. Joe presented two tickets for first cabin passages. Ned and Joe needed to walk quickly to avoid being caught by men. They decided to find an express office to send their baggage. Joe had a dollar and planned to buy food after sending the baggage. They met a knowledgeable boy shortly after leaving the express office.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: A District Messenger Boy and a Necktie Party

text: Walter identified one of the combatants as Sewatis and the other as Jim Albert. Sewatis overpowered Jim Albert and restrained him using a blanket. Walter discovered a warrant for his arrest in Jim Albert's possession. Stephen confirmed the authenticity of the warrant after examining it. Sewatis took Jim Albert and the warrant back to his tribe. Walter realized he was not secure from Sam Haines even in the woods. Walter found a trail leading eastward across the river after waking up.

George and Ralph were riding when they noticed black clouds forming in the sky. They sought shelter under a shed as a heavy rainstorm began. The storm included vivid lightning and loud thunder. George and Ralph were unaware of the potential dangers posed by lightning to nearby oil tanks. A lightning strike hit a large derrick, causing it to break apart and scatter debris. Ralph expressed fear at the power of the lightning strike. George was captivated by the storm and focused on the largest oil tank in the valley.

The uncle mentioned a gun that was previously kept in the garden. The uncle's sister had a child named Horatio, who was killed at Waterloo before birth. The uncle claimed that the house they were in was haunted. The ghost was said to be that of a man who killed a Christmas wait with a lump of coal. The uncle recounted that the man had also killed a solo cornet-player. The cornet-player was known for playing only two tunes, 'Annie Laurie' and 'Home, Sweet Home'. The cornet-player was last seen entering the uncle's house but was never seen leaving.

The text discusses the behavior of people towards their dogs, highlighting excessive adulation. Young women are described as engaging in affectionate behavior towards dogs when young men are present. Elderly spinsters are mentioned as caring for a dog they refer to as a German sausage on legs. The text notes that families often center their lives around their dogs, discussing their actions extensively. Cats are portrayed as less affected by adulation compared to dogs, which seem to encourage it. The narrative describes how gaining a dog's approval is essential for social interactions with its owners. The text reflects on the transformation of dogs due to their treatment, contrasting their innocent beginnings with their current state.

source.author: Jerome Klapka Jerome
source.title: Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow

text: The text is titled 'Passing of the Third Floor Back' and was written by Jerome K. Jerome. The book was published by Dodd, Mead & Company in New York in 1909. The setting is Bloomsbury Square on a November afternoon. A stranger is observed walking in the neighborhood, attracting the attention of a young lady and a constable. The stranger asks the constable for directions to Mrs. Pennycherry's boarding house at Number Forty-eight. Mrs. Pennycherry prepares to meet the stranger after he rings the bell at her boarding house. Mary Jane, a servant, expresses that the stranger is not the usual type of boarder.

source.author: Jerome Klapka Jerome
source.title: Passing of the Third Floor Back

text: Mrs. Pennycoop believes that kindness costs nothing. Mr. Pennycoop has twenty years of experience as an auctioneer. The couple discusses their vicar, Mr. Cracklethorpe, who has made his congregation dislike the church. Mrs. Pennycoop expresses sympathy for Mr. Cracklethorpe despite his disagreeable nature. Mr. Pennycoop feels that personal insults can be tolerated, but actions are more concerning. Mrs. Pennycoop suggests that Mr. Cracklethorpe's unpleasant demeanor may be due to health issues. The couple plans to visit Mr. Cracklethorpe before he leaves.

The text discusses the concept of forgetfulness in relation to success and virtue. The author suggests that virtue is not necessarily linked to success. Life is described as a gamble, with rules for success compared to systems used in gambling. The author emphasizes the importance of self-control and courage in facing life's challenges. The text critiques the idea of planning for a world of reasonable creatures, stating it is unrealistic. The author argues that if everyone were reasonable, many societal issues would not exist. The text concludes with a reflection on personal choices and their consequences.

source.author: Jerome Klapka Jerome
source.title: The Second Thoughts of An Idle Fellow

text: Aunt Maria does not allow the children to hear inappropriate language. Uncle Podger attempts to hammer a nail into the wall but injures himself in the process. Aunt Maria expresses a desire to leave the house during Uncle Podger's home repairs. Uncle Podger takes pride in his work despite the mess he creates. Harris is expected to be similar to Uncle Podger when he grows up. George suggests focusing on essential items for their trip rather than unnecessary ones. The text discusses the burdens of material possessions and societal expectations.

The manager suggested publishing the author's work as a serious educational book for schools. The author agreed to the manager's proposal after altering the title and adding a vocabulary. The book, titled 'Ahn', became widely used in English philological education. The British educational method includes a native French gentleman, often a Belgian, as a language instructor. The native French gentleman is typically ineffective at teaching and is viewed as a source of amusement. The text contrasts the British method of teaching French with the German method, which involves daily lessons without comic instructors. The German method aims to provide students with a practical understanding of the language, enabling them to discuss various topics.

Mr. Korner traveled from the city to Ravenscourt Park. Mr. Korner was determined to clarify his future with Mrs. Korner. Mrs. Korner expressed surprise and concern when Mr. Korner demanded his supper. Mrs. Korner did not have any kidneys available for Mr. Korner's meal. Mrs. Korner's friend suggested poaching eggs as an alternative for Mr. Korner. Mr. Korner expressed dissatisfaction with the meal options presented to him. Mrs. Korner and her friend worked to prepare a meal for Mr. Korner despite the challenges.

Ulrich is a character who expresses a desire to marry the whole village. Germany was united in a common cause against French forces during the war. Ulrich's profession is a wheelwright, and he is called to a distant town. Ulrich discovers five human figures in a wood, two of whom are German Landwehr and three are French soldiers. Four of the men are dead, and one Frenchman is alive but severely wounded. Ulrich tends to the wounded Frenchman for nearly a week before helping him escape. Ulrich decides not to return to his village, feeling ashamed of his change in perspective on the war.

A dog named Tiny choked on money he swallowed. Hollis attempted to help Tiny using a long pair of pincers. Tiny resisted the attempts to help him, believing he was being robbed. Despite efforts to save him, Tiny died. The narrator describes a dream about discovering a hidden room filled with gold. In the dream, the narrator kills a friend who is kneeling before an open chest of gold. The narrator frequently dreams about being urged to act in a play at the Lyceum.

Munich experiences a significant exchange of people every Sunday, with villagers and mountaineers arriving in the morning. The author prefers visiting low-ceilinged beer-halls over crowded cafes to observe the life of the common people. The author believes that common people exhibit more individuality and character compared to the upper social classes. The author enjoys watching the interactions and activities of patrons in the beer-halls, including games and conversations. The author describes various characters in the beer-halls, including an eager card player and a cross-looking old woman. The atmosphere in the beer-halls is lively, with laughter, singing, and camaraderie among the patrons. The author finds value in observing the daily lives of common people rather than adhering to the norms of upper-class society.

The young man expresses sorrow to his father, who responds sharply. Grindley junior embraces his father, indicating emotional support. Old Grindley visits Solomon at the big house in Nevill's Court. Solomon calls for Janet Helvetia after a meeting with old Grindley. Grindley junior studies the printing business and eventually becomes the printer and publisher of _Good Humour_. Miss Ramsbotham is described as plain but pleasant looking, with qualities that make her an ideal wife but not a romantic partner. Miss Ramsbotham has a keen sense of humor and a practical approach to life, including a slight American accent acquired during her travels.

The narrator observed a pair referred to as 'Kipper' and 'Carrots' who considered themselves sweethearts. Kipper was approximately fifteen years old and Carrots was about twelve years old. Carrots had run away from an old woman in Limehouse who used to beat her. Kipper got Carrots a lodging with an old woman who had an attic in the same house where he slept. The narrator left the coffee shop for a place in the city and did not see Kipper and Carrots for five years. The narrator later encountered Kipper and Carrots at a restaurant in Oxford Street. The restaurant was described as a dismal place with a lot of love-making among the patrons.

Camelford replaced his glass on the table and did not look at his wife. Mrs. Camelford expressed her lack of desire to drink and sought her husband's gaze. Camelford urged Mrs. Camelford to drink, stating it was only a dream. Armitage recounted a narrative in the Club smoking-room about a painful sensation he experienced. He described a gradual return of light and sound, eventually finding himself seated beside a young girl. The girl introduced herself as Alice Blatchley, and they exchanged names on each other's programmes. Armitage recalled a past connection with Alice Blatchley, involving love and subsequent distance between them.

The music-hall stage often features family acts, typically consisting of parents and multiple siblings. Performers on the music-hall stage may have strong family ties, as seen in acts with multiple sisters performing together. A male performer described his wife's violent behavior during a comedic routine, indicating a troubled domestic life. The humor in performances often revolves around the misfortunes and troubles of others. A female performer shared a story about her lover's betrayal, which elicited laughter from the audience. A male performer humorously presented a scenario where his wife left him for the lodger, which was well-received by the audience. The text reflects on the nature of humor, suggesting it often stems from the troubles experienced by others.

source.author: Jerome Klapka Jerome
source.title: The Angel and the Author - and Others

text: The character experiences a prophetic curse that affects those around her. She becomes a famous 'artiste' known for delineating coster character. The character does not identify as Signora Ballatino and does not play the zithern. The narrator expresses a preference for melancholy aspects of life and nature. The narrator recalls childhood memories of a dreary marshland by the sea. The sea is described as being prone to anger, often tossing large stones during storms. The narrator has a fear of a mysterious underwater feature known as the Bar.

Malvina's activities during the midsummer weeks may never be fully revealed. The Doctor believes that the events have been grossly exaggerated. Dawson, R.A. is described as a lovable man with a habit of punning. Dawson smashed a Dutch interior over the head of Mrs. Dawson. Mrs. Arlington attempted to reform herself but felt she had failed. Mrs. Arlington felt an intuitive desire to take a walk to the Cross Stones. A diminutive figure appeared to Mrs. Arlington at the Cross Stones and assisted her.

Jim was devoted to her but could not meet her romantic expectations. Jim attempted to engage in romantic gestures but was naturally clumsy. The Old Maid commented on young girls being attracted to superficial qualities. A young married woman experienced a loss of affection from her husband after marriage. The Girton Girl suggested that silence about relationship issues can lead to misunderstandings. The Woman of the World intervened in a couple's communication issues by encouraging open dialogue. A friend of the young married woman explained to her husband how his behavior was affecting their relationship.

The narrator describes an extraordinary dream involving a theater and a cloak-room attendant. In the dream, the attendant insists that the narrator leave his legs behind in the lobby. The narrator expresses annoyance at the absurdity of the request but prepares to comply. The attendant demonstrates that the narrator's legs can be unscrewed and removed easily. The narrator recalls another dream about being hanged, where his relatives are not surprised by the situation. The narrator reflects on how Knowledge and Experience influence surprise in waking life but do not exist in dreams. In dreams, the narrator suggests that anything is possible and there is no astonishment.

Lady Mogton believes the candidate for the upcoming election should be Annys. Annys expresses a desire to consult Geoffrey before making a decision. Lady Mogton insists that the choice of candidate is a matter of duty, not preference. Geoffrey enters the room and reveals he has been appointed to the Under-Secretaryship for Home Affairs. Phoebe expresses delight at Geoffrey's news and congratulates him. Geoffrey mentions that his appointment may necessitate a bye-election. Lady Mogton and St. Herbert consider the implications of Geoffrey's appointment.

Rushing River is a chief who holds unconventional views about women, believing they should not be mere servants to men. Moonlight is a captive who shows emotional distress upon seeing Rushing River's injured form. Rushing River has a mother named Umqua, who is described as rudely intellectual and self-assertive. Rushing River has been more stunned than injured, with a serious injury to his little finger. Umqua expresses concern about Rushing River's emotional state after his injury, suggesting he may be stunned. Rushing River acknowledges his feelings for Moonlight, indicating he has found a mate in her. Umqua advises Rushing River to take Moonlight to his tent, recognizing her intelligence and worth.

The Kafirs engaged in battle by throwing assagais and stones from cliffs. The white men were mostly expert shots and suffered few casualties. Many Kafirs were killed during the conflict before retreating. Hintza agreed to proposals from the Governor, including the return of 50,000 cattle and 1,000 horses. Hintza's agreement was insincere, as he intended to fulfill none of his commitments. After the Governor's departure, Hintza's people massacred about thirty Fingoes. The Governor ordered Hintza and his followers to be held as hostages for the safety of the Fingoes.

Jackman teaches an old man how to use a repeater rifle. The repeater rifle can fire sixteen shots without reloading. The old man expresses concern about how to keep track of the shots fired. Jackman advises the old man to continue firing until the rifle refuses to fire. MacRummle prefers fishing to hunting but is motivated by the enthusiasm of others. Barret and Junkie find a spot to observe the hunting pass without being seen. Barret mentions to Junkie that their cousin Milly fell in the same spot while trying to get flowers.

Hilda expresses mixed emotions about the impending war, feeling both exultation and sorrow. Ada dismisses Hilda's concerns about the future and encourages her to focus on the present. A hermit informs the girls that King Harald is approaching with his fleet and urges them to seek safety. Ada's foster-father sent the hermit to fetch them to a place of safety. Alric warns the girls that they are in danger and urges them to leave quickly. Erling offers to lead Hilda away from the mound to avoid detection by the King's people. Glumm asks Ada to decide if he will be her protector before he goes into battle.

Mrs Butterfly asked Mr Bull-frog to sing more quietly during a gathering. Mr Bull-frog became overly excited and continued to sing loudly despite being asked to be quieter. A Snail attempted to dance a minuet but was laughed at and retreated. Some Gnats, Midges, and other flies left the ground to dance in the air. Spiders descended from the oak tree to join the dancers, causing more chaos. The Glow-worm provided light as evening fell, prompting the dancers to continue their activities. The Black Beetle suggested sending for the Glow-worm's friends to increase the light.

Bertram's sketch-book was examined by the trappers for nearly an hour. Few educated men had penetrated far into the western wilderness during that time. Old Redhand recognized many landscapes in Bertram's sketches and could trace his route to the Saskatchewan river. Redhand described adventures related to the scenes in the sketch-book. Redhand identified an Indian named Big Snake as a thief who had stolen horses. Bounce was stringing the claws of a grisly bear to make a necklace. Gibault expressed that he was in love, which prompted a discussion among the others.

source.author: R M Ballantyne
source.title: The Wild Man of the West

text: Ned Sinton and old Mr. Shirley worked diligently on their farm and built good relationships with their neighbors. Ned Sinton fell in love with Louisa Leslie, who eventually became Mrs. Sinton. Tom Collins, a successful merchant, requested Ned to purchase a farm near his own after making a fortune. Ned bought a farm three miles from his own for Tom Collins. Larry O'Neil returned to San Francisco after struggling with farming in California and became Tom Collins' butler. Nelly Morgan became a desirable partner and married a hardworking man in the district.

The characters express a desire for mitts, comforters, and helmets but reject the associated religion. David Duffy suggests that they should appreciate the gifts they receive. Fink argues that the kindness shown through gifts is a result of the love of God. The mate mentions that they have received a large case of books. The box contains old periodicals and volumes of various titles. Joe Stubley expresses skepticism about the value of books and learning. Pat Stiver dismisses the need for books, stating that some people only want food and drink.

Peterkin dropped a whole oyster into deep water while fishing. Peterkin attempted to catch a fish that took the bait but released it before being hauled up. Jack suggested that Peterkin try to haul the fish up by the mouth gently. Peterkin successfully caught a fish after it swallowed the bait completely. The three individuals fell into the water while trying to secure the caught fish. Jack warned Peterkin about a shark approaching them in the water. The group paddled frantically to reach the shore while trying to fend off the shark.

The wedding feast was attended by the bride, known for her thriftiness and modesty, and the coxswain, who has saved many lives.
