Old Mrs Massey, the bridegroom's bed-ridden mother, was present at the wedding feast and appeared to enjoy herself despite her condition. The coxswain, Robert Massey, was encouraged to dance in his rescue clothing instead of wedding garments. A gold watch and a purse of fifty sovereigns were presented to Massey by the grateful grandfather of a girl he saved. The wedding feast was conducted on teetotal principles, promoting total abstinence. The sudden death of Old Mrs Massey occurred shortly after the wedding, significantly affecting Robert Massey. Robert Massey expressed a desire to leave the village due to memories of his mother, but hesitated because of his wife, Nell.

The narrator expresses a desire for revenge and reflects on his feelings when meeting certain white men. The narrator has been a wanderer, seeking to be useful to himself or others. Will Big Ben agrees to have the narrator accompany him on a journey across the mountains. Big Ben is ready to start immediately if they can divert their route to a fur-traders' outpost. The group approaches Rocky Mountain Fort, located near the eastern spurs of the Rocky Mountains. Larry O'Hale spots a black bear and decides to pursue it on horseback. Larry misses his shot at the bear, causing it to flee in response to his charge.

Tom displayed a relaxed demeanor while walking through the forest. He carried a heavy double-barrelled gun and wiped his brow with a handkerchief. Tom had not yet succeeded in shooting a lion despite hearing their voices and seeing them at night. He cautiously approached what he believed to be a lion, only to discover it was a yellow stone. After this realization, Tom resumed his walk without further incident. He observed a wide stretch of the river that appeared calm and mirrored the surrounding scenery. The area was populated with various living creatures, including alligators, cranes, herons, and waterfowl.

A significant number of islands in the South Seas have been influenced by Christianity, while others remain in a state of degradation. Some inhabitants of the South Seas continue to practice cannibalism, consuming both enemies and their own slaves. Natives prepare for war with human sacrifices to the god of war and perform various bloody and superstitious rites. Warriors use weapons such as slings, pikes made from sting-ray bones, and clubs made of hard wood. Battles often begin with celebrated warriors challenging each other before engaging in combat. The fighting involves four ranks: the bravest men with spears, men with clubs, young men with slings, and women carrying stones and weapons. Orators of battle encourage troops with passionate speeches and are actively involved in the fight.

The hermit wore a loose short hunting-coat of brown cotton. The hermit prepared a meal that included cold meat, a hot steak of venison, coffee, cream, cakes made from coarse flour, fruits, and honey. The hermit identified the meat resembling chicken as armadillo, which is difficult to catch. The hermit explained that the cream comes from a cow that grows in the ground. The hermit sourced coffee from local trees and made cakes from the mandioca-root, which he grows. The hermit mentioned that many Negroes are slaves and some Indians are also enslaved in the area. The hermit indicated that various fruits and roots grow in the forest, including plantains, bananas, yams, cocoa-nuts, oranges, and plums.

The Bell Rock rises only a few feet out of the sea at low tide. The foundation of the lighthouse was three feet three inches above low water of the lowest spring-tides. The landing of the stones for the lighthouse was a delicate and difficult process due to their weight and brittle nature. Various methods for landing the stones were proposed, including floating them with buoys and using a cofferdam. Mr. Stevenson decided to use praam boats to transport the stones to the rock. The stones were cut in the workyard at Arbroath and transported to the rock using sloops and praam boats. The landing-master was responsible for transferring the stones from the boats to the rock using ropes and blocks.

Mountain pastures are called saeters. Milk is carried down from the saeter by girls for daily use. The milk is put into round flat tubs and allowed to sour and thicken. The hut is built of rough logs and contains basic furniture. The old man in the hut wears a complete suit of brown homespun and a red nightcap. Fred Temple caught three yellow trout while fishing. The friends planned to consider their sleeping arrangements after eating.

The vessel received severe shocks from passing floes and was near a large berg. A mass of ice, referred to as a 'calf,' struck the hull of the brig, nearly damaging it. The brig was blown into loose ice after the wind shifted, causing the cables to snap. The brig was at risk of destruction due to the grinding masses of ice around it. The brig was freed when the mass of ice holding it struck a submerged tongue of the berg and split in two. Captain Harvey ordered the crew to prepare an anchor as they passed close to the berg. The brig was eventually secured under the shelter of the berg until the storm subsided.

Gaff is leading his son, Billy, to write a letter. Tottie is preparing to assist in writing the letter. The Bu'ster is curious about the letter and chooses to hold the blotting paper. Gaff and his wife discuss how to address the letter. Tottie discovers that the ink is red. Billy is punished by his mother for cheering about the ink.

The party halted at a fork in the road while the guide, Glendinning, considered the two divergent paths. Glendinning was unacquainted with the region beyond the river Cluden. The officer in command decided to divide the party to explore both paths. Glendinning chose Will Wallace as his companion for the right path. Will Wallace expressed dissatisfaction with his role in the military actions he had witnessed. Wallace described witnessing acts of torture and robbery committed by troops in the King's name. Glendinning was unaware of Wallace's character and experiences prior to their current mission.

A mother and two children were observed in a room, with the boy naked and the girl slightly better dressed. The mother and the room were described as tattered, draggled, and dirty. The children lived in a court where the Frogs reside. Bobby, a boy referred to as a brat, declined a job offer from Sir Richard. Bobby was described as smart but impudent, and he spoke boldly to Sir Richard. Sir Richard offered Bobby a position as under-gardener out of charity. Bobby expressed that he did not want to receive charity and questioned the offer.

Contributions from remote and obscure places often contain fresh and original ideas. Artistic and literary atmospheres do not necessarily create artists or writers. Editors tend to seek contributions from rural areas, as they often promise novelty. Young contributors should be receptive to editorial suggestions, as they can lead to learning. Revising and rewriting work can significantly improve its quality. Editors appreciate contributors who demonstrate trustworthiness and creativity. Writing solely for the editor is not advisable, as effective writing should engage a broader audience.

source.author: William Dean Howells
source.title: The Editor's Relations With The Young Contributor

text: Bromfield Corey was introduced to Mrs. Brinkley. Alice was engaged in two or three dances and appeared serious and pale. Alice left the event early due to a headache. Mavering felt he had ruined his chances with the women at the event. Mavering received a note that he anticipated contained significant information. Boardman suggested Mavering visit Mrs. Pasmer. Mavering expressed that he could not give up on Alice.

The subject attempted to write a story in both verse and prose. He wrote the first chapter of a novel but did not finish it. He believed that if he had completed the novel, it would have been a failure. His writing style was lyrical and meditative, with a tendency towards allegory. He was sensitive to criticism, especially from those he respected. He often reverted to his original lines after revising his poetry. He once submitted a poem to a magazine that had a similar motive to another recently published work.

Ludlow took Wetmore to see Cornelia's sketches. Wetmore believes Cornelia might get one of her sketches into the Academy exhibition in the spring. Cornelia felt listless and lacked enthusiasm after Ludlow's visit. Cornelia returned to her work at the Synthesis but did so aimlessly. Ludlow's criticism had previously served as inspiration for Cornelia. Mrs. Maybough struggled to justify Ludlow's behavior to her friends. Mrs. Westley invited Cornelia to pour tea at her January Thursdays.

Verrian reported to his mother that the story was gaining popularity among high-quality readers. The editor Armiger indicated that there had been an increase in sales attributed to Verrian's story. The publishing house expressed interest in publishing a book based on Verrian's story. Mrs. Verrian expressed pride in her son's adherence to his artistic standards. Verrian mentioned that newspapers focused on the love interest and incidents in the story rather than its artistic merit. Armiger inquired if Verrian had heard from a girl involved in a previous correspondence, to which Verrian replied he had not. Mrs. Verrian hoped that the letters Verrian had received were not of a troubling nature.

Willis makes jokes about absent-mindedness and boasts about California desperadoes. Mrs. Roberts expresses curiosity about what Willis would have done if a garotter had taken his watch. Roberts claims he saw one garotter and describes knocking him down. Mrs. Roberts believes there were more than one garotter present. Willis comments on Roberts' actions during the incident and suggests he showed presence of mind. Mrs. Roberts expresses excitement and concern about the doorbell ringing, fearing it is the garotters. Mr. Bemis enters the scene, stating he has just been robbed of his watch.

The text is titled 'Bride Roses' and is authored by W. D. Howells. The scene takes place in a florist's shop. A lady enters the shop and greets the florist, Mr. Eichenlaub. The lady expresses concern about the flowers freezing due to the cold weather. The florist mentions using a refrigerator to protect the roses from sunstroke. The lady requests flowers for an event on the upcoming Saturday and wants to discuss the order. The florist explains that he often manages flower quantities well and can sell leftover flowers at funerals.

The characters are in Sillery for the summer due to the husband's business. Kitty is experiencing her first housekeeping and finds it strange. Kitty mistakenly believes that her interactions with Mr. Arbuton may be perceived as romantic. The hostess mentions that they are the only American couple visiting Sillery that summer. Kitty feels a mix of dread and enjoyment when left alone with Mr. Arbuton. Kitty engages in conversation about the scenery and village as they travel. The village has a mix of French and Irish communities.

The representatives of the French people are expected to offer reparation to the memory of Émile Zola. The government did not participate in Zola's funeral, which was seen as a missed opportunity. A monument to Zola is anticipated to be constructed to honor his contributions. Criticism of Zola's work focuses on its nature and quality rather than determining his literary status. M. Chaumie stated that Zola's work was driven by a desire for sincerity and truth, influenced by feelings of pity and justice. Zola's methods in writing were more artistic than scientific, as he created fiction from his observations. Zola's characters are perceived as having intense reality and individuality, distinct from typical fictional characters.

Kitty Morrow is characterized as both tiresome and vivacious. Kitty Morrow has a cold-hearted nature but is not cold-blooded. Knellwood is a celibate young ritualist whom Kitty Morrow loves. Mary Fairthorne is described as a good girl with higher beauty than Kitty Morrow. Yuki is a half-caste heroine in 'A Japanese Nightingale' who marries Bigelow. Yuki marries Bigelow to help her brother through college in America. The story of Yuki and Bigelow is described as having a charm and freshness unique to its art.

source.author: William Dean Howells
source.title: A Psychological Counter-current in Recent Fiction

text: Miss Ramsey asks Nora to bring a bottle and some glasses and to invite Mr. Ashley. Mr. Ashley enters and expresses that he could have waited all day to see Miss Ramsey. Miss Ramsey offers Mr. Ashley a cigarette and a cocktail, but he declines both. Miss Ramsey comments on the smoking habits of Englishwomen and American ladies. Miss Ramsey attempts to pour a cocktail but realizes the bottle is not opened. Miss Ramsey feels faint and requests Mr. Ashley to open the window. Mr. Ashley offers Miss Ramsey tea, which she accepts with specific instructions.

Willis declares he is going to strike. Mrs. Roberts expresses concern that Edward may have the grippe. Mrs. Campbell suggests that drowsiness may be due to having spent the night on a sleeping-car. Mrs. Roberts decides to make Edward a cup of tea. Mrs. Campbell advises against starting a fire while wearing gloves. Mrs. Roberts suggests whiskey-and-water as a remedy for Edward. Mrs. Roberts is unable to remember something important before leaving.

Mrs. Roberts expresses gratitude to Willis for his help. Lawton questions how sending for Aunt Mary helps the rest of the group. Curwen holds up a glove and confirms it is the right one. Mrs. Roberts urges Mrs. Miller to see her baby. Lawton hears a cry and believes it may be a cry for help. Roberts goes to check the source of the noise and returns with a mysterious whisper. The elevator contains Mrs. Roberts's Aunt Mary, Mrs. Curwen, Miss Lawton, Mr. Miller, and Mr. Alfred Bemis.

The narrator did not give up their place at Venice but decided not to return if they could find work at home. The narrator traveled to Ohio to seek employment and considered returning to their trade as a printer if necessary. The narrator believed they would have an advantage with readers from the West, although they doubted this would apply in their own region without an Eastern imprint. After three weeks in Ohio without finding work, the narrator returned to the East, specifically New York, to pursue opportunities. The narrator sought a salaried position on a paper and began writing editorials for various publications, primarily for the Times. The narrator was never offered a permanent position despite receiving praise from the editor-in-chief of the Times. The narrator was offered a basis at a new literary paper but was later informed that the engagement would not proceed.

The children fell on a bed of India-rubber about twenty feet deep. Forty or fifty thousand boys and girls had been banished for making a mess. The young Khan and Khant of Tartary entered the kingdom with a magnificent retinue. The choice of the Khan and Khant for a bride and groom fell upon the Prince Butterflyflutterby and Princess Flutterbybutterfly. The Khan and Khant were brother and sister. The Khan and Khant made a mess while traveling through the kingdom and camped out in the back yard of the palace. The General-in-Chief kept his men under arms night and day due to the excitement caused by the Khan and Khant.

source.author: William Dean Howells
source.title: Christmas Every Day and Other Stories

text: Ethel Reed is distressed and hiding her face in her hands. Miss Spaulding expresses concern for Ethel Reed's well-being. Grinnidge comments on the situation occurring on the other side of the wall. Miss Reed insists on keeping the register open despite the heat. Ransom reveals he wrote a rude note to a woman and ended their acquaintance. Miss Reed finds Ransom's comments humorous and expresses approval. Ransom acknowledges he should have been more honest about his feelings.

Gaites inquired about the freight train's departure time. The station-master informed Gaites that the freight would leave in about ten minutes. The freight conductor allowed Gaites to travel to Lower Merritt. Gaites entered the caboose, which had a table, chairs, and leather-covered benches. The conductor shared information about the Desmond family and their property near Lower Merritt. Gaites noticed changes at the hotel in Lower Merritt, which was now called an Inn. The Inn featured new electric lighting and an aesthetically designed parlor.

Mrs. Somers and Mr. Campbell are alone together in a drawing-room. Mrs. Somers offers tea to guests, including Mrs. Canfield, Miss Bayly, and Mrs. Wharton. Mrs. Wharton declines tea, stating her only objection to afternoon tea is the tea itself. Mrs. Somers mentions her Bramford portrait, prompting Miss Bayly and the other ladies to express interest in seeing it. Mr. Campbell expresses a desire to leave, but Mrs. Somers does not explicitly wish him to go. Mrs. Curwen arrives and indicates she is leaving, complimenting Mrs. Somers' portrait. Mrs. Curwen offers Mr. Campbell a ride in her coupé, which he accepts.

Fulkerson invited March to dinner at Maroni's to discuss a financial plan. March expressed discomfort with the idea of Dryfoos being involved in the plan. Fulkerson clarified that he did not persuade Dryfoos for his own benefit. Dryfoos wanted his son to have a productive occupation rather than being idle. Dryfoos's son had aspirations to study for the ministry, which his father opposed. Fulkerson suggested visiting Dryfoos before he left for the West. March decided to wait for his wife before visiting the Dryfoos family.

The likelihood of being let in is higher for a lady than for a gentleman. The speaker plans to take a coupe and instruct the driver to go quickly. The speaker wants to prevent Willis from buying tickets for himself and Amy. The cook has been hired for six dollars a week and will not do any laundry. The cook is described as respectable, neat, and lady-like, and is Irish and Catholic. The cook is expected to arrive at half-past three. The train departs at ten minutes to four.

Christ's Cross is as broad as the whole world, as He died for the whole world. The length of Christ's Cross lasts through all time, as long as there are sinners to be saved. The height of Christ's Cross is as high as the highest heaven and the throne of God. The depth of Christ's Cross reaches deep enough to save the deepest sinner. Christ descended into hell and preached to the spirits in prison. Without Good Friday, there can be no Easter Day, as self-sacrifice is necessary for blessedness. The belief in the Resurrection includes the idea that humans will have new bodies on a new earth.

Reginald attempted to obtain the hermit's story from Godric, who initially resisted sharing his life details. Godric described his past life as one of vice, including being a cheat, usurer, and hypocrite. Reginald visited Godric several times and eventually persuaded him to share his life and miracles. Godric blessed the book Reginald wrote about him but warned him to conceal it until after his death. Godric was born in Walpole, Norfolk, to parents AEilward and AEdwen, who were described as poor and pious. Godric preferred wandering as a pedlar rather than working in the fields, eventually selling goods in villages and towns. Reginald noted a miraculous event in Godric's life involving three stranded porpoises.

Hearts were hardened due to spite and stubbornness. Individuals took delight in doing wrong despite knowing it was wrong. They would respond to questions about their actions with various forms of denial or insolence. Pharaoh hardened his heart and rejected the Lord's message, driving Moses and Aaron away. People may become angry with preachers for delivering unpleasant truths. The speaker emphasizes that the messages are from God, not personal opinions. God will chastise individuals for their sins as a form of love and guidance.

The text lists various forms of the name Theodoric, including Teodrich, Tiadric, and Tiedrich. It distinguishes between Low-German and High-German forms of names, noting that forms with Th-d are Low-German and those with D-t are High-German. The text states that High-German emerged later than Low-German, with its literary presence not established until the eighth century. The name Dietrich is used in both Low-German and High-German forms in the oldest German poem, the song of Hildebrand and Hadebrand. Johannes von Muller referred to Theodoric of Verona as Dietrich von Bern to connect with the popular name known from legends. Theodoric had a gold plate made with the first four letters of his name incised, which were [Greek text]. The text discusses the historical practice of spelling proper names based on their appearance in historical documents rather than their original forms.

The text discusses the relationship between the working class and the middle class in England and Scotland. It argues that both classes share the same spirit and ancestry, leading to a more homogeneous society. The author suggests that the English nation is well-suited for equal political rights due to its lack of a caste system. The text highlights the importance of education for all citizens, regardless of their social class. It claims that social drawbacks hinder the development of the working classes' manhood. The author expresses concern about manhood suffrage potentially allowing individuals who are not fully mature in mind to vote. The text advocates for reasonable household suffrage based on the ability to afford a certain standard of living.

Felix was a governor known for violence, misrule, extortion, and cruelty in Judaea. Felix caused the murder of the high-priest in Jerusalem out of spite. Felix took Drusilla, his wife, from her lawful husband, a Syrian king. St. Paul appeared before Felix to plead for his life and was recognized as innocent by Felix. Felix showed interest in the faith in Christ and sought to understand it. St. Paul likely spoke to Felix about righteousness and temperance. Felix, raised as a slave in Rome, may not have been familiar with concepts of righteousness and temperance.

Mr. Jasper Mayne expressed an opinion about Ben Jonson's style in relation to Shakespeare. The text discusses the works of Cartwright, particularly his poems and plays. Cartwright's writing is characterized by thought, fancy, force, and varied learning. The play 'The Ordinary' is noted for its similarities to the works of Rabelais and Aristophanes. Cartwright's play 'Love's Convert' presents noble and pure sentiment. The 'Royal Slave' is regarded as Cartwright's masterpiece by both the Court and his contemporaries. Cartwright's humor is described as being of high quality, though he can also be crude when necessary.

Jonathan had cause to hate and envy David but chose to support him instead. Jonathan learned that Samuel had anointed David to be king, putting his own future at risk. Jonathan opposed his father Saul's plans against David while remaining respectful. Jonathan believed in the Lord's choice of David as king and accepted it despite personal loss. Jonathan helped David escape from Saul by agreeing on a secret sign involving arrows. Saul became angry with Jonathan for supporting David and attempted to harm him. Jonathan and David parted ways after a heartfelt farewell, promising loyalty to each other.

The Grotto del Cane is located near Naples and is known for keeping a dog that is exposed to carbonic acid gas for visitor amusement. Breathing out produces impure air that contains an excess of carbonic acid, which does not support life. A simple experiment with lime-water can demonstrate the presence of carbonic acid in exhaled breath. Oxygen is necessary for combustion processes in living beings, fires, and candles, while carbonic acid is a byproduct that can extinguish flames. An average fire requires as much oxygen as several human beings, and candles and gas-burners also consume significant amounts of oxygen. Carbonic acid accumulates in poorly ventilated spaces, posing a risk of poisoning to occupants. Death can occur from lack of ventilation when a person is exposed to burning charcoal in a sealed room.

source.author: Charles Kingsley
source.title: Sanitary and Social Lectures and Essays

text: The narrative describes a character who struggled with sin and found redemption through the influence of a saintly figure. The character sought the saint's tomb and experienced a transformation that led him to become a chivalrous knight dedicated to helping widows and orphans. Conrad, another character, expresses satisfaction at having trained a saint but also feels a sense of sadness and doubt about the means used to achieve this. The story highlights the saint's charitable acts, including teaching, caring for the sick, and feeding a dying slave. The community reacts emotionally to the saint's story, with expressions of grief and admiration, leading to a proclamation of her sainthood. Conrad reflects on the complexities of creating a saint and the moral implications of his actions in the process.

Plotinus was a significant figure in Neoplatonism, known for his moral character and practical life. He died around 200 A.D. and refused animal food, abstained from baths, and declined medicine during his last illness. Plotinus revered Plato and attempted to develop his ideas, although his dialectic was superior to that of his followers. Iamblichus became the head of a Neoplatonist school that emphasized theurgy and magic, overshadowing Porphyry's more rational approach. Porphyry expressed a dislike for magic and superstitions, which he associated with Christianity as a religion for the common people. Plotinus reportedly summoned a familiar spirit in the temple of Isis, which he described as a god rather than a daemon. The writings attributed to Abamnon, Anebos, and Iamblichus reflect a blend of old superstitions with new philosophical ideas.

Professor Ramsay's work involves understanding the confusion of different geological beds. The text discusses volcanic rocks such as Felspathic Traps, Quartz Porphyries, and Greenstones intermingled with volcanic ashes and fossil-bearing Silurian beds. The summit of Snowdon contains volcanic ashes that include fossil shells. Submarine eruptions can produce jets of high-pressure steam and gases that create clouds and heavy rain. Eruptions can hurl fragments of rock and melted lava into the air, which then fall into the sea and form beds of mud or breccia. The eruption of Vesuvius in 1822 produced a steam jet that rose more than four miles into the air. The ash-beds of Snowdonia were likely laid down at the bottom of an ancient sea over long periods.

The text discusses the use of reason and common human faculties in understanding and communication. M. Jourdain is referenced as someone who has spoken prose without awareness of it. The educated individual is described as someone who becomes conscious of common human faculties and learns to use them accurately. The text suggests that the purpose of education is to teach the right use of reason to the less educated. Socrates is mentioned as a figure who attempted to teach the Athenian youth the importance of questioning and understanding. The conversation concludes with a suggestion to study Plato and apply learned principles to everyday understanding.

Tom read a letter written in a hasty ill-formed hand. The letter expressed concern for a friend whose father is blind and ruined. The writer feels a burden to their benefactors and describes their dependence on them. The writer mentions restrictions on their reading and lifestyle due to their situation. The writer reflects on the harshness of the Canadian winter and their longing for the South. The writer contemplates the nature of women and their relationships with men. The writer expresses a desire to live freely rather than in a dull existence.

The text references the warm rich youth of nations, characterized by childlike virtue and faith. The speaker expresses a desire to return to the roots of manhood and the mothers who nurtured them. The speaker envisions a future where man conquers evil, death, and shame, returning to a state of purity. Earl Haldan's daughter is depicted as looking across the sea and laughing, seeking a marriage fee of six princesses' locks. A knight arrives, claiming to have won the locks of five princesses and seeking to complete the tale. The knight takes Earl Haldan's daughter's locks, completing the tale and instructing her to weep. The text includes an ode to the North-East Wind, welcoming it and expressing weariness of summer's heat.

Lancelot expresses feelings of starvation and neglect towards his children. A stranger advises Lancelot to invest money in ways that create employment for English workers. The stranger claims to have a connection with the Begum of the Cannibal Islands, who has excess money. The stranger recounts a story about the new king of the Cannibal Islands being eaten by his ministers. Lancelot acknowledges his past writings in a review about George Sand. Lancelot admits that his sins stem from selfishness and sloth. The banker warns Lancelot to be respectful in his conversation with the stranger.

The text discusses the consequences of societal corruption and the potential for revolution and anarchy. It emphasizes the importance of fearing God as a means of deliverance from societal issues. Joseph is presented as an example of someone who adheres to God's laws despite personal suffering. The text outlines the sacred nature of human relationships and the responsibilities that come with them. Joseph refuses the advances of his master's wife out of fear of God and a sense of honor. Even in prison, Joseph maintains faith in God's justice and providence, remaining active and helpful. The text concludes by highlighting that faith in God is what makes individuals gallant.

The robin's breeding song is noted for its force, variety, and character of melody. The garden warbler and the willow wren have similar voices, making them difficult to distinguish. The garden warbler's song begins with high and loud notes and ends lower and softer. The willow wren's song is characterized by a sudden outbreak of cheerfulness and hesitating hilarity. The wood wren is described as a slender, graceful, yellow warbler that appears restless and anxious. The wood wren's journey includes a long migration from Morocco, facing various hardships along the way. The wood wren is considered a delicate bird that is uncommon in England compared to its cousins.

The text discusses the concept of fearing God due to His mercy rather than His wrath. It references a Psalm that states there is forgiveness with God. The text contrasts superstitious beliefs about God with the idea of Him as a merciful Father. It mentions that some people, in times of distress, turn to saints or other entities instead of God. The text encourages individuals to remember God's mercy and compassion. It describes God as compassionate, long-suffering, and generous. The text states that God helps those who are humble and call upon Him.

Henry VIII would have been viewed positively by history if he had died before the divorce was proposed. Mr. Froude argues that Henry VIII was well-suited to govern England due to his birth conditions. Mr. Froude suggests that Henry VIII's moral character had not been fully tested during his early years. Henry VIII's later actions are debated among historians, with differing opinions on his character. Mr. Hallam's views on Henry VIII's relationship with Parliament are questioned by Mr. Froude. The text raises questions about the fairness of historical judgments regarding Henry VIII and his Parliament. The Parliament had a mixed response to Henry VIII's demands for money, sometimes granting and sometimes refusing them.

Dave Porter was found alongside a railroad track by farming people who assumed he had been put off a train. Dave was taken to a poorhouse and later lived with kind people who sent him to a boarding school. An old sailor named Billy Dill recognized Dave and mentioned a crazy nurse and a lost child. Dunston Porter confirmed that Dave was found near a railroad about thirteen years ago in the eastern United States, near Crumville. Dunston Porter revealed that Dave is the son of his twin brother, David Breslow Porter. David Breslow Porter is currently traveling in Europe for his health and has a daughter named Laura. Dunston Porter and David Breslow Porter were once business partners in a chemical works.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: Dave Porter in the South Seas

text: Pop sent the colored man away to work with a caution to be more careful in the future. The colored man left the vicinity and went to New York, where he shipped on an outward-bound ocean vessel. Several weeks later, Randolph Rover sent each of his three nephews a bicycle. The Rover boys enjoyed cycling and decided to ride to Chardale on a half-holiday. The road to Chardale required crossing several bridges and descending a long hill. Tom Rover sped down the hill without a brake, unaware of the approaching train. Dick and Sam Rover attempted to warn Tom about the train as he approached the railroad tracks.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys in the Jungle

text: Certain papers had to be signed. A fire occurred at the sawmill during which the papers disappeared. Lush Barrock claimed to have procured the missing papers from someone else. Andrew Felps was offered the papers by Lush Barrock for one thousand dollars. Two men belonging to the Felps crowd appeared during the conversation. Lush Barrock fled when he saw Snap and his friends. The boy hunters lost Lush Barrock's trail at a brook.

The Rover boys, Sam, Tom, and Dick, went on various adventures including a chase on the ocean and a journey to Africa. They discovered a treasure document on an island in the Great Lakes and later found a box containing gold, silver, and precious stones in the Adirondack Mountains. A scarlet-fever scare led to the closure of Putnam Hall, prompting Mr. Rover to send his sons to California for their health. In 'The Rover Boys on Land and Sea,' the boys and Dora Stanhope were cast away on a deserted island and rescued by a United States warship. The boys returned to Putnam Hall in 'The Rover Boys in Camp' and participated in the annual encampment, facing hazing and a bully named Lew Flapp. Captain Putnam and George Strong oversaw the military academy's activities and praised the cadets for their performance during the encampment. Dick Rover addressed Captain Putnam on behalf of the cadets at the end of the encampment.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on the River

text: James Morris decided not to send for more goods from the East until late in the fall. Louis Glotte was allowed his liberty and disappeared immediately. Dave and Henry were eager to go on a hunting trip with Barringford, which was arranged for several weeks later. The hunting tour was planned to last a week or ten days. The group started their trip on horseback, as advised by Barringford. On the first evening, they only saw small game and made their meal from fish caught by Henry. Henry and Dave engaged in a swimming match while waiting for their evening meal to be prepared.

Job Haskers expressed frustration over a trick played on him and refused to apologize to Poole. Doctor Clay advised Haskers to be more careful in his treatment of students and threatened resignation if he did not comply. Haskers felt angry and humble after the confrontation with Doctor Clay. Gus Plum received a letter from Nick Jasniff postmarked London, which mentioned Dave Porter. The letter from Jasniff indicated he was enjoying his time in Europe and had financial gains. Dave Porter was intrigued by the letter, particularly the mention of his father and sister. Dave decided to copy part of the letter and send it to his uncle, inquiring about a trip to London.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: Dave Porter in the Far North

text: The group initially considered returning but decided to walk along a frozen watercourse. Gif expressed interest in encountering brook mink or ducks during their outing. The group covered a quarter of a mile and successfully hunted two rabbits. Spouter attempted to shoot a squirrel but was unsuccessful. Gif suggested a shortcut through the woods to the Lodge for more hunting opportunities. While deep in the forest, the group spotted flying partridges and attempted to shoot them. Andy climbed a tree to retrieve a dead partridge and heard a peculiar sound suggesting the presence of a wild animal.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on a Hunt

text: Tom demanded the return of a ball from the mate of the yacht. The mate initially refused to return the ball and threatened Tom. Tom stated he would report the matter to Captain Barforth if the ball was not returned. The mate eventually threw the ball to Tom but warned him to be careful with it. Tom decided not to report the incident to the captain to avoid further conflict. The group on the yacht engaged in various activities, including fishing and singing. A storm was anticipated, but it turned out to be damp and foggy without thunder or lightning.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on Treasure Isle

text: The mist began to rise, causing concern among the group. Sam expressed worry about their situation and asked Dick for a solution. Dick hoped a steamer or sailing vessel would come to rescue them. Tom spotted a vessel in the distance as the mist lifted. The group identified the vessel as a steam yacht but saw no signs of life on board. The boys attempted to call out to the yacht but received no response. Tom insisted on boarding the yacht despite the lack of crew or response.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys in Southern Waters

text: Watson recalls that the buffalo population has significantly decreased. Watson experienced a buffalo stampede while on Crazy Tom Mountain. During the stampede, Watson was thrown from his horse into a thorn bush. Watson observed more than twenty buffalo around him during the stampede. Five buffalo were trampled to death during the stampede. The group halted for dinner around one o'clock. Slavin appeared pale and expressed a need for rest.

Ben called out to Dave after emerging from the restaurant. Dave reported seeing Ward Porton, who ran away when approached. Dave expressed a desire to talk to Porton and mentioned the possibility of having him arrested. The group of young people decided to take a route back to Crumville that avoided Conover's Hill. Jessie expressed concern for Dave's safety regarding Ward Porton. The sleighing party was in good spirits despite the earlier incident. Dave was attending a civil engineering class and receiving private tutoring from Mr. Ramsdell.

Broxton suggested returning the coach after realizing they had lost track of their target. Leo Dunbar followed Broxton and Griswold ashore and sent a telegram to Carl to come immediately. Leo informed the chief of police about the situation, and they proceeded to the hotel where Broxton and Griswold were staying. Leo knocked on the door of Broxton and Griswold's hotel room, claiming there was a fire next door. Griswold attempted to escape but was tackled by Leo, resulting in a broken leg. Broxton was captured and handcuffed by Carl and the police. Griswold confessed that Nathan Dobb hired him to attack Leo Dunbar.

Tom and Sam discussed a story involving a jibberjacker. The jibberjacker was thrown against a wall and went through the side of a building. The jibberjacker sustained injuries and could not escape. Tom and Sam used a cross-cut saw to remove the jibberjacker's head. Larry mentioned that only a few boys left the Hall due to a scarlet fever scare. The boys planned to elect new officers once all members returned. Fred Garrison and George Granbury joined the boys for dinner in Ithaca.

Roger pulled Phil's sleeve and motioned for his friends to crouch behind rocks. Link Merwell, Sol Blugg, Job Haskers, and Larry Jaley appeared on the opposite ledge. Roger suspected that the group was searching for the Landslide Mine. Phil stated that the mine belonged to Roger's mother. Link Merwell expressed frustration about not locating landmarks. Larry Jaley pointed out the presence of Dave and his friends behind the rocks. Roger warned the group not to remove any of his uncle's landmarks if they found the mine first.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: Dave Porter in the Gold Fields

text: The governor assured the sea hero that the people of New York and vicinity were eager to honor him. A naval parade was arranged for the first day of the reception, followed by a land parade on the next day. The naval parade course was up the Hudson River past Grant's Tomb and included the _Olympia_, the Admiral's flag-ship, and several other war-ships. The banks of the Hudson were filled with people who applauded as the war-ships passed by, and every war-ship fired a salute at Grant's Tomb. Admiral Dewey and Theodore Roosevelt were prominent figures in the naval parade, receiving enthusiastic cheers from the crowd. The land parade started at Grant's Tomb and ended at Washington Square, lasting between five and six hours. On January 3, 1900, Governor Roosevelt sent his last annual message to the State legislature addressing various issues including trusts.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: American Boy's Life of Theodore Roosevelt

text: Hal is looking for Macklin at quarter to six. Hal follows Ferris after he leaves a tenement. Hal loses track of Ferris in a crowd at Broadway. Hal sees Mr. Caleb Allen while following Ferris. Allen enters a small mansion that is brightly illuminated inside. An old German vendor informs Hal that nobody lives at the mansion. The vendor suggests that the mansion is a gambling place.

Dave calculated he had gone two or three miles on the pony. The pony continued to run due eastward despite Dave's attempts to turn it back. After another two miles, the pony began to slacken its speed. Dave attempted to turn the pony again but was unsuccessful. The bronco eventually dropped to the ground and lay on its side. Dave urged the pony to get up and continue back to the ranch. Dave saw what he initially thought were buildings in the distance, but they were actually moving cattle.

Matt left Andy in charge of the store and went to the post-office to look for a letter from Ida Bartlett. Ida Bartlett's letter indicated that Mr. Fenton was disturbed by Mr. Gaston's departure and a potential exposure. Ida Bartlett had written to Mr. Gaston but had not yet received a reply. Matt expressed a strong desire to learn about his father and the missing papers. Andy encouraged Matt to remain hopeful about the situation regarding his father. The auction business was busy for the first two days, but it began to rain on the third day. A drunken man entered the store and requested to buy a pistol, alarming Matt.

Dan Baxter followed Dick and Tom from the hotel to the theater. Dick and Tom attended a performance of a light opera at the Columbia Theater. After the performance, Dick and Tom decided to eat at a nearby restaurant. Dan Baxter intended to confront Dick and Tom but had no specific plan. Dan Baxter had moved to the West to escape trouble in the East and to seek financial help from a relative in Australia. Dan Baxter attempted to access Room 324 at the hotel where Dick and Tom were staying. Dan Baxter successfully opened the door to Room 324 using a key, although it could not be removed afterward.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on Land and Sea

text: The Rough Riders fought on foot and did not have horses. Pictures of the Rough Riders are considered to be artistic exaggerations. Some individuals enlist in the army and navy after seeing such pictures. Nagasaki was bustling with soldiers preparing to depart for Manchuria. The _Shohirika_ left Nagasaki to join a squadron bound for the western coast of Korea. Life on the Japanese warship was similar to life in the American navy, with various drills and exercises. Japanese sailors and soldiers are reported to be among the healthiest in the world.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: At the Fall of Port Arthur

text: Edwards is a convict that the Texas marshal was pursuing. Cavanagh is accused of harboring Edwards. The sheriff believes Cavanagh is concealing Edwards to avoid law enforcement. Dalton defends Cavanagh, stating he is a capable ranger. Cavanagh has resigned from his position, but the Supervisor has not accepted the resignation. Dalton intends to offer Cavanagh a promotion instead of punishment. Lee expresses concern for Cavanagh's well-being amidst the situation.

Rose smiled at the Doctor, who expressed admiration for her. The Doctor invited Rose to share her story and offered to introduce her to people in Chicago. Rose shared details about her college work and her father with the Doctor. The Doctor suggested that Rose bring something of hers to show to an editor. Rose promised to dine with the Doctor the following Sunday at six. After leaving, Rose felt taller and stronger as she walked down the street. Rose observed the men and shop windows around her with a changing perspective.

The characters discuss the potential consequences of advising others. The youth and the woman wash dishes together and postpone a discussion. The woman inquires about the morning Star and retrieves a paper from the stairs. The youth expresses concern for the woman's safety due to threats against her. The woman believes that her father will protect her from real danger. The youth agrees to sit with the woman as she seeks advice. The woman demonstrates a method involving a slate that she claims can be vitalized by her touch.

The original plan for dealing with the Indians involved their removal from land to less desirable areas. Elsie was raised with a strong sense of race hatred but later became influenced by artists who valued Native Americans. Elsie was impressed by the success of Maurice Stewart in sculpting Native American subjects. Wilfred J. Buttes achieved financial success after working with the mountain Utes. Elsie expressed her desire for fame and recognition in her artistic pursuits. She wrote a letter to her father expressing her frustration with Captain Curtis and her uncle's situation. Captain Curtis considered changing his dining arrangements due to Elsie's hostility towards him.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: The Captain of the Gray-Horse Troop

text: Matilda Fletcher expresses regret about her life and the lack of happiness she has experienced. She feels that her children have not provided her with comfort and expresses a desire to rid herself of her burdens before death. Martha, who is present with Matilda, reflects on her own feelings of dissatisfaction and acknowledges that Matilda's life has been harder. Matilda expresses a strong aversion to her husband, Joe Bent, and does not want to see him. Joe Bent inquires about Matilda's condition and is told by Martha that she seems quite strong. Martha decides that the family should go to bed while she stays with Matilda, following the doctor's instructions. Matilda is later heard muttering to herself about memories of happier times in the meadow.

Humiston was hurt and financially distressed by the failure of his exhibits in Pittsburg and Chicago. Moss objected to Humiston's diatribes while Mrs. Moss attempted to change the subject. Humiston expressed that the only place for an artist to live fully was Paris. Bertha felt mentally weary and confused by the conversation and was grateful to Mrs. Moss for intervening. Humiston invited Bertha to visit him in New York, and she agreed to send him a message if she did. Bertha compared Ben Fordyce to Humiston and found Fordyce more appealing. Bertha was unaware that her wealth attracted attention from those around her, including artists.

The ranger plans to visit the courthouse. The ranger believes he has the support of certain witnesses. Hanscom's actions have angered Abe, who is seeking revenge. The ranger feels a strong desire for money and recognizes his own weaknesses. The ranger has developed from a capable boy into an unambitious man. Kitsong and his followers are waiting for the ranger and are in a dangerous mood. Kitsong confronts the ranger with hostility regarding his actions.

A man's figure swathed in white drapery was observed, but the face was not visible. Mrs. Miller began singing 'Annie Laurie' during the session. The psychic exhibited signs of suffering, which culminated in a moment of silence. During the silence, a table moved toward the observers without any apparent contact from the psychic. Miller expressed his belief that the phenomenon could be a case of telekinesis. A pencil and a megaphone on the table began to move, raising questions about the psychic's ability to interact with them. Mrs. Miller mentioned a box of candy located out of reach of the psychic.

The cartridge failed to go in during an encounter with a creature in the forest. Burton yelled, causing the creature to vanish into the dark. The smell of frying meat attracted a hungry beast from its den. The camp was set, fire lighted, and supper eaten before watching the sunset. The narrator expressed feelings of nostalgia and wrote verses during the evening. The group arrived in Quesnelle on the eleventh day of their journey. The narrator took a pony and dog-cart to inspect a mine in the Caribou Mining district.

The dusk fell and the air grew chill as the bottom bundle was pitched up. Will knelt down to help scrape loose wheat into baskets. David called for the men to turn out and they uncoupled the tumbling rods. Mr. Dingman invited Will to supper, but Will decided to go home instead. The county fair was scheduled for Thursday, a significant event in the country districts of the West. Will prepared for the fair by washing the carriage and polishing the horses' harnesses. Will looked forward to the fair with anticipation of showing his regret and love to Agnes.

Bill and his hired hand engage in a confrontation with Jim. Jim attempts to attack Bill in a fit of rage. Bill manages to subdue Jim during the struggle. Ike and Jack witness the altercation and react to it. Jim is injured during the fight but eventually regains consciousness. Jim questions the fairness of the fight after being hurt. Jim acknowledges Bill's strength and concedes defeat.

Blanche felt girlishly happy while laughing at Si Peasley and his misadventures in the city. Blanche expressed a desire to live in town during the winter. Blanche enjoyed the companionship of the Clayton girls, who invited her to spend the night with them. The next morning, Estelle accompanied Blanche while she did a little shopping. Blanche felt heavy-hearted as she returned to the prairie after her outing. Willard Burke attempted to ask Blanche a question about their relationship during dinner. Blanche experienced feelings of anger and isolation as she faced her circumstances.

Clement capitalized 'The Biddy' at two hundred thousand dollars. Clement issued three checks for forty-five thousand dollars each. Biddy received a check from the cashier. Eldred stated that the check provided him the means to fight. Clement reminisced about past struggles with Dan and Biddy. Clement tore up the checks given to him by Dan and Biddy. Clement announced that Biddy would become a quarter owner in 'The Witch'.

The road winds up a divide after leaving the Grande River before descending into Ute Park. Ute Park is located between the Continental Range and the Bear Tooth plateau. The landscape consists of ridges and ravines, sparsely covered with pinons, cedars, and aspens. In late August, the hills display various colors from aspen, fire-weed, huckleberry beds, and asters. A pale young man rode beside the driver Bill McCoy, who was a good driver. The young man was in the area for health reasons and lived in Connecticut. Two horsewomen approached the stage, which led to a misunderstanding by the young man.

Douglass felt the impact of Helen's words about the performance. Royleston struggled with his lines during the play. Helen Merival's performance was well-received by the audience. The audience applauded Helen for her portrayal, which was close to her true self. Douglass was concerned about the audience's reaction to the play's message. The second act received less enthusiastic applause compared to the first act. Helen's performance improved as Royleston became more confident in his role.

Harold expressed a desire to be with General Custer and to be a scout. Harold and his sweetheart, Dot, were both pupils at a local seminary. Harold admired the Wild West and fantasized about its adventurous lifestyle. Harold had mixed feelings about Native Americans, sometimes viewing them as noble and other times wishing to kill them for fame. Harold was perceived as a bad influence among village boys, often blamed for mischief he did not lead. The real leaders of the mischief were the shoemaker's two sons, who manipulated others into trouble. Harold's temperament was not suited for leadership, as he preferred to avoid responsibility.

The woman instructed Bob to tell his father that he must milk the remaining cows himself. After feeding the children, the woman attempted to feed the calves, but most of the milk was spilled. The woman became overwhelmed and fell to the ground, sobbing. Burns was described as tired, hungry, and ill-tempered while working with his team at the well. The woman took her children to bed after they had their supper and reflected on her harshness. The woman contemplated suicide but ultimately decided to milk the cows instead. While milking the cows, the woman experienced physical exhaustion and cried into the pail.

The child wept silently and felt that the strangers were her friends but wanted her mother. Gearheart and Ans discussed the need to secure the shanty and retrieve the girl's belongings. Gearheart expressed reluctance to handle the dead woman and suggested Ans take care of the child. Gearheart opened the door of the cottage to find the dead woman inside, with a frozen face and rigid eyes. Gearheart observed the clean clothing of the dead woman, which was finer than expected. Gearheart found a long box in the barn and used it to create a coffin for the dead woman. Gearheart felt an unreasoning fear of the dead and could not bring himself to touch the body.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Little Norsk; Or, Ol' Pap's Flaxen

text: Ida mentioned the presence of Congressman Mr. Talcott from Iowa at the event. Bradley spoke about the decline of the Grange and the challenges faced by farmers. Bradley expressed his emotional connection to the farmers' movement and the need for unity among the poor. Bradley declared his commitment to the movement after being encouraged by Ida. The audience responded with applause to Bradley's declaration. Ida and Bradley reflected on the significance of the event and its potential impact on the reform movement. Ida noted that the movement provided hope and a new perspective for the farmers.

The character expresses a desire to leave and not stay for dinner. The character mentions having murder charges against him, which he claims are wrong. The female character expresses sadness at the male character's departure and promises to sing for him. The male character renounces any claim to the female character as he prepares to leave. The male character reflects on his journey back to the West, feeling a sense of freedom and connection to the land. He observes changes in the environment and people as he travels, noting the transition to the cow country. The male character experiences a longing for the peaks of the West as he approaches his destination.

Falder admitted to altering both the cheque and the counterfoil. The cheque-book remained in Mr. Walter's pocket until he returned from Trenton on Tuesday morning. Cokeson expressed surprise and concern over Falder's actions. James stated that the case against Falder was serious and suggested prosecution. Cokeson mentioned that a woman visited Falder, who was not related to him but was married. Walter expressed a desire to give Falder a chance despite the situation. James concluded that Falder's actions warranted legal consequences due to their calculated nature.

SEELCHEN asks LAMOND if God is present. LAMOND suggests that the only road to life is through love. SEELCHEN expresses that she does not love. LAMOND describes love as a pursuit of wonder. SEELCHEN agrees to come to LAMOND. SEELCHEN appears pale and weary as she speaks of her heart being old. LAMOND expresses jealousy over the sound of cowbells.

Halliday invited Ashurst to stay the night and have a bathe. Ashurst had previously rowed in his college boat, played in his college football team, and won his college mile. The two little girls, Sabina and Freda, wanted Ashurst to see their cave. The cave featured a pool where the children wanted to catch creatures. Ashurst realized it was past three o'clock and that he could not cash his cheque that day. Ashurst sent a wire to Mrs. Narracombe stating he was detained for the night and would return the next day. Ashurst swam in the sea with Halliday and the three girls after borrowing a bathing dress.

The characters in the text include ST ERTH, CANYNGE, BORRING, COLFORD, WINSOR, and DE LEVIS. COLFORD reports that DE LEVIS has accused Ronald Dancy of robbing him. CANYNGE instructs BORRING to ensure that Dancy does not leave the Club. ST ERTH questions whether Kentman provided the police with the numbers of certain notes. WINSOR confirms that the police have not yet traced the notes. DE LEVIS expresses frustration with CANYNGE and accuses him of letting him down. CANYNGE states that both DE LEVIS and Dancy cannot remain members of the Club.

Barbara experiences emotional turmoil after a conversation with Courtier. Harbinger expresses feelings of frustration and confusion towards Barbara. Barbara acknowledges her familiarity with Harbinger's world and her desire for power. Miltoun is resigning his seat due to a conflict with his conscience. Lord Valleys dismisses Barbara's concerns about Miltoun's decision. Barbara expresses concern for Miltoun's future and the impact of his choices. Lady Valleys prefers not to think about their family member, Granny.

WANDA has keys that may belong to Larry. A policeman advises WANDA to keep her outer door shut after dark. KEITH expresses concern about WANDA's relationship with Larry. WANDA claims that Larry is her life and pleads not to be separated from him. KEITH warns WANDA that Larry is not reliable and may endanger her. WANDA insists that she would go away if Larry asked her to, but she could not live without him. LARRY enters the scene after WANDA goes to bring him in.

The text discusses the concept of 'Realism' and its distinction from 'Romanticism'. The author questions whether various writers, including Turgenev, Ibsen, Tolstoy, Dostoievsky, and Stephen Crane, can be classified as realists. The author argues that realism is not solely tied to naturalistic technique or imaginative power. Realism is characterized by an artist's focus on revealing the actual inter-relating spirit of life, character, and thought. The audience for realist art is described as those who require an enlightening quality in art to evoke emotion. The text suggests that there is a division between realist and romantic artists, but pure examples of either are rare. The author notes that even the most determined realist may possess romantic qualities and vice versa.

A couple, described as a large man and wife, walked side by side in silence amidst a busy street. The couple appeared unconcerned with their surroundings and engaged in conversation about dining and theatre plans. Shelton observed that the couple embodied the characteristics of well-bred individuals from country houses. The couple supported charities and exhibited clear judgment, with a disdain for breaches of morality. Shelton felt a sense of discomfort and irritation towards the couple, despite their well-mannered demeanor. He noted a resemblance between himself and the couple, reflecting on their calm and healthy appearance. Shelton returned to his rooms feeling moody and expressed his impressions to Antonia, describing a sense of meanness.

Gyp had a deep love for her father, Winton, which significantly influenced her development. Winton's frequent absences caused Gyp emotional distress, which subsided upon his return. Gyp cultivated sympathy for her poorer neighbors, influenced by Winton's open-hearted nature. At the age of nineteen, Gyp attended a hunt-ball with her governess and wore a pale maize-colored dress. Gyp's appearance at the ball was striking, showcasing her beauty and confidence. During the ball, Gyp prioritized her governess's feelings over her own enjoyment by sitting with her instead of dancing. Gyp overheard comments at the ball suggesting that she and Winton were perceived as father and daughter.

The figure moves from the lamp-post to the doorway. The figure is young and wears ragged clothes. The figure identifies himself as Ferrand and mentions a past encounter with Wellwyn in Paris. Ferrand expresses that he is in poverty and recalls receiving ten francs from Wellwyn. Ferrand states he has not yet achieved success and feels exploited by the bourgeois. Wellwyn offers Ferrand tea and rum, which Ferrand accepts. Ferrand expresses feelings of discouragement and reflects on the nature of life.

Sir William has given Dunning until tomorrow to decide on his actions. Studdenham informs Sir William that Dunning is hanging partridges. Lady Cheshire expresses concern about Freda's health. Sir William mentions the previous year's game count, which included 253 pheasants. Dunning acknowledges that he understands the situation but feels he never meant any harm. Sir William warns Dunning that if he leaves, he will not receive a character reference. Mabel Lanfarne invites Bill to join her for pool.

Mr. Lavender knocked on a door and entered a room with two young ladies who were tapping typewriters. Mr. Lavender asked to see the President but was informed that the Secretary would suffice. One of the young ladies left the room and returned shortly after. Mr. Lavender entered a room with two men, one pacing and talking in a powerful bass voice. The pacing man expressed concerns about politicians interfering with their plans. The Secretary asked the pacing man whom he would choose from France for their plans. Mr. Lavender proposed that the pacing man should be the League of Nations.

MAUD examines her expression in the mirror before returning to the table. TOPPING informs MAUD that lunch has been ready for some time. MAUD expresses disinterest in lunch and inquires about a message given to a young party. TOPPING mentions a horse race called the Cesarwitch and describes it as a dark horse at twenty to one. MAUD asks TOPPING to place a bet of ten shillings on the race. MAUD discusses a film project with TOPPING, seeking his opinion on a psychological aspect of her character. MAUD reveals that she has the Fanshawe diamonds and contemplates where to conceal them.

Edward is at Hannibal. A maid named Martha enters and returns a wedding ring to a character referred to as SHE. SHE is startled when she realizes she left the ring in the bathroom. A young officer in khaki enters with a girl who is dressed in a discreet dark dress and hat. The girl is identified as Russian and expresses sadness about the war. The young officer has just come out of the hospital and is a little lame. The conversation between the girl and the young officer touches on themes of war and personal connections.

The characters in the text include Katherine, More, Henry, and Olive. More is preparing to deliver a speech and is experiencing indecision about its content. Katherine expresses concern about More making a speech and its implications. Street musicians are playing outside, which captures the attention of More and Olive. Olive, a child, enters the room and interacts with More, asking about his speech. More breaks a wine-glass while speaking passionately about his beliefs. The text explores themes of patriotism, justice, and the consequences of war.

The conversation involves a discussion about the nature of revelation and existence. Gratian and George have a relationship that includes mutual respect despite their differing views. Gratian's father, Pierson, did not oppose her marriage to George, whom he considers honest and trustworthy. Gratian and George had a brief honeymoon before George returned to France. Pierson struggles with how to communicate George's health status to Noel. Thirza advises Pierson to allow the publication of banns to delay the marriage. Pierson ultimately decides to oppose the marriage, believing it to be a serious mistake.

MRS. MILER observes a gentleman on the first floor pretending to knock at number two. MRS. MILER describes the gentleman as a nasty, smooth-looking man wearing a billycock hat. MALISE expresses detached appreciation for MRS. MILER's comments. CLARE arrives and inquires if Mr. Malise is in. MRS. MILER informs CLARE that Mr. Malise is dressing and offers her a chair. MRS. MILER mentions that Mr. Malise prefers his claret fresh-opened. MALISE enters the room with a thread of tobacco hanging from his cheek.

Ivy expresses reluctance to dance. Mrs. Bradmere enters the scene after knocking and ringing a bell. Mrs. Burlacombe informs Mrs. Bradmere that Mr. Strangway is upset. Burlacombe describes Mr. Strangway as being in a precarious mental state. Mrs. Bradmere insists on seeing Mr. Strangway immediately. Burlacombe mentions that Mr. Strangway's situation is widely known. Mrs. Bradmere acknowledges Mr. Strangway's distress and attempts to offer support.

The characters SCANTLEBURY, EDGAR, WANKLIN, WILDER, TENCH, and ANTHONY are involved in a discussion about a dispute. WILDER suggests that the dispute should be handed over to Mr. Simon Harness for settlement. EDGAR expresses his refusal to withdraw his statements regarding cowardice and starvation. ANTHONY has been the Chairman of the Company for thirty-two years and claims to have never been beaten by the men. ANTHONY asserts that there can only be one master in a house and rejects the idea of equality between masters and men. ANTHONY believes that the interests of Capital and Labour are fundamentally opposed. ANTHONY states that the Board is the machine that leads and determines actions without fear.

source.author: John Galsworthy
source.title: The Project Gutenberg Plays of John Galsworthy, Complete

text: Fellows mentions he has had a twinge in his cork wrist. Hillcrist expresses concern about the Jackmans wanting to see him. The Jackmans inform Hillcrist that they have received notice to quit their cottage. Jackman states that they must vacate the cottage this week. Mrs. Jackman explains that they have lived in the cottage for thirty years. Hillcrist is upset about the situation and plans to write to Mr. Hornblower. The Jackmans believe Mr. Hornblower wants the cottages for his workmen.

Mr. Porter attempted to cook dinner but faced difficulties with sausages that fell into the fire. The dinner was unsuccessful, with portions of sausages returning to the pan as cinders. Mr. Porter reprimanded his eldest son for not focusing on his lessons. Mr. Porter completed some household chores after the children left for school. Mr. Porter changed his grocer twice and was threatened with slander by his fishmonger during shopping. Mr. Porter went to bed at eleven o'clock and later admitted his wife home. The next morning, Mr. Porter discussed a difficult situation with Mr. Bert Robinson at work.

George, Bob, and Benson walked through the grass to the well. Benson tied a rope to a candlestick and lowered it into the well. The string parted, causing the candlestick to fall into the water. Benson prepared to descend into the well despite George's concerns about his health. Benson instructed George and Bob on how to assist him while he was in the well. After a period of silence, a violent tug on the rope indicated Benson was in trouble. George and Bob attempted to pull Benson up, but a dead man's face emerged from the well.

source.author: William Wymark Jacobs
source.title: The Well, The Lady of the Barge and Others, Part 4

text: Mrs. Prince was informed by Joe Barlcomb about an incident involving six men. Mrs. Prince initially reacted with alarm, thinking there was a fire. Joe Barlcomb visited Mrs. Prince the following evening to provide details about the incident. Mrs. Prince exhibited unusual behavior, including making strange noises and appearing to be in a fit. Mrs. Prince attributed the trouble to Bill Jones and instructed Joe to take a bottle to him. Joe was told to befriend Bill Jones and give him beer mixed with gin to break a spell. At the Cauliflower, Joe successfully reconciled with Bill Jones after initially facing hostility.

source.author: William Wymark Jacobs
source.title: Breaking A Spell, Odd Craft, Part 6

text: Charlie Tagg is contemplating how to begin a conversation with Emma while thinking of another girl. Old Cook mentions that Charlie has returned home at an opportune time. Mrs. Cook informs Charlie about a significant bargain in the chandlery line. Old Cook expresses regret about missed opportunities in his youth. Mrs. Cook suggests that Charlie should go on more voyages after marrying Emma while she manages the business. Charlie Tagg expresses skepticism about the chandlery business and its future prospects. Charlie refuses to enter the shop that is being shown to him, stating he does not like its appearance.

source.author: William Wymark Jacobs
source.title: The Nest Egg, Captains All, Book 3

text: The fourth story was told by an old hand in a quiet setting with the gas turned out. George, the waiter, left the room unexpectedly during the storytelling. An old gentleman mentioned that he knows people who have seen apparitions. The ghost story connected with the house involves Jerry Bundler, a London thief. Jerry Bundler was captured in the house eighty years ago and was found dead by hanging. The old gentleman's father claimed to have seen Jerry Bundler's ghost in the house. The narrator could not specify which bedroom Jerry Bundler haunted.

Joan tended to her stepfather, who was in a weakened state and required assistance to turn in bed. Gunn's power diminished after Mullet's death, prompting him to seek immediate financial gain. The nurse predicted that Mullet had only four days to live, and Gunn planned to take advantage of this. Gunn entered Mullet's room while Joan was away and attempted to extract information about Mullet's money. Captain Rogers confronted Gunn in Mullet's room, revealing that he was aware of Gunn's intentions. Rogers incapacitated Gunn and planned to frame him for murder after Mullet's death. The nurse awoke the next morning and discarded the medication meant for Mullet, unaware of the events that transpired.

source.author: William Wymark Jacobs
source.title: Captain Rogers, The Lady of the Barge and Others, Part 7

text: A significant number of women in Little Haven were gathered near a fence and in groups on the road. Mr. Quince informed the farmer that he had given him incorrect advice earlier. Mr. Rose expressed concern about potentially acting against the law based on Mr. Quince's advice. Mr. Quince suggested that Mr. Rose should release the prisoner and apologize. Mr. Rose could not find the key to the stable where the prisoner was held. Mr. Hogg confirmed that he had seen the key earlier but did not know its current location. Mr. Quince left without addressing the identity of the prisoner in the stable.

Sam is surprised when a detective officer recognizes him as a detective. The detective officer, identified as Detective-Sergeant Cubbins, is in the area to protect sailors from being robbed. Cubbins mentions that he is trying to catch two criminals named Long Pete and Fair Alf. Cubbins offers Sam a five-pound note for helping him catch the criminals. Cubbins plans for Sam to appear as a drunk man walking up Tower Hill to lure the criminals. Sam has twelve pounds in his possession and agrees to participate in Cubbins' plan.

Miss Truefitt expresses that she is glad Mr. Catesby is present. Mrs. Porter enters the room looking for knife-powder and recognizes Mr. Catesby. Mrs. Porter claims Mr. Catesby is her husband who left her eighteen months ago. Mrs. Porter embraces Mr. Catesby, causing him distress. Mrs. Truefitt and Prudence comment on the situation with amusement. Mr. Catesby attempts to leave but is physically restrained by Mrs. Porter. Mr. Catesby decides to apologize to Mrs. Truefitt before leaving.

The narrator confronts a boy on the wharf for throwing coke. The boy claims he has as much right to be on the wharf as anyone else. The boy throws coke at empties while the skipper and crew encourage him. The narrator threatens to report the boy for wasting coke. The boy pretends to be sorry and offers to pick up the coke. The narrator's wife, referred to as 'missis,' is shy and prefers to be alone. The situation escalates into a struggle, attracting attention from others on the jetty.

Old Sam went out wearing a cap after leaving a mission-hall. Ginger Dick and Peter Russet followed Old Sam but left him when he entered a shop. Old Sam bought a button-hole for his coat at the corner of Commercial Road. Ginger and Peter waited for Old Sam outside a tobacconist's shop. A woman named Mrs. Finch came out of a parlour at the back of the shop. Peter recognized Old Sam's foot while looking at a boot in the shop. Ginger and Peter met Old Sam inside the shop and discussed a half crown.

The night-watchman expressed frustration about a dog on the ship Henry William. The night-watchman recalled a past experience with a dog that caused trouble. Three men, Sam Small, Ginger Dick, and Peter Russet, were at a public house after being turned out of a music hall. A big black dog entered the public house and approached Sam, licking his hand. Sam shared an arrowroot biscuit with the dog, which then jumped on his lap. Peter Russet and Ginger Dick also fed the dog, and they speculated about its owner. Sam suggested that there might be a reward for the dog and proposed to take care of it.

A man named George Dixon returns home after a long absence. Charlie initially does not recognize George due to his beard. George tells Charlie he has had a terrible time since he left home. George's wife, Julia, expresses surprise at seeing him again. Julia questions George about his past actions, including telling her to get rid of her relations. George mentions he has suffered greatly, including being shipwrecked and fighting for his life. Old Burge criticizes George for frightening people upon his return.

The carman accidentally bumped his bad shin against the narrator's foot while in a hurry. A thin little woman was passed out during a speech she was making, and a policeman was about to assist her. The skipper insisted that the woman would come on his ship, and the narrator agreed as long as she left his wharf. The skipper and his mate helped the woman to the ship after the narrator fetched a pint for the policeman. The narrator went to the jetty and found the woman calling out for 'Bill' while sitting on the deck of the John Henry. The narrator encountered his wife on the doorstep while the woman attempted to walk arm-in-arm with him. The narrator's wife and the woman began arguing about the narrator's actions upon entering the house.

The narrator wrote a letter to a man named Bill, pretending it was from a woman named Dorothy. The letter invited Bill to meet at Cleopatra's Needle at eight o'clock. The narrator could not find an envelope to send the letter and kept it in his pocket. Upon returning home, the narrator's wife displayed signs of anger and confronted him. The wife accused the narrator of being unfaithful and questioned his actions. The narrator attempted to explain that the letter was a mistake and not meant for him. The confrontation escalated as the wife recalled past grievances against the narrator.

Bill expressed a desire to buy the second mate's mattress as a keepsake. The second mate initially refused to sell the mattress but eventually agreed to sell it for two pounds. Bill promised to pay the second mate for the mattress after they were paid off. Bill and the second mate agreed to keep the transaction a secret from the skipper. Bill and another character, Jimmy, planned to deceive Jimmy about their intentions regarding the mattress. The group was towed to London after four days of travel. Bill and the narrator drew ten shillings each to go ashore with.

source.author: William Wymark Jacobs
source.title: Bill's Paper Chase, Lady of the Barge and Others, Part 3

text: His lordship had dinner at 1 p.m. Miss Rose was sewing in the living-room while his lordship watched her. His lordship expressed dissatisfaction with the dullness of the place. Mr. Rose complained about his lordship's treatment of him in front of his daughter. His lordship promised Mr. Rose to treat him differently. Miss Rose expressed a desire to hear about his lordship's mansion. His lordship described his ideal life in a humble setting.

A boy approaches a man and asks if he is looking for a cabin-boy. The boy has run away from home and is afraid of being pursued. The boy's father is likely offering rewards for his return. The man attempts to persuade the boy to return home but is unsuccessful. The boy expresses a desire to see the world and experience adventures. The boy provides his father's name, Mr. Watson, and his father's occupation as a draper. The man decides to inform the boy's father about his whereabouts after the boy has set sail.

source.author: William Wymark Jacobs
source.title: Manners Makyth Man, Ship's Company, Part 12

text: The letter is addressed to Miss Minnie Miller, 17, John Street, Mile End Road. Joe is on guard and is asked to deliver the letter. The gal offers Joe a shilling for bus fare to deliver the letter. Joe initially refuses to leave his post but eventually agrees to deliver the letter. The narrator locks the gate after Joe leaves. Miss Butt is looking for the key to her box, which is padlocked. The narrator observes that the hatch is closed and locked after Miss Butt leaves.

Mr. Bodfish noted the presence of two caked rims of mud on the stairs. Mr. Bodfish's niece stated that Emma had not been outside the house all day. Mr. Negget suggested that the mud cakes were rather large for a woman. Mrs. Negget testified that Emma's box had been thoroughly searched. Mr. Bodfish inquired about Mrs. Driver's purpose for visiting that morning. Mr. Negget expressed an idea that Mrs. Driver was after a wedding ring. Mr. Bodfish reacted with confusion and anger to Mr. Negget's suggestion.

source.author: William Wymark Jacobs
source.title: Cupboard Love, The Lady of the Barge and Others, Part 5

text: Slinn exhibited forgetfulness regarding Don Caesar, indicating a lack of memory about the incident.
