Mulrady focused on financial gain despite lacking special skills and often fell prey to unscrupulous financiers. Mulrady's luck allowed him to succeed in his ventures, making his mistakes appear insignificant. He sank a new shaft at great expense, ultimately finding a significant volume of water that benefited his mine and neighbors. Mulrady purchased a league of forest and canyon land from Don Ramon's heirs at a high price, believing it contained gold. Despite being sneered at, Mulrady's shares were bought, and he was respected by various social classes. The rainy season revealed the crude conditions of Rough-and-Ready, with mud invading buildings and the landscape appearing unattractive.

The text is titled 'EXCELSIOR' and is authored by Bret Harte. The work is presented by Enoch Morgan's Sons Co. in New York. The narrative features a youth carrying a stencil-plate that reads 'SAPOLIO.' Various cleaning applications for 'SAPOLIO' are mentioned throughout the text. The youth interacts with several characters, including an old man and a maiden. The text references 'Bixby's Blacking,' 'Mustang Liniment,' and 'Simmons' Pills.' The word 'SAPOLIO' is repeatedly emphasized in different contexts within the narrative.

Miss Porter left before the man could explain himself. The Sheriff of Calaveras interrupted a trial and took Joe away. The evidence from a previous inquest was read before Joe was taken. Joe laughed when shown a ring during the trial. The Judge asked Joe if the ring belonged to him, but Joe did not respond directly. Cass Beard became bitter and hard after losing his good humor. Cass decided to leave Blazing Star to focus on making money.

Mr. Hathaway holds a large business card in his hand. Mr. Hathaway offers to show the largest business in canned provisions and domestic groceries in the State. Mr. Hathaway mentions having entertained Governor Fiske and Senator Doolan. Captain Stidger describes the city's growth and future potential as a metropolis. A rivalry develops between two groups in the parlor, each supporting their respective admired individuals. Hathaway invites his party to refreshment in a private room before they leave. Captain Stidger identifies a group of young ladies from the Convent of Santa Clara.

source.author: Bret Harte
source.title: A Ward of the Golden Gate

text: The scene takes place on a veranda with a sister observing the surroundings. The sister has a refined appearance with soft gray shadows and dark gentle eyes. She is described as taller and thinner than her sister, Kate, who has a matronly demeanor. Mrs. Hale suggests that Kate should change her dress and ride to meet John. Kate expresses reluctance to leave Mrs. Hale alone without a man for protection. Mrs. Hale mentions the Chinese field hands and their education in their own country. Kate refuses to take Manuel with her, citing concerns about his behavior.

Randolph left the cabin after believing that Miss Avondale had seen and was avoiding him. He felt responsible for her changed fortunes and longed to speak with her. Miss Avondale slipped away with other passengers when the boat reached the Alameda wharf. Randolph wandered in the hotel garden and main street hoping to meet her again. He recognized Miss Avondale as she ran toward the wharf during a rainstorm. Randolph shared an umbrella with Miss Avondale as they rushed to board the last boat. Miss Avondale mentioned she left her little cousin with friends due to the weather.

Mr. Hamlin waited for a phenomenon to repeat but it did not occur. Mr. Hamlin read a letter that instructed him to be at the corral with the buggy at three. Brown awoke from a dream in which he and Sue were getting married again. Mr. Hamlin advised Brown to sell all his possessions and leave the country with his wife. Mr. Hamlin left quickly after advising Brown, demanding his horse be saddled. Brown's hostler was concerned for Mr. Hamlin's welfare as he prepared to leave. The morning after, residents near the Wingdam turnpike heard a voice singing.

source.author: Bret Harte
source.title: The Luck of Roaring Camp and Other Tales

text: The wounded man fell into Gideon's arms with a bullet in his chest. The crowd attempted to assist the wounded man, but he warned them to stand back. The surgeon and a younger man arrived to attend to the unconscious prisoner. The surgeon informed the sheriff that the wounded man would not survive long enough to return to jail. Jack Hamlin agreed to be responsible for the wounded man. The wagon carrying the wounded man, Gideon, Jack Hamlin, and the surgeon arrived at the 'Palmetto Shades' in Martinez. Gideon felt troubled by the luxurious surroundings of the 'Palmetto Shades' while attending to the wounded man.

Christie and Jessie searched for items in the dining-room. They found several books, including works by Thackeray and Dickens. Jessie discovered letters tied with a ribbon, addressed to 'My darling Fairfax.' Christie expressed disapproval of the letters and the familiarity implied by the use of a first name. Mr. Carr returned home late with a package for his daughters containing a silver spoon and a battered silver mug. Jessie humorously suggested the items were a reminder of Kearney's christening. Christie lay awake at night, reflecting on memories and the sounds of the wind.

Percy Briggs expressed concern about the state of the camp and the lack of a wagon road. Tom Rollins denied involvement in a recent performance that caused disturbance in the camp. Briggs emphasized the need to improve the camp's reputation and eliminate undesirable elements. Rollins and Briggs discussed the importance of maintaining order without resorting to violence. Mosby, the grocery proprietor, expressed caution about the potential impact of new families on his business. A rider approached the camp, characterized by a shotgun and a navy revolver, and appeared intimidating.

A large pane of ordinary window glass was found stuck in the fork of a tree. The young girl observed her reflection and the surrounding landscape in the glass. She retrieved a large piece of yellow soap and some yards of rough cotton sheeting from her supplies. After undressing, she transformed into a young woman named Flip, who was modishly attired. Flip's appearance was enhanced by the colors of her gown and the natural surroundings. A sound from the trail below caused Flip to hide quickly. After some time, Flip returned to her homespun garments as the spell was broken.

James North was met by Joe in the morning. Joe suggested that North stay with him until the child was better. Miss Bessy had not closed her eyes the previous night. North spent a week at Joe's cabin before returning to his own quarters. Miss Bessy invited North to spend the next evening at her house for a dance. North was left to take care of the baby while Miss Bessy attended the dance. Joe listed several people who would be at the dance, including Widder Higsby and Polly Doble.

Enriquez admires his wife Urania excessively. Enriquez collects geological specimens to please Urania. Urania dislikes gold and what she calls 'vulgar mining.' Enriquez possesses several specimens of gold-bearing quartz and mining shares. Enriquez's grandfather and father worked the mines before the American speculators. The mines Enriquez refers to were originally silver mines worked by peons and Indian slaves. Enriquez believes that it takes a gold mine to work a silver mine.

Elijah Martin was known as a shiftless and worthless individual in Redwood Camp. He entered Redwood Camp carrying his belongings in a red handkerchief on a shovel. During a flood in 1856, he drifted away on a plank while others either escaped or drowned. Elijah Martin was overlooked by the census and ignored by the tax collector. He was referred to by vague names such as 'him,' 'Skeesicks,' or 'that coot.' On March 15, 1856, he found himself adrift in a swollen tributary of the Minyo. After being swept away, he was eventually cast ashore on an unexplored wilderness.

Jovita expresses anger towards Sandy regarding John Oakhurst. Sandy is bewildered and questions Jovita about mentioning John Oakhurst's name. Jovita feels terrified after accidentally mentioning John Oakhurst's name. Sandy admits to being confused and states he will not drink anymore that night. Jovita plans to signal Don Juan from the flat roof of the upper corridor. Don Jose observes Jovita and Diego with a sarcastic smile and comments on the situation. Concho informs Don Jose that two caballeros have arrived seeking his presence.

Billy was relegated to the rocky crags above the camp after an incident involving a fallen bough. M'Ginnis appeared with a wheelbarrow but without Billy the day after Billy was relegated. Billy had a longing for posters and would appear whenever a circus, concert, or political meeting was advertised. Billy once removed a theatre bill and was pursued by an advance agent while carrying it on his horns. Colonel Starbottle visited a young actress known as the 'Sacramento Pet' during his election business. Billy's visits became less frequent as Rocky Canyon changed due to the arrival of Southwestern families. A traveler reported seeing a wild-looking animal resembling a small elk in the mountains, which was believed to be Billy.

source.author: Bret Harte
source.title: Mr. Jack Hamlin's Mediation and Other Stories

text: The Judge admired the features of his daughter while smoothing her hair. A tall figure entered the doorway, revealing the form of an Indian man. The Indian wore a blanket over one shoulder and had a beaver hat adorned with a feather. The Indian questioned the Judge about the presence of the Pale Face among the Red Man. Genevra Tompkins engaged in a dialogue with the Indian, comparing food sources. The Indian expressed sadness about the Red Man's retreat before the Pioneer. Genevra Tompkins watched the Overland Mail stage leave, fearing for her father's safety.

Salomy Jane inquired about Phil Larrabee, who is known to be an enemy of her father. Mr. Clay mentioned that he had been thinking about Phil Larrabee and heard from a Chinaman that Larrabee was seen at Sawyer's Crossing. Mr. Clay found tracks in the far pasture that he believed were not his and suspected they belonged to Larrabee. Salomy Jane offered to investigate and find out where Larrabee was hiding. Mr. Clay insisted that Salomy Jane should not engage in the investigation as he believed it was not suitable for women. That night, Salomy Jane sat by the window and heard the sound of a horse's shoe on flinty ground. Salomy Jane took her father's shotgun and went outside to investigate the source of the noise.

The woman has clear eyes that are ringed with suffering. The coverlet has slipped from her shoulder, startling the man. The woman struggles to sit up and expresses a sarcastic remark about her situation. The man identifies himself as a Northern general and the woman as a Southern spy. The woman expresses bitterness about being betrayed by another woman. The man explains that a flower was used as a signal in a plot against her. The woman realizes that the signal was changed and questions the loyalty of another woman.

Polly was hanging onto the pigtail of Wan Lee while laughing. The tunnel-men expressed a desire not to cut off a Chinaman's pigtail again. The children reached the entrance of one of the tunnels but became frightened by the darkness. Wan Lee scattered red paper slips and set off fireworks at the tunnel entrance. The children reacted with awe and fascination to Wan Lee's actions. Polly realized she had forgotten her doll, Lady Mary, which was damaged. Hickory humorously suggested that Lady Mary's hair was lost due to being scalped by Injins.

source.author: Bret Harte
source.title: The Queen of the Pirate Isle

text: Romulus was acknowledged as the king and focused on organizing the people and framing the constitution of society. The community under Romulus consisted of a mix of ignorant peasants, refugees from justice, and individuals of wealth and influence. As the city building progressed, more respectable individuals joined the community, leading to a more organized commonwealth. The institutions of the Roman state likely developed gradually over time rather than being formally established by Romulus. Romulus is said to have created a republican system with elected civil and military offices. The population was divided into three tribes, each selecting three presiding officers, likely with Romulus making the final selections. The remaining population was divided into Patricians, an aristocratic class, and Plebeians, who were further divided into patrons and clients.

Josey is instructed by Jonas to give hay to the old General, a large white horse. The old General was named after a general who used to ride him during parades. Josey puts hay into the old General's crib and checks on him. Oliver opens the barn doors and begins to clear snow from in front of them. Josey joins Oliver in shoveling snow from the barn doors and clearing paths in the yard. After working for half an hour, they go inside to find breakfast nearly ready. Oliver and Josey plan to use the old General to haul wood after breakfast.

source.author: Jacob Abbott
source.title: Jonas on a Farm in Winter

text: Elizabeth was jealous, petulant, and irritable. Elizabeth envied others the love and domestic enjoyments. Elizabeth questioned her maids of honor about marriage. One young lady expressed her desire to marry a certain gentleman. Elizabeth offered to speak to the young lady's father about her marriage. The young lady's father consented to the queen's arrangement. Elizabeth ultimately denied the young lady the opportunity to marry.

ROLLO ON THE RHINE is a book written by Jacob Abbott. The book was published in Boston by Taggard and Thompson in 1864. Jacob Abbott entered the book according to the Act of Congress in 1855. The book is part of a series titled ROLLO'S TOUR IN EUROPE. The main character, Rollo, is twelve years old. The story includes Rollo's family members, including his parents, younger brother, and cousin. The book contains chapters that describe various locations and experiences along the Rhine River.

The tollman stands on the abutment of the bridge and swings a wooden shoe to passing boats using a long line from a pole. The helmsman in the boat takes hold of the shoe to put money into it, which the tollman later retrieves. The tollman carries the collected money to a small toll house located on the pier. Rollo encounters a bridge with a narrow movable section that allows masts and rigging of ships to pass through. In areas with heavy ship traffic, there are ferries instead of bridges, using flat-bottomed boats for crossing. Rollo finds the ferries entertaining and describes crossing one as similar to crossing a street by water. Rollo and Mr. George spend several days in Rotterdam, enjoying the sights and taking a walk around the town.

Rollo decided not to engage with books for a month. Rollo planned to help Jonas with his work during this time. Jonas was digging a canal in the marsh to drain off water. Rollo took a piece of bread and a tin dipper to gather water from the brook. Rollo walked along a green lane with raspberry-bushes on each side. Jonas had previously planted raspberry-bushes in the lane after ploughing the ground. Rollo gathered raspberries to take to Jonas while he worked.

Peasants in Switzerland greet strangers pleasantly when they meet on the mountains. Strangers in most other countries typically pass each other in silence. The guide spoke to a girl named Ninette in German. Ninette carried a basket that was small at the bottom and larger at the top. The basket was secured to Ninette's back with two flat strips of wood. Mr. George and Rollo considered buying the straps that held the basket. Ninette indicated that her father, who lived nearby, could sell them a pair of straps.

James was waiting for Rollo and his mother on the front steps of his house. Rollo offered James the front seat in the carryall, which James accepted. Rollo's mother proposed to give a lecture on playthings instead of telling a story. Rollo and James were unsure what a lecture was but agreed to listen to their mother. Rollo's mother explained that the value of a plaything lies in the pleasure it brings to the mind. Rollo mentioned a plaything called a 'kicker,' which was a pasteboard man that could move its arms and legs. Rollo's mother noted that the pleasure from the 'kicker' diminished over time as it became familiar.

Sectarianism and bigotry in religion focus on external rites rather than spiritual interests. Genghis Khan organized two grand celebrations to illustrate his victories in Western Asia. The first celebration was a grand hunt intended to keep soldiers occupied. The hunt took place in a vast uninhabited region infested with wild beasts. Soldiers were organized in a military formation to drive the animals toward the center of the hunt area. The soldiers were prohibited from killing animals and were tasked with driving them out of their hiding places. As the hunt progressed, the animals became agitated and began to attack each other.

King Richard's second wife was called the little queen because she was about nine years old at the time of their marriage. Richard's courtiers advised him to marry again after the death of Queen Anne. Richard considered marrying Isabella, the Princess of France, despite her being very young and the daughter of his enemy. The marriage proposal was intended to establish peace between England and France, which had been in conflict. An embassage consisting of an archbishop, two earls, twenty knights, and five hundred horsemen was sent to propose the marriage. The embassadors were received honorably in Paris and dined with the French king. Objections to the marriage included Isabella's young age and her prior engagement to another duke's son.

Robert experienced intense rage and revenge after an insult from his brother. Robert drew his sword and attempted to confront his brother, causing alarm in the courtyard. The king intervened to prevent a fight between his sons, requiring force to separate them. Robert felt that his father was against him and sought sympathy from his mother. Robert organized a group of young nobles to rebel against his father and aimed to seize Rouen. The king sent an armed force after Robert's group, which failed to surprise Rouen. Matilda maintained secret communication with Robert while trying to mitigate the conflict between him and the king.

Mary directed supper to be prepared and divided her money into parcels for her attendants. During supper, Mary conversed cheerfully while her friends were silent and sad. Mary drank to the health of her friends and asked them to forgive her for any past grievances. She spent the evening writing letters to her relatives in France and making her will. Mary wished to have her body taken to France for burial at either Rheims or St. Denis. Arrangements were made for her execution in the great hall where she had been tried. Mary requested a delay to finish her devotions before proceeding to the hall of execution.

A black cone thirty feet high is located in the center of the crater. The cone has a fiery furnace mouth at the top that emits steam and lava. Mr. George and Rollo are observing the crater from a narrow ridge. Rollo and Josie descend into the crater with a group led by a mountain guide. The floor of the crater is covered with black lava that is hard enough to walk on. Rollo and Josie buy pieces of lava from local boys near the cone. Rosie expresses concern for Rollo and Josie's safety when they are obscured by vapor.

The event featured games, shows, and military and civic spectacles for thousands of spectators. A procession included twelve statues of gods and a thirteenth statue representing Philip as a god. Philip arranged to walk in a conspicuous space during the procession, wearing white robes and a crown. The procession was moving toward a theater where games and spectacles were to be exhibited. An officer of the guards, Pausanias, stabbed Philip to the heart, resulting in his death. Pausanias was cut to pieces by the guards before he could escape. Alexander was proclaimed king shortly after Philip's death, despite being between nineteen and twenty years old.

Rollo expressed a desire for Allie to join him and their mother on a trip. Allie showed enthusiasm about seeing the Tarpeian Rock, despite not knowing what it was. Mrs. Beekman initially refused to allow Allie to walk to the Tarpeian Rock. Rollo offered to take a carriage to the destination. Mrs. Beekman reluctantly consented to the children's proposal after some persuasion. Rollo negotiated the fare with the coachman in Italian before getting into the carriage. Rollo had studied the map and Guide Book to ensure he knew the way to the Tarpeian Rock.

Rollo and his father discussed a tree that was growing around a rock. Rollo expressed interest in experimenting with putting a cent into a tree. Rollo's father suggested making a small cleft in the bark to insert the cent. Rollo followed his father's instructions and inserted the cent into the tree. While working, Rollo talked to his father about a book he found interesting. Rollo mentioned a story about Aladdin and his lamp from Henry's book. Rollo's father did not express a desire for an Aladdin's lamp.

A corps of armed chariots was built and equipped for warfare, resembling modern artillery in expense and design. The chariots were heavy, drawn by two horses, and featured scythe-like blades on the axle-trees for combat. Each chariot contained a driver and one or more armed warriors who fought with javelins and spears. Abradates prepared a hundred chariots at his own expense and made a larger chariot for himself drawn by eight horses. Panthea contributed a helmet, corslet, arm-pieces of gold, and additional armor for the horses from her private treasures. Panthea kept her contributions a secret until the day Abradates was to go into battle for the first time. The appearance of Abradates in his splendid armor and chariot drew admiration from the spectators.

The Parliament assembled in November 1640. The king attended the Parliament in a quiet and unostentatious manner. Strafford was left in command of the army at York during the Parliament. The Commons began to attack Laud and Strafford shortly after the opening of Parliament. The speakers condemned the government's actions during the intermission of Parliaments, blaming Strafford and Laud. The king hesitated about signing the bill of attainder against Strafford. Strafford was executed following the proceedings against him.

Rollo left the parcel his mother gave him on the other side of the brook. Rollo asked Jonas for advice on what to do after watching the fishes. Jonas suggested that Rollo build a wigwam, which is a small house made of bushes. Rollo chose a smooth spot under a great oak tree to build his wigwam. Rollo realized he left his hatchet on the other side of the brook and went to retrieve it. Jonas helped Rollo by trimming the bridge to make it easier to cross. Rollo used a piece of twine from his parcel to strike a circle for the wigwam.

The princess was prepared for her embarkation after much hesitation. The queen took leave of her mother at the palace without shedding tears. The princess was accompanied by a procession through the streets to the pier. The bridal party boarded a ship after salutes were fired by English ships. The fleet was unable to set sail on the first day due to contrary winds. Catharine wrote to Charles upon her arrival at Portsmouth, causing excitement in London. Charles delayed meeting Catharine for five days and was reportedly indifferent to the event.

source.author: Jacob Abbott
source.title: History of King Charles II of England

text: A lady's father was suspicious of her lover and took measures to keep her in sight. The lovers devised a plan to escape to Gretna Green during a dance. Mr. McDiarmid, a Scotch journalist, elicited stories from a Springfield priest over drinks. Priests in Springfield charged varying fees for marriage services, sometimes up to £100. Joseph Paisley married three couples from his deathbed and died with three hundred pounds. Gretna Green experienced a high volume of marriages, with fifty occurring monthly. A toll-keeper built a hotel to attract couples getting married at Gretna Green.

source.author: James Matthew Barrie
source.title: A Holiday in Bed and Other Sketches

text: Peter went to the young lady's chamber and threatened to open the curtains if she did not get up and dress. Wendy invited the boys to come with her, suggesting that she could get her parents to adopt them. The boys were excited about the invitation but were primarily thinking of themselves. Peter initially refused to go with Wendy and pretended to be indifferent. Wendy attempted to coax Peter into going by mentioning finding his mother. Peter expressed a desire to remain a little boy and have fun, rejecting the idea of finding a mother. Peter told the others that he was not coming, which made them doubt their decision to leave.

Granny signals to Barbara and the Colonel to leave. Barbara kisses the Colonel's hands before departing. The Colonel advises Barbara not to go to the alder pool. Barbara and her husband leave, and the Colonel expresses eagerness to hear his wife's opinion. The Colonel suggests cutting down the alder tree, stating there is no boy present. Ellen offers to read to the Colonel, who requests something funny. A woman speaks to her dead son in a dark room where a man sits quietly with an evening paper.

Sanders was known for his neat dress and rarely wore corduroys. Nanny was described as a slattern due to her heavy workload and lack of care for her appearance. Sanders often hinted that Nanny's slovenly ways troubled him, but she remained silent in public. Nanny earned the family's income through weaving, washing, and cooking, while Sanders was perceived as having a reputation for generosity. Sanders attended church regularly, while Nanny gradually stopped attending after their marriage. Nanny ceased to go to church because she lacked appropriate Sabbath clothes. The doctor discovered that Nanny had never been well during the last week of her life.

Margaret expresses confusion about the connection between her laugh and her father, Dearth. Dearth states that children's laughter lasts as long as they have perfect faith. Margaret recalls her earliest memory of seeing the stars. Dearth mentions that he wanted Margaret's earliest memory to be significant. A vagrant woman named Alice approaches Dearth and Margaret. Alice is searching for leftover food from tourists. Dearth gives Margaret a coin to help Alice, despite their financial situation.

The children were in bed while Mrs. Darling sewed by the fire. Mrs. Darling had bathed and sung to the children before they fell asleep. Mrs. Darling dreamed of a strange boy from Neverland while she slept. A boy named Peter Pan entered the nursery through the window accompanied by a strange light. Nana returned from her evening out and growled at Peter Pan as he leapt through the window. Mrs. Darling found Peter Pan's shadow after he left the nursery. Mrs. Darling decided to roll up the shadow and put it away in a drawer.

The speaker reflects on the state of a group facing dire conditions, including frozen feet and lack of food. The group has decided to die naturally rather than take their own lives despite their desperate situation. The speaker recalls a story about Scott and his comrades, comparing their enduring spirit to a youth lost in a glacier. The text mentions a legend told by explorer Nansen about a monk who became entranced by a lark's song, losing track of time. The monk discovered that he had been absent from the monastery for over a hundred years after listening to the lark. The narrative includes a reflection on a student at St. Andrews who feels a deep connection to beauty and life. The student is described as being somewhat isolated from his peers due to his unique perspective on life.

The character Miss Phoebe dances and expresses a desire to celebrate Waterloo. Miss Phoebe refers to herself as her niece while dancing. Captain Brown, also known as Valentine, mistakes Miss Phoebe for Miss Susan. Valentine brings a bottle of medicine for Miss Phoebe's headache. Miss Phoebe's father is Mr. James Throssel, who resides at Great Buckland. Valentine offers Miss Phoebe a chance to attend the ball with her Aunt Susan. Miss Phoebe expresses a wish to inspire admiration from gentlemen at the ball.

Sam'l Dickie is known in Lang Tammas's circle. Little Sanders is a coal-carter who is distinguished from his father by his name. Sam'l's mother named him Sam'l while he was still in his cradle. Sam'l Dickie wore a blue glengarry bonnet with a red ball on Saturday evening. Eppie Fargus was knitting stockings on an adjoining dyke. Sam'l has been courting Bell for a year or two. Eppie warned Sam'l about the potential consequences of his actions with Mysy Haggart.

Andrew caught Lord Randolph in the heel and carried away his shoe. Andrew's face struck the steps and he heard the word 'Fenian.' The president instructed Andrew to tie a muffler around his neck. Andrew held his thesis in his hand while discussing it with the president. The Society for Doing Without has been in existence for some years. Andrew proposed that everyone should die upon reaching the age of forty-five. Andrew criticized the current policies of the society and suggested that killing off parents would revolutionize the world.

Blackie sometimes instructed students to invite each other to tea instead of breakfast. The professor recommended a cold bath at six o'clock every morning. Only one student reportedly followed the professor's advice on cold baths, and he died. Blackie's classroom experienced demonstrations whenever he mentioned a distinguished politician. A notebook containing the professor's jokes was passed down among students each year. The Hellenic Club now takes the place of the classroom, with Blackie as the chair. A junior reporter who reviewed Professor Calderwood's book later attended Edinburgh University and ranked 144th in moral philosophy.

Crichton is on an island and is gathering firewood. Lady Mary expresses concern about the implications of equality. Crichton believes there must always be one to command and others to obey. Tweeny finds cocoa-nuts and shares her thoughts on their growth. Crichton reassures Tweeny that he will not give her up despite her vulgarity. Crichton attempts to kindle a fire using a lens from his watch. Ernest warns Crichton about a tiger-cat approaching.

Pettigrew has been married for years. Pettigrew's wife encourages his smoking. Pettigrew keeps cigars in a cupboard beneath a bookcase. Pettigrew's wife gives him cigars as birthday presents. Pettigrew pretends to smoke Celebros cigars. Pettigrew prefers Villar y Villar cigars over Celebros. Pettigrew's wife is unaware of his true smoking preferences.

The club requires a membership fee of thirty pounds. Members of the club pay extra for dinners, which cost five or six shillings. The club does not provide any benefits such as weekly allowances or free items. The committee that elects new members consists of about a dozen individuals. The narrator's mother expresses skepticism about the value of the club. The narrator's mother reacts with sarcasm upon learning of the narrator's election to the club.

The narrator observes a woman laughing, noting that her laugh resembles David's. The narrator believes the woman has influenced David's character since they first met. David is described as being easily lost when not guided, likened to an arrow. The woman is portrayed as anxious while watching David engage in risky activities. David holds a high admiration for the woman, believing she can help him attain heaven. The text discusses a specific time between six and seven when children assess their mothers. The narrator reflects on the challenges mothers face during this judgment hour.

The Emperor believes he has honored Culture and contributed to Germany's prosperity. Culture asserts that she is not bound to any single nation and has many homes, including France. The Emperor expresses a desire for Germany to expand and believes it is a divine mission. Culture warns the Emperor that jealousy, not love of money, is the root of all evil. The Emperor decides to sign a document to maintain peace, but ultimately tears it up. Culture returns to the Emperor, revealing the consequences of his actions and the devastation caused by war. The Emperor dreams of a peaceful Germany but is confronted by Culture about the reality of his decisions.

Maimie believed the Duke would choose her and warned her friend not to follow. Maimie saw a light made of glow-worms above a fairy ring. The Duke of Christmas Daisies appeared to be in love, as indicated by the reactions of the Queen and court. Peter Pan was late because his boat was stuck on the Serpentine in ice. The fairies were unable to dance due to their sadness. Brownie insisted on being presented to the Duke and was led before him. The doctor declared that the Duke was in love, causing excitement among the spectators.

source.author: James Matthew Barrie
source.title: Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens, Version 1

text: Amy is searching for someone and questions Richardson about her whereabouts. The little maid leaves the room while carrying dishes. Amy looks behind drawn curtains and finds no one there. Steve enters and is surprised to see a strange lady, addressing her as Alice. Amy refuses to disclose her name to Steve. Amy accuses Steve of having a secret regarding a woman who dined with him. Amy demands that Steve return her letters in exchange for keeping his secret.

Peter is a character who is central to the story and is associated with music. The princess's coming-of-age ball is celebrated on the second birthday and occurs every month thereafter. The Queen grants Peter a wish for playing beautifully, but he hesitates to choose what to wish for. Peter's first wish is to visit his mother, with the condition that he can return to the Gardens if he finds her disappointing. The fairies grant Peter the power to fly by tickling him on the shoulder. Peter flies over various landmarks before reaching his mother's window, which he finds open. Peter observes his mother while she sleeps and feels a connection to her.

source.author: James Matthew Barrie
source.title: Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens, Version 2

text: David has a respect for education and has purchased a library. Alick also respects education but struggles to read the Contemporary Review. James does not respect education, while Maggie has an open mind. David has raised his family members, Alick, James, and Maggie, to their current position. David is nearly forty years old and has a brisk manner. The family members share a resemblance and are described as having inquisitive blue eyes. David is preoccupied and does not engage with the game being played.

The whig wing of the cabinet, led by Lord Spencer, supported a modified renewal of the Coercion Act along with a land purchase bill and limited self-government. The radical wing opposed coercion and the purchase bill but was open to a milder form of coercion in exchange for a central board with significant administrative functions for Ireland. A strong radical contingent in the House of Commons was expected to resist any form of coercion. A liberal member of parliament indicated intentions to move for the rejection of any proposals for the renewal of exceptional law. Mr. Gladstone informed the Queen about the whig section's growing dislike for special legislation for Ireland. Mr. Gladstone expressed strong support for a Central Board of Local Government in Ireland during a conversation with Lord Granville. Mr. Gladstone indicated that he was prepared to resign if necessary, but he did not want to connect the Irish issue with his resignation.

source.author: John Morley
source.title: The Life of William Ewart Gladstone (Vol 3 of 3)

text: The text discusses the author's inclination to attend religious assemblies for the emotions of fellowship. It suggests that individuals without definite convictions may benefit from conforming to public beliefs. The author emphasizes the importance of individual conscience in matters of conformity and belief. The text mentions the author's constant reading of the Bible and the _Imitatio_. The author expresses a sense of loss regarding the inability to practice family prayer. The teaching of Comte influenced the author's ideas, providing them with systematization and definiteness. The author acknowledges the value of Wordsworth's work and its impact on her thoughts.

source.author: John Morley
source.title: Critical Miscellanies, Volume 3, Essay 4, The Life of George Eliot

text: Burke dated the significant events to the Sixth of October 1789. The moral authority of the sovereign ended on that day. The Count d'Artois fled after the insurrection of July 1789. Three hundred members of the Assembly sought to resign after the events of October. The people of Paris became the masters of France following the events of October. Robespierre's position changed as the people were recognized as sovereign. Robespierre opposed the property qualification for electors based on the principle of equality.

Two thousand unhappy individuals have struggled with their artistic endeavors. Parrocel is considered a dauber when compared to Vernet, but he possesses rare talent relative to many others. Diderot expresses that producing even mediocre art requires immense labor and patience. Diderot criticizes the occupation of criticism for its tendency to hinder enjoyment of art. Diderot does not spare criticism for Boucher, despite Boucher's popularity and income. Diderot acknowledges Boucher's skill but calls for more disciplined taste and variety in his work. Fragonard is mentioned in the context of the discussion about art and criticism.

Vauvenargues believed that the thought of death distracts from living fully. He was known for his meditative temperament, which distanced him from the libertinism of his time. Turgot was another prominent figure who could have countered the moral laxity of the era. Vauvenargues's approach to morality was characterized by delicacy and sympathy, unlike typical moralists. He emphasized sincerity in moral writing, criticizing authors for lacking authenticity. Vauvenargues's style was moderate and persuasive, contrasting with the hardness of La Rochefoucauld and La Bruyère. He had a tendency to overlook grandeur and originality if they were expressed too boldly.

The lectures were intended to provide a dogmatic exposition of the Positive Philosophy. The lectures attracted notable figures such as Humboldt, Poinsot, and Blainville. Comte experienced a severe attack of cerebral derangement after the third lecture. Comte was rescued after attempting to throw himself into the Seine during a period of profound melancholy. In 1828, Comte renewed his lectures, and the first volume of the Course of Positive Philosophy was published in 1830. Comte was appointed examiner for boys aspiring to enter the École Polytechnique in 1833. Comte proposed establishing a chair of general history of the sciences, which was initially welcomed but ultimately rejected.

source.author: John Morley
source.title: Critical Miscellanies, Volume 3, Essay 10, Auguste Comte

text: There are several distinct interpretations and meanings of evidence that can lead to different conclusions. Certain types of facts can only be proved in specific ways. It is important to know what one intends to show or dispute before starting an argument. Many argumentative objections can exist against a proposition, yet the balance may favor its adoption. Neglecting to practice attention on logical matters allows interest and prejudice to influence reasoning. A class for the study of Logic, Reasoning, and Evidence could be beneficial in educational institutions. Using legal instances as a medium for teaching practical logic could enhance understanding of the legal system.

source.author: John Morley
source.title: Critical Miscellanies, Volume 3, Essay 1, On Popular Culture

text: The Historic Method is often misrepresented by caricatures that people accept as true philosophy. The newspaper press influences public discussion by promoting low-level discourse and reinforcing prejudices. Removing taxes on knowledge is viewed as imposing a tax on independent opinion. The proliferation of journals contributes to a decline in individuality in public opinions. Material prosperity has increased while sincerity of spiritual interest has declined, creating a dual negative effect. New wealth often leads to a lack of public duty and a focus on luxury and ease. The pursuit of comfort tends to overshadow the pursuit of truth in societal values.

Shaftesbury's philosophical ideas influenced Diderot's notions on morals and art. Diderot appreciated Shaftesbury's optimistic harmony as a way to escape disordered theological concepts. Naturalistic religion was seen as a relief for those disillusioned by traditional religious practices. Voltaire praised Pope's Essay on Man, attributing its substance to Shaftesbury's Characteristics. Shaftesbury's philosophy aimed to make morality independent of religion and associated it with beauty and harmony. Diderot maintained the idea of virtue and goodness being inherent in human nature throughout his work. Diderot's writing, Promenade du Sceptique, was confiscated by a police agent and was not published until after his death.

Turgot believed that an oath, regardless of its importance, should not be treated lightly. Turgot rejected the idea that one could maintain a respectable public image while compromising personal integrity. He criticized the prevailing sophisms of his time that justified falsehood and hypocrisy. Turgot argued that individuals should not have to lie to protect themselves from societal punishment. He expressed that maintaining personal honesty is essential, regardless of societal expectations. Turgot's only public literary equivocation was in the letters titled _Le Conciliateur_, which advocated for religious toleration. Before gaining prominence, Turgot was recognized for his contributions to philosophical thought.

The text discusses the relationship between means and ends in moral and social contexts. It asserts that the means prepare the end and that the end is shaped by the means. The text identifies two sets of relations that require regulation through coercion: criminal individuals and nations. Criminal individuals are described as having unsocial propensities that threaten social order. Nations are characterized as being in a state of nature, bound by self-interest and material power. Mr. Carlyle is mentioned as having contributed to the understanding of these concepts in his historical work. The text emphasizes the need for moral relationships to evolve from the recognition of pathological necessities.

Condorcet was instructed by the Jesuits at Rheims and excelled in mathematics at the age of fifteen. Condorcet's curiosity extended beyond geometry and algebra to political sciences by the age of seventeen. Condorcet wrote essays on integral calculus while reflecting on human societies and moral obligations. Condorcet abandoned hunting due to his moral objections to inflicting pain on sentient creatures. Condorcet valued knowledge as a means to social action and prioritized social aims in his life. Condorcet expressed disappointment at having to shift from public labor to studying geometry. Condorcet remained alert to new ideas and developments that could promote virtue and justice in society.

Harriet Martineau had a scientific approach to social organization and its institutions. Martineau's writing focused on political economy and was characterized by rapid and clear storytelling. She moved from Norwich to London to gain a better understanding of England's social state. Martineau attended dinner parties in London and engaged with prominent individuals of her time. She maintained a critical and independent attitude towards society and its norms. Martineau expressed disdain for pretentiousness and the superficiality of certain literary figures.

source.author: John Morley
source.title: Critical Miscellanies, Volume 3, Essay 6, Harriet Martineau

text: De Maistre was familiar with the works of his philosophical opponents but held a strong antipathy towards them. De Maistre criticized the philosophers of the eighteenth century, claiming they lacked honesty and probity. He viewed Voltaire as a corrupting influence and associated admiration for him with divine disfavor. De Maistre expressed contempt for Locke, describing him as weak and lacking clarity in thought. He considered Hume to be particularly dangerous among the philosophers of the last century. De Maistre wrote a lengthy refutation of Bacon's ideas, criticizing his morality and intellectual integrity. He believed that his opponents were worse citizens than they were philosophers, which fueled his resentment.

source.author: John Morley
source.title: Critical Miscellanies, Volume 2, Essay 4, Joseph de Maistre

text: The Duke of Brunswick was compared to the Duke of Cumberland in the context of fighting for the crown of England. The French king and queen attempted to escape over the frontier, undermining confidence in their loyalty to the new order. Mirabeau stated that the new constitution was too democratic for a monarchy and had too many kings for a republic. Foreign intervention ultimately led to the downfall of the French monarchy and the hope for an orderly resolution. In the spring of 1792, France declared war in response to the invasion preparations by Austria and Prussia. The French people associated the monarchy with the foreign enemy, leading to distrust in the king's loyalty. The manifesto issued by the Duke of Brunswick incited a violent response from the people of Paris on the 10th of August.

The Assembly was characterized by a predominance of plain sylvan strength and earnestness. From 1820 to 1844, New England experienced a general criticism and attack on institutions. Calvinists and Quakers began to split into old school and new school during this period. Swedenborg's speculations began to influence the minds of thousands, including Emerson. Geology and astronomy contributed to a shift in understanding regarding divine justice and the universe. A temper of scrutiny and dissent emerged, prompting individuals to question conformity and its legitimacy. Various movements arose proposing radical changes in agriculture, diet, and social institutions.

The text discusses the combination of two ingredients that are salutary when separated but produce a poisonous compound when combined. The first ingredient is the significant advancements in physical science during the eighteenth century. The second ingredient is the fixed classic form of French intelligence. The classic spirit applied to scientific advancements produced the philosophy of the century and the doctrines of the Revolution. Classicism is characterized by the exclusion of particulars and the preference for general, vague, and typic representations. The text argues that the revolutionary movement in literature began with the breakdown of classic form and spirit. Rousseau and Diderot are noted for their contributions to literature that rejected classicism.

source.author: John Morley
source.title: Critical Miscellanies, Volume 3, Essay 8, France in the Eighteenth Century

text: Johnson advised someone to focus on their own affairs and not concern themselves with Corsica. At the end of 1765, Rousseau was in Paris instead of Motiers, prompting a letter from a devoted admirer. The admirer expressed gratitude to Rousseau for sending them to Corsica and claimed the experience was beneficial. Rousseau's interest in Corsica diminished due to personal issues and rumors about his invitation to help the islanders. France acquired Corsica from the Genoese senate in 1768, which Rousseau criticized as unjust. The condemnation of Rousseau by the Council in 1762 led to a political division in Geneva between his supporters and opponents. The conflict in Geneva was rooted in political issues rather than theological ones, with ongoing tensions between popular and aristocratic factions.

The elder Mill maintained an undiminished interest in life and his convictions on religion until his death. His principal satisfaction was the thought of improving the world, while his chief regret was not having more time to do so. Mr. Mill believed in the possibility of happiness and did not consider human life to be poor for those who know how to make the best of it. He identified tranquillity and some excitement as essential components of a satisfied life, attainable by many individuals. Hindrances to happiness include ignorance, bad laws or customs, and the positive evils of life such as poverty and disease. Mr. Mill learned from Turgot and Condorcet about the improvability of the human condition and the potential for progress. He believed that many sources of human suffering are conquerable through human care and effort, despite the slow pace of change.

The speaker proposes a toast in support of a policy that requires whole-hearted support from the service. An Indian gentleman has been appointed to the Council of the Viceroy, which is noted as a significant event. Two Indians were previously appointed to the Council of India at Whitehall. The Councils Act has been passed through Parliament in the last six to eight months. Nine Indian gentlemen were arrested on December 13 under a law from 1818 and are currently detained. A Bill has been introduced in the House of Commons that criticizes the policies of the speaker and Lord Minto. Historical comparisons have been made regarding the Secretary of State's actions, referencing figures such as King Charles I and Cromwell.

John was a clerk who had a considerable sum of money belonging to other people. John entrusted a letter with bonds to a fellow-clerk who had a drinking problem. The fellow-clerk became heavily intoxicated and was ejected from the boarding-house. The fellow-clerk ended up in a hospital in Sacramento and was unconscious for several days. John was identified as the absconding clerk two months later, but his letter remained unopened. John went on holiday without informing anyone and was later found to have amassed a large sum of money. The bank's correspondent in Edinburgh was alerted about John's disappearance and scandal.

source.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
source.title: The Works of Robert Louis Stevenson - Swanston Edition, Volume 10

text: The narrator describes a green gloaming environment while stepping off onto the PIERRES PERDUES of the foundation. A helmeted figure takes the narrator by the hand and gestures encouragement. The narrator sees Bain's face through a window, indicating a connection between them despite being in separate worlds. Bob is working with another diver to settle a stone of the sea-wall when he notices his companion in distress. The companion is trapped under fifteen tons of rock, causing him pain. The narrator learns about the effects of water density on weight and agility during their submarine experience. The narrator experiences a sensation of weightlessness while attempting to leap onto a stone, aided by Bob.

The town is situated between Mulinuu to the west and Matautu to the east. Mulinuu is described as a flat promontory with a village and is the residence of the Samoan kings. The village of Mulinuu is noted to be the property of a German firm. The walk from Mulinuu to Matautu includes passing through Matafele, which has German businesses and a Catholic mission. The bridge of Mulivai serves as a frontier between Matafele and Apia proper. The walk features various nationalities, including American and English merchants, and a significant presence of sailors. The native population is described as living in a foreign town, with few visible native houses along the beach.

source.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
source.title: The Works of Robert Louis Stevenson - Swanston Edition, Volume 17

text: The neutral territory and tripartite municipality of Apia were viewed negatively by the German consulate and Brandeis. Becker admitted to landing Tamasese's warriors at Mulinuu, which violated treaties. Sewall protested twice against the landing of Tamasese's warriors. Becker's strategy involved seating a puppet king under German colors to frame any rebellion as a war against Germany. Otto Martin was serving as magistrate in the municipality beyond his term, which should have been succeeded by an American. Becker refused to attend municipal meetings when Sewall sought Martin's removal, effectively suspending the municipality. On October 10th, a chief Tamaseu was arrested and later released by Sewall after a bail request was denied by Martin.

Mrs. Ogilvy mentions James More as a kinsman of hers. Mrs. Ogilvy expresses a negative opinion about James More. Catrine is described as a good-hearted lass who is influenced by her father. The narrator, Davit Balfour, has met Catrine once and saw her again from a window. Mrs. Ogilvy questions Davit Balfour's intentions and identity. Mrs. Ogilvy initially suspects Davit Balfour of being a spy. Mrs. Ogilvy comments on Davit Balfour's lack of understanding of women.

The text includes various poems and illustrations. The speaker expresses a desire to find a soldier who remains silent. The poem 'Autumn Fires' describes the transition from summer to autumn. The gardener is depicted as serious and uninterested in conversation. The poem 'Historical Associations' references battles and adventures in a garden setting. The speaker addresses cousins Willie and Henrietta, reminiscing about childhood play. The speaker also addresses their mother, recalling memories of the past.

source.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
source.title: A Child's Garden of Verses, Verse 154

text: The drum is noted for its martial voice and physiological effect. Drums are often covered with asses' skin, which is described as an irony. The text discusses the historical use of donkey skin for drums in military contexts. The narrator mentions that people in Landrecies had shown interest in their boats. The Juge de Paix invited the narrator and companions to dinner at his home. The Judge's house is described as well-appointed with a collection of old brass warming-pans. The wine served by the Judge was praised as excellent.

The letter discussed exhibits profound goodness and tenderness. The author conveys a sober truthfulness about Frank without exaggeration. Whitman's style is characterized by rough, unrhymed, lyrical verse. Whitman believes in breaking down the barriers between prose and poetry. His verses are referred to as 'recitatives' in reference to a musical form. Whitman's writing contains a mix of plain grandeur, sentimental affectation, and nonsense. The challenge of showing beauty in common things is noted as a rare talent.

source.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
source.title: The Works of Robert Louis Stevenson - Swanston Edition, Volume 3

text: Robert Louis Stevenson mentions the arrival of the first mosquito of the season. Stevenson planned to return to Edinburgh by the last week of May. A member of the Russian party in Mentone tried to persuade Stevenson to study law under Professor Jhering at Göttingen. Stevenson describes the weather in Mentone as beautiful and his health as very good. Stevenson has philosophical discussions with a Prince who talks extensively about his theories. Stevenson expresses sadness about leaving a dear friend in Mentone. Stevenson plans to attend a course of lectures in Göttingen during the summer.

source.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
source.title: The Works of Robert Louis Stevenson - Swanston Edition, Volume 23

text: Fleeming was interested and keen to help his children with their projects. He encouraged his children to understand scientific principles and to complete their work thoroughly. Fleeming assisted his son Frewen in building a toy steamboat, starting with a proper drawing. Fleeming dedicated time to play with his children, ensuring it did not interfere with his work. Frewen and Bernard engaged in various scientific experiments and projects, including soap-bubbles and parachutes. The boys enjoyed riding and shared their adventures, discussing their experiences with horses. Fleeming expressed appreciation for his sons' contributions and maintained a supportive relationship with them.

source.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
source.title: The Works of Robert Louis Stevenson - Swanston Edition, Volume 9

text: The text discusses the duality of human nature, suggesting that man is not truly one but rather two distinct entities. The author reflects on their scientific studies, which led them to explore the mystic and transcendental aspects of consciousness. The author expresses a desire for the separation of the two natures within themselves to alleviate the struggles of consciousness. The text mentions the burden of life that is inescapable for mankind, which cannot be cast off without returning with greater pressure. The author describes their discovery of a drug that could alter their identity and control their dual nature. The author acknowledges the risks associated with testing their theory, including the potential for death. Wolf tries to seek comfort from Madge after failing to get a response from the men. Wolf feels neglected and depressed by the lack of attention from the humans. Wolf waits for Skiff Miller to reappear after he goes out of view.

source.author: Jack London
source.title: Love of Life and Other Stories

text: The narrator and Lop-Ear encountered Saber-Tooth in the forest early in the morning. They followed Saber-Tooth from the safety of the branches and made noise to warn other forest-dwellers. The narrator and Lop-Ear engaged in tiger-baiting, which was common among their group. They chased Saber-Tooth across three miles of forest until he fled from them. The narrator and Lop-Ear ventured across open ground to the edge of the rocky hills. They discovered three wild dog puppies playing in the sun near their lair. The narrator and Lop-Ear captured two of the puppies, realizing the danger of tampering with wild animals' young.

The Yukon was covered by three feet of ice. The weather was sharp and clear, with a gray sky and no sun visible. At a quarter before twelve, the sun appeared above the horizon but did not rise perpendicularly. Daylight and Kama had irregular eating habits, sometimes gorging and sometimes going without food. The dogs ate once a day, rarely receiving more than a pound of dried fish each. By three in the afternoon, the twilight faded into night, and stars became visible. Daylight and Kama were on the first day of a sixty-day journey.

Sheldon experienced loneliness and frequently checked the sea for the whale-boat. The loss of the _Jessie_ significantly impacted Berande's capital and plantation expenses. Pete Oleson, the skipper of the _Flibberty-Gibbet_, was suffering from fever and declined to go to Sydney. Oleson expressed a desire to return to his home country but believed he would not survive there. Joan arrived at the beach in a whale-boat during a heavy squall and was cheerful despite the weather. Joan planned to buy Pari-Sulay and had already selected a site for her bungalow. Sheldon and Joan agreed to avoid future arguments during their dinner together.

The text discusses a specific portion of the Salvation Army located on Blackfriars Road near the Surrey Theatre. Men in the crowd were forced to stand for hours despite being weak, famished, and exhausted. A significant number of men in the crowd were American sailors looking for ships. American sailors often desert their ships in the New World due to low wages and poor treatment. English ships sign sailors for the entire voyage, which can last up to three years, preventing them from signing off until they reach England. The crowd included both American sailors and non-sailors, with the latter referred to as 'tramps royal.' One American tramp royal was noted for his distinctive hat and had traveled through several European countries.

The island of Talofa means love and is referred to as the Isle of Love. The king of Talofa is an old man who drinks squareface gin out of grief. The princess of Talofa is named Tui-nui and is the only child of the king. The princess's brother was lost in a hurricane while returning from a voyage to Samoa. Among the Polynesians, royal women have equal rights with men to rule and trace their genealogies by the female line. Percival Delaney describes his romantic experiences with Princess Tui-nui, highlighting her elusive nature. Percival Delaney recounts his past prowess in swimming and squidding while trying to impress the princess.

Peter Tonsburg was running the boat _Chill III_ when he was caught and fired by the East Coast outfit. Mr. Frisbie is safe at the Southern Hotel with a five-inch scalp wound from a brick. Peter agreed to help after learning that Miss Drexel was in Panuco town. The _Topila_ is a federal gunboat that opened fire on the _Chill_. The constitutionalists on the north shore also fired at the _Chill_ with rifles and a machine gun. Peter estimated they would reach Panuco town in less than three hours if they did not hit a log. The _Chill II_ was steered by Peter, who was familiar with the river's layout.

The chronometer had a losing error of seven-tenths of a second when the journey began from Hawaii. The chronometer unexpectedly accelerated and caught up with itself by three minutes. Henry developed rheumatism in his back during the voyage. The Snark was forty-three feet on the water-line and fifty-five feet overall. The Snark was ketch-rigged and carried multiple sails including a flying-jib and spinnaker. The Snark was partly built in San Francisco and was delayed by six months due to anarchy. The Snark was libelled in San Francisco and fined for breach of quarantine in the Solomons.

Dorothy Sambrooke spent a month in the tropics, engaging in activities such as riding horses, climbing volcanoes, and learning surf swimming. During this time, she was in the company of Stephen Knight, an athlete and surf-board rider. Dorothy was unaware of the changes in her feelings towards Steve, who had been her playfellow. Steve exhibited a different demeanor during their goodbye, appearing excited and disconnected. Dorothy noticed a new intensity in Steve's gaze, which she found both terrifying and alluring. The transport's whistle signaled the departure, prompting a crowd to gather at the dock. Steve had previously entertained a Senatorial party by demonstrating surf riding at Waikiki Beach.

The militia shall consist of every able-bodied male citizen of the respective states, territories, and District of Columbia, who is more than eighteen and less than forty-five years of age. Any enlisted man of the militia who refuses or neglects to present himself to a mustering officer when called shall be subject to trial by court martial. Courts martial for the trial of militia officers or men shall be composed of militia officers only. The militia, when called into actual service, shall be subject to the same rules and articles of war as regular troops of the United States. The bill was introduced in the House of Representatives on June 30, 1902, by Representative Dick of Ohio. The bill was passed unanimously by the Senate on January 14, 1903, and approved by the President of the United States seven days later. E. Untermann published a pamphlet on the 'Militia Bill' in July 1903, which had a small circulation among workingmen.

The text discusses the concepts of strength and weakness in relation to personal pleasure and profit. The speaker argues that one cannot wrong another person, only oneself. Altruism is defined as an act performed for the welfare of others, contrasting with selfish acts. Wolf Larsen acknowledges having read some of Herbert Spencer's works, particularly _Data of Ethics_. Larsen summarizes Spencer's view that a man must act for his own benefit, then for his children, and lastly for his race. Larsen rejects the idea of acting for the benefit of his race and children, viewing it as unnecessary sentiment. The speaker reflects on the implications of immortality on the concept of altruism.

The scene takes place on a ship where Dag Daughtry, a steward, is involved in a dispute with Captain Duncan over a dog. Captain Duncan accuses Daughtry of stealing the dog and suggests that Daughtry's accomplice helped the dog board the ship. Daughtry refuses to give up the dog, arguing that it would be detrimental to his reputation as a captain to be involved in dog theft. Captain Duncan offers ten pounds for the dog, but Daughtry declines, mentioning a cat in Sydney that needs a home. Daughtry teaches the dog, Michael, a trick that impresses Captain Duncan, leading him to offer fifty pounds for the dog. During a demonstration, Michael does not recognize Daughtry and reacts aggressively towards him, prompting Daughtry to express his anger. Daughtry claims that the trick he performed is one he has heard about but never seen executed before.

Draper states that Italy lost 15,000,000 people during the Gothic war. The reign of Justinian is said to have diminished the human species by 100,000,000 due to wars, famines, and pestilences. Germany lost 6,000,000 inhabitants during the Thirty Years' War. In 1886, the bursting of the dikes of the Yellow River resulted in the drowning of 7,000,000 people. The famines in India during 1896-97 and 1899-1900 caused a population decrease of 21,000,000. In the United States, between 30,000 and 35,000 worker deaths occurred due to accidents in 1908. The current global population is approximately 1.75 billion.

source.author: Jack London
source.title: The Human Drift and Other Stories

text: The Nishinam people keep their young warm with deer-skin and campfire. The Modoc frequently come against the Nishinam in strength. The strength of the Nishinam is derived from the collective strength of all its members. Red Cloud emphasizes the importance of kindness among the Nishinam. Dew-Woman and Red Cloud express their love and connection through a mating song. The War Chief believes that councils of men should not include women. Red Cloud argues that as men grow in kindness and wisdom, women should also grow and be included in councils.

Genevieve felt a conflict between her desire to express love and a sense of sin associated with physical affection. Joe experienced a desire to hurt Genevieve, which was contrary to his nature. Joe's intention in physical confrontations was never to cause harm, but rather to win the match. Genevieve found a mix of surprise and pain in Joe's embrace, which left her feeling both delighted and aware of sin. Mrs. Silverstein expressed strong disapproval of Joe Fleming, referring to him as a prize-fighter. Genevieve was shocked to learn that Joe was a prize-fighter, as it contradicted her perception of him. Silverstein defended Joe, arguing that he was a good boy who made and saved money.

Buck was found by Thornton, who discovered he had three broken ribs. Thornton decided to camp until Buck's ribs healed. During winter in Dawson, Buck performed a notable exploit that increased his fame. A conversation at the Eldorado Saloon led to a wager about Buck's strength. Matthewson bet a thousand dollars that Buck could not start a sled with a thousand pounds. Thornton borrowed a thousand dollars from Jim O'Brien to accept the wager. The sled with a thousand pounds of flour was frozen to the ground, complicating the challenge.

The old man and the boy observed a bear from a distance. The boy indicated for the old man to step aside from the trail. The boy expressed excitement about the bear, referring to it as 'a big un.' The old man reminisced about a time when bears were rare and people visited the area in large numbers. The boy produced a silver dollar and asked the old man about money. The old man identified the coin as minted in 2012 and recalled historical events. The boy successfully hunted a rabbit and handed it to the old man.

Graham commented on the value of a horse and its breeding potential. Dick mentioned that breeders offered him thirty-five thousand dollars for the horse last year. Paula is described as tough and has never had accidents. Dick and Paula have been married for ten or a dozen years. The lunch was a stag event while the women were engaged in a separate activity. Graham was captivated by the image of Paula against the backdrop of a swimming stallion. Dick Forrest arrived just after the second gong to initiate cocktails.

source.author: Jack London
source.title: The Little Lady of the Big House

text: Dough and Slim sent younger men to buy alcohol. The group consumed a large quantity of beer and cheap wine. The group was arrested by constables after a drinking event. The group was taken to court the following morning. Judge Sol Glenhart presided over the court proceedings. L. C. Randolph was questioned about his occupation as a newspaper man. Randolph was sentenced to sixty days in prison for local color in his work.

The hangman entered the prison with a bag. The prisoners experienced fear and remorse throughout the night. The warders observed the prisoners praying, despite them not having prayed before. Phantoms and grotesque figures appeared to the prisoners during the night. The prisoners felt a sense of guilt and fear as they awaited their fate. At six o'clock, the prisoners cleaned their cells. At seven o'clock, the Lord of Death entered the prison.

Charity is viewed as degrading and demoralizing. It is considered immoral to use private property to alleviate the evils caused by private property. Socialism aims to eliminate poverty and improve living conditions for all members of society. Under Socialism, individual prosperity and happiness are expected to be shared among all members of the community. Individualism is seen as necessary for the full development of life, beyond what Socialism can provide. The existence of private property allows some individuals to develop a limited form of Individualism. The poor are often forced into degrading work due to lack of private property and are viewed as less important in society.

source.author: Oscar Wilde
source.title: Miscellaneous Aphorisms; The Soul of Man

text: The text discusses themes of love, nature, and immortality. It describes how love influences the natural world, such as flowers and animals. The speaker expresses a desire for a connection with nature after death. Imagery of various flowers and animals is used to convey emotions and experiences. The text suggests that love is essential for the beauty and vitality of nature. It portrays a vision of unity with the universe and eternal life through nature. The poem 'Impression--Le Reveillon' describes a dawn scene with vivid imagery.

The future Individualism will develop through joy. Christ did not attempt to reconstruct society and preached Individualism that could only be realized through pain or solitude. Mediaevalism is characterized by a worship of pain and self-torture, which is seen as real Christianity. The Renaissance introduced ideals of beauty and joy that conflicted with Christ's message. In modern Russia, pain is often necessary for self-realization, especially for artists. The modern world seeks to eliminate poverty and suffering through Socialism and Science. The new Individualism aims for a harmonious existence where man can live fully and perfectly without causing harm to others.

The Man claims to have performed miracles similar to those attributed to another figure. The Man is judged by God in the House of Judgment. God accuses the Man of living an evil life and showing cruelty to those in need. The Man acknowledges God's accusations and admits to his wrongdoings. God states that the Man has repaid good with evil and has betrayed those who helped him. God decides to send the Man to Hell as a consequence of his actions. The Man asserts that he has always lived in Hell.

Pearl is described as having a blue vein's tapestry and a breast that sways like a wind-stirred lily. Pigeons spread their wings as a bright car soars into the sky, passing over the Aegean. Venus acknowledges the loss of a fair maid from her retinue and instructs her servants to carve a cedar chest. The cedar chest is intended to hold the bodies of the maid and is located where olive trees grow near Paphos. Queen Venus prays to Proserpine for a favor to allow Desire to cross Charon's icy ford. Young Charmides is found lying by a Lethaean well, plucking blossoms from the asphodel. Charmides experiences a moment of intimacy with a figure that approaches him, leading to a passionate encounter.

The author believes that additional height in shoes is necessary for wearing long gowns in the street. The author criticizes modern high-heeled boots for only adding height to the heel and not to the sole. The author compares modern high-heeled boots to the clogs of the time of Henry VI, noting their design flaws. The author acknowledges the artistic value of clogs and suggests they can be both beautiful and comfortable. The author discusses the divided skirt and its decorative elements, viewing them as unnecessary and counterproductive to ease of movement. The author agrees with Mr. Wentworth Huyshe that Greek dress is not suited to the climate but believes modifications can be made. The author cites Mr. E. W. Godwin's work on dress, emphasizing that principles of Greek dress can be adapted for modern use.

Little Hans walked for three hours before arriving at the Doctor's house. The Miller's son fell from a ladder and requested the Doctor's assistance. The Doctor rode off to the Miller's house with little Hans following behind. Little Hans lost his way in a storm and drowned in a moor. His body was found the next day by goatherds and returned to the cottage. The Miller was the chief mourner at little Hans' funeral. The story concludes with a discussion about the moral of the tale.

source.author: Oscar Wilde
source.title: The Happy Prince and Other Tales

text: The Violets remarked that the little Dwarf was extremely plain. The old Sundial had once told the time to Emperor Charles V. The Peacock agreed with the Sundial's statement about social status. The Birds liked the little Dwarf despite his ugliness. The Dwarf had been kind to the Birds during a harsh winter. The Lizards took a fancy to the Dwarf and played with him. The Flowers were annoyed at the behavior of the Birds and Lizards.

GUIDO expresses that a certain man is not worthy of attention and describes him as an eloquent fool. BIANCA wishes for Death to take the man mentioned by GUIDO. SIMONE advises against speaking of Death in a merry house and reflects on the nature of marriage and infidelity. SIMONE acknowledges his aging and desires to enjoy the present evening. GUIDO declines to play the lute that night, suggesting a more private moment with BIANCA. SIMONE insists on the power of music to uplift the soul and encourages GUIDO to play. SIMONE comments on a stain on the cloth and discusses the qualities of wine from Naples and Tuscany.

The speaker expresses a sense of unworthiness and a lack of right to feel happy. The speaker reflects on their mission of helping the poor, despite not feeling it was their true calling. The speaker believes that the sick and dying do not judge the purity of those who care for them. The speaker has a deep emotional connection to Gerald, which they attribute to their own disgrace. Gerald expresses surprise at the depth of his mother's love for him and vows to be a better son. Hester urges the speaker to leave Gerald's father and suggests there are better places to live. Gerald expresses disdain for his father and struggles with the decision of what to do next.

Prince Paul presents two documents: a proclamation from the Czar and a plan of the Winter Palace. The group discusses the urgency of their plans, indicating that action must be taken that night. Michael expresses skepticism about the Czar's intentions and suggests that the Czar would not have kept his crown if he truly cared for the people. The President reads from the group's rules and declares that Alexis, the Czar, is guilty. The group unanimously decides that the penalty for Alexis is death and prepares to act that night. Vera argues against killing Alexis, stating he has risked his life for the group and is not a tyrant. The President and others counter Vera's defense, labeling Alexis a traitor.

Willie Hughes is connected with Shakespeare's plays and is noted for his immortality through them. Shakespeare's works suggest that Willie Hughes had a significant impact on his audience. Willie Hughes is described as having mastery over dramatic art in Shakespeare's A Lover's Complaint. Thomas Knell recounts that William Hewes played music for the Earl of Essex the night before his death. The name Hews is associated with music and the stage in Elizabethan literature. The first English actress was Margaret Hews, who was loved by Prince Rupert. There is speculation about Willie Hughes's death and his potential travels to Germany to perform.

source.author: Oscar Wilde
source.title: Lord Arthur Savile's Crime and Other Stories

text: The text describes the emotional state of men awaiting execution in prison. The prisoners experience feelings of guilt and fear as they await their fate. The execution is scheduled for eight o'clock, which is referred to as the stroke of Fate. The Chaplain does not attend the execution due to his emotional distress. The prisoners are released from their cells and observe the sky with sadness. Some prisoners feel they deserve to be executed more than the man who is actually being hanged. The text reflects on the nature of sin and its consequences.

The setting is a seaside resort in Sussex. Jack was found in a hand-bag at Victoria Station. The hand-bag was given to Mr. James or Thomas Cardew in mistake for his own. Lady Bracknell advises Jack to acquire relations and produce at least one parent. Jack claims he can produce the hand-bag at any moment. Lady Bracknell refuses to allow her daughter to marry someone associated with a cloak-room. Algernon expresses a disdain for relations and finds them tedious.

The art of a civilization may not accurately reflect the true nature of its people or their society. The decline of the Roman Empire was not solely due to the vices of Tiberius or the virtues of the Antonines. Abstract and ideal arts are suggested to better express the spirit of an age than imitative arts. Imitative arts may only represent the styles of individual artists or specific schools rather than the actual appearance of people from that time. The portrayal of Japanese people in art is described as a deliberate creation by artists rather than an accurate representation of reality. The actual appearance of Japanese people is compared to that of ordinary English people, lacking extraordinary features. Experiencing Japanese art is suggested to be more about understanding the style than visiting Japan.
