Charles Baudelaire stated that the heart contains passion while the imagination contains poetry. Theophile Gautier emphasized that everyone is affected by a sunrise or sunset. The distinction of the artist lies in their ability to render nature rather than just feel it. Art maintains a separate realm from real life, which is essential for aesthetic charm and great imaginative work. The artist can draw from all of history and existence, selecting what is beneficial for their spirit. True artists exclude harsh or disturbing subjects from their work, focusing instead on beauty. Keats exemplified the spirit of artistic choice, particularly in his work ODE ON A GRECIAN URN.

The scene takes place in the Library of Lord Goring's house. Phipps is the butler who is known for his impassivity and has been called the Ideal Butler. Lord Goring enters wearing evening dress, a silk hat, and an Inverness cape. Lord Goring discusses fashion and self-love with Phipps. Lord Goring receives three letters from Phipps. One letter is from Lady Chiltern, written on pink notepaper, expressing her trust and desire to see him. Lord Goring contemplates the implications of Lady Chiltern's letter and his plans for the evening.

Virginia expresses a lack of interest in America due to its absence of ruins and curiosities. The Ghost reveals that he has not slept for three hundred years and feels lonely and unhappy. Virginia shows compassion towards the Ghost, asking if he has a place to sleep. The Ghost describes a beautiful garden beyond the pine-woods, which he refers to as the Garden of Death. Virginia recognizes the garden as the Garden of Death and reflects on the beauty of death. The Ghost shares an old prophecy that requires Virginia to weep for his sins and pray for his soul. Virginia decides to ask the angel of death to have mercy on the Ghost.

For Love of the King is a masque written by Oscar Wilde. The masque was invented in 1894 as a personal gift to Mrs. Chan Toon. Mrs. Chan Toon was previously known as Miss Mabel Cosgrove and was related to the King of Burma through her marriage. The masque was not published until after Mrs. Chan Toon's death and following an arrangement with its owner. The principal characters of the play include King Meng Beng, U. Rai Gyan Thoo, and Shah Mah Phru. The setting of the play is the palace of the King of Burma during the Sixteenth Century. The first act takes place in the Hall of a Hundred Doors.

A Fair Penitent is a story by Wilkie Collins that first appeared in Charles Dickens' magazine, Household Words, on July 18, 1857. The story was published anonymously but was attributed to Wilkie Collins by Anne Lohrli through her analysis of the magazine's financial accounts. Charles Pineau Duclos was a French writer who lived during the first half of the eighteenth century and served as secretary to the French Academy. Mademoiselle Gautier was a French actress who later became a Carmelite nun and is described as having a handsome appearance and a violent temper. Mademoiselle Gautier had a significant romantic relationship with actor Quinault Dufresne, which ended when he cooled towards her after she mentioned marriage. After the end of her relationship with Dufresne, Mademoiselle Gautier fell into deep melancholy and abandoned her previous life to become a nun. The narrative of Mademoiselle Gautier's conversion is considered of particular interest for the study of human nature.

Small creatures, possibly cats or rabbits, escaped from a laboratory. A large dog, limping and injured, also escaped and attempted to approach its master. The master threatened the dog and it left, disappearing into darkness. The master stood alone, captivated by the stars, before returning to the laboratory after hearing a railway whistle. The servant, feeling guilty about his master's actions, was troubled by the fate of the injured dog. A fire broke out in the laboratory, leading to suspicions of incendiarism and suicide during an inquest. The jury ultimately ruled the death as misadventure despite evidence suggesting foul play.

Leah and William discuss the idea of writing a book based on their experiences. William expresses concern about their lack of experience in writing for publication. Leah believes that many people succeed in writing despite initial inexperience. Leah suggests consulting a doctor as an arbitrator to settle their doubts about the project. The doctor supports Leah's plan and encourages them to proceed with writing the book. The doctor offers to help by showing their completed work to the editor of a local newspaper. Leah realizes she has not thought of a title for the book, which the doctor emphasizes is important.

Lady Clarinda expresses surprise about Mrs. Beauly. Mr. Dexter is known for mystifying people and misleading them. Helena Beauly's adventures are mentioned in connection with Mr. Dexter. Lady Clarinda has a maid named Phoebe who speaks foreign languages. Helena Beauly was staying at a place near Edinburgh called Gleninch. Helena was engaged to dine with friends visiting Edinburgh while a masked ball was occurring. Mr. Macallan disapproved of the masked ball, believing it compromised a lady's reputation.

Miss Rachel and the Moonstone are at a dead-lock. Mr. Seegrave is struggling to investigate the theft of the Diamond. Samuel, the footman, and the narrator's daughter knew where the Diamond was kept. The narrator believes that all servants may have known where the Diamond was located. Rosanna Spearman is considered trustworthy by the narrator. Superintendent Seegrave examined the servants' characters but found no useful information. Penelope, the narrator's daughter, felt accused by Superintendent Seegrave after her second questioning.

The doctor asked if there was anyone staying with the household besides the regular members. The doctor inquired if Mr. Philip Dunboyne had made any enemies since living in the town. The doctor stated that he has made a discovery indicating that someone is trying to poison Mr. Dunboyne. The doctor advised that Mr. Dunboyne should be taken to the hospital for his safety. Mr. Philip Dunboyne expressed a desire to see Euneece before he dies. The narrator felt unable to face Helena due to the situation. Mr. Dunboyne threatened to haunt the narrator if she refused to let him see Euneece.

The girl expresses a longing for happiness and companionship in a beautiful world. She feels grief and pain due to her father's restrictions on her happiness. The girl fears death because she has not yet found the happiness she believes is meant for her. Hermanric offers the girl warmth, food, and protection after witnessing her distress. The girl feels gratitude towards Hermanric for his kindness. She reveals that she was expelled from her home by her father in anger. The girl hesitates to share the details of her past due to an instinctive sense of caution.

Arnold warns Anne about Mistress Inchbare's inquiry regarding her husband. Anne feels compelled to accept the landlady's correction and refers to Arnold as her husband. Mistress Inchbare expresses relief after Anne's response and waits for further conversation. Arnold assists Anne in leaving the room and assures her he will handle the situation. Anne requests water after feeling faint, but none is available on the table. Mr. Bishopriggs brings water and informs them about a group of gentlemen on horseback nearby. One of the gentlemen has inquired about the lady who arrived alone at the inn.

Captain Stanwick claims Bertha as his promised wife without her justification. Bertha expresses her intention to marry Mr. Varleigh instead of Captain Stanwick. Bertha's aunt believes both gentlemen are in love with her and expresses concern about the situation. Mr. Varleigh has left the hotel due to a disagreement with Captain Stanwick. Captain Stanwick confronts Bertha about her feelings for Mr. Varleigh. Bertha denies giving Captain Stanwick any reason to claim her affections. Bertha's aunt intervenes during Captain Stanwick's confrontation to demand he alter his tone.

The narrator expresses trust in a person despite concerns about being distrusted. The narrator decides to reply to a letter in person rather than in writing. The narrator consults his watch to ensure he can return before dinner. The narrator encounters a kitchen-maid while crossing a glade in Fordwitch Wood. The kitchen-maid informs the narrator that he mistakenly took her for a stranger. The narrator finds the Lodger at the cottage with a handkerchief covering his face. The Lodger instructs the narrator to wait in the boat-house before he approaches.

A lady asked Monkton if he had ever seen his uncle's ghost, which he responded to with a scowl. The lady fainted at Monkton's reaction, leading to a scene of hysterics. Monkton is referred to as 'Mad Monkton' and is considered a privileged lunatic in Neapolitan society. Monkton is English, good-looking, and has an income of thirty thousand a year. Monkton frequently inquires about the location of a mysterious duel. During a conversation, Monkton expressed regret for his past behavior towards the narrator. The narrator and Monkton developed a friendship, enjoying rides and sailing together.

The character expresses joy and a sense of youthfulness while enjoying nature. The character rolls down a bank, reminiscent of childhood behavior, while a dog plays with him. Old Sharon engages Isabel in conversation about Lady Lydiard. Moody observes that Old Sharon is not paying attention to Isabel's story. Old Sharon abruptly asks Isabel about sealing Lady Lydiard's letter, interrupting her narrative. Isabel decides to explain how she sealed the letter, believing it is relevant to their discussion. Old Sharon shows signs of distraction during Isabel's explanation and attempts to set another trap.

The narrator hears a door close and then feels a match-box on a table beside Margaret. The narrator strikes a match and notices a second locked door in the room. The narrator suspects a stranger has approached Margaret while the room was dark. The narrator resolves to prevent the stranger from approaching Margaret's bedside. Margaret's condition changes, and her breathing becomes calm and slow. Margaret opens her eyes and expresses anguish and shame upon recognizing the narrator. Margaret pleads for the narrator to leave her, feeling unworthy of forgiveness.

Lady Janet is determined to keep Horace Holmcroft in ignorance of the truth regarding Mercy's identity. Horace Holmcroft is engaged to marry Mercy in a week's time. Lady Janet cannot allow Horace to marry Mercy under false pretenses. Julian believes that Lady Janet will succeed in persuading Horace to break off the engagement. Horace's distrust of Julian may lead him to take actions he would not normally consider. Julian intends to meet Horace to prepare him to hear Mercy without anger. Mercy refuses to leave Julian alone with Horace due to concerns for Julian's safety.

Lady Loring and Stella had a disagreement regarding Stella's visit to Romayne. Lady Loring expressed irritation and decided to return to Stella after a brief period of reflection. Stella left without leaving a message and went to Camp's Hill, Islington. Stella was initially daunted by the appearance of the street but was motivated by her desire to help Romayne. Stella knocked on the door of No. 10 and inquired about Madame Marillac. Stella ascended to the second floor where she found a clean room occupied by two women working on embroidery. The elder woman in the room recognized Stella and asked if she had come for the work.

Mr. Meadowcroft's eldest son is named Ambrose. Ambrose Meadowcroft greeted Mr. Lefrank at the station. Ambrose mentioned that a new member of the family had come to live with them. The new family member is Naomi Colebrook, Mr. Meadowcroft's American niece. Naomi Colebrook has been living with the Meadowcrofts for less than two months. Mr. Meadowcroft is a confirmed invalid due to chronic rheumatism. Mr. Meadowcroft's only unmarried daughter is described as a melancholy, middle-aged woman.

The narrator is investigating the reputation of Sir Percival's mother. The narrator has found one fact that vindicates her reputation. The narrator considers inquiring about 'Miss Elster of Knowlesbury' to further the investigation. The clerk informs the narrator that the clergyman from 1803 is deceased. The clerk mentions that he obtained his position through the previous clerk. Young Mr. Wansborough is identified as a lawyer in High Street, Knowlesbury. The distance from the current location to Knowlesbury is approximately five miles.

The narrator received a marriage proposal from a young gentleman at the table d'hote. The young gentleman has white eyelashes, red hands, and large front teeth. The narrator refused the proposal and has since been verbally abused by the gentleman. Doctor Allday visited the narrator and inquired about Mrs. Ellmother. Doctor Allday requested the narrator to write to Mrs. Rook. The narrator expressed indignation towards Alban Morris for plotting against her. Doctor Allday recommended Mr. Morris as a suitable sweetheart.

The port of departure was Mangerton-on-the-Mud. The intended destination was the Scilly Islands. Preparations for the voyage were made in Bristol. The travelers brought clothes, wrappers, tobacco, French novels, and Egyptian cigars. They purchased various supplies including food and nautical equipment in Bristol. The travelers visited a large country-house to gather additional provisions. They were accompanied by two boys during their preparations.

Madame Pratolungo is not present to teach the narrator. The narrator expresses disappointment in a conversation with a character named Oscar. Oscar apologizes for offending the narrator and expresses feelings of unworthiness. The narrator insists that Oscar should stay longer, but he refuses. Oscar mentions wanting a lock of the narrator's hair. The narrator recalls giving a keepsake of hair to the true Oscar. The narrator cuts off a lock of her hair to give to Oscar.

ANNAJANSKA is a theatrical piece written by George Bernard Shaw. The play was first performed at the Coliseum Theatre in London on January 21, 1918. Lillah McCarthy played the role of the Grand Duchess in the performance. Henry Miller portrayed Schneidekind and Randle Ayrton played General Strammfest. The setting of the play is a military station office on the east front in Beotia. The dialogue includes discussions about the political situation and various governments. The characters express differing views on the revolution and its implications.

Lavinia expresses doubt about always being a Christian. Spintho claims that dying in the arena will make one a martyr and that all martyrs go to heaven. Ferrovius agrees with Spintho that faithfulness to the end is necessary for salvation. Lavinia feels she will not enter heaven easily and acknowledges her moments of weakness. Spintho becomes terrified at the thought of dying and desires martyrdom instead. Androcles suggests that all humans are sinners and tries to console Spintho. Ferrovius insists that Spintho should pray and expresses disdain for him.

The lady leaves the premises in a hurry. The lady calls for Lord Augustus from the street. The lady requests to use the telephone to contact the War Office. Augustus connects the lady to Lord Hungerford Highcastle, referred to as Blueloo. The lady claims to have won a bet and has a list in her wallet. The lady admits to having switched a list of guns for a blank piece of paper. The lady invites Augustus to tea at Rumpelmeister's.

Catherine enters in full Imperial regalia. The soldiers fall on their knees upon her entrance. Catherine orders the soldiers to seize Edstaston and throw him at her feet. Edstaston expresses his anger and refuses to be intimidated by Catherine. Catherine warns Edstaston about the limits of her patience. Naryshkin kneels in fear and pleads for mercy from Catherine. Catherine dismisses the soldiers and expresses disdain for instruments of torture.

Divine right does not require authority. Home is described as a prison for girls and a workhouse for women. Modern civilization is criticized as a disease built on poor foundations. Gambling is identified as a popular method of wealth distribution, primarily benefiting the house. Poverty is stated to be the main issue for the poor, while uselessness is the issue for the rich. The text suggests that sincerity can be dangerous unless accompanied by ignorance. Self-sacrifice is portrayed as a means to enable the sacrifice of others without guilt.

MRS. BANGER is the organizing secretary of the Anti-Suffraget League. LADY CORINTHIA FANSHAWE is the president of the Anti-Suffraget League. The Anti-Suffragets plan to fight against the Suffragets. General Sandstone's project to remove women from a two-mile radius has been abandoned. MRS. BANGER and LADY CORINTHIA intend to enforce the removal project despite the government's decision. MRS. BANGER possesses an XVIII century horse pistol that she claims was carried by her grandmother at Waterloo. MRS. BANGER asserts that women need the right to military service rather than the right to vote.

Morrison announces Mr. Undershaft has arrived at the door. Lady Britomart instructs Morrison to let Mr. Undershaft in. Lady Britomart discusses financial arrangements for her children with Mr. Undershaft. Mr. Undershaft expresses disinterest in their son Stephen. Lady Britomart defends Stephen's character and capabilities. Mr. Undershaft states that the Undershaft tradition disinherits Stephen. Lady Britomart insists that Stephen could manage the foundry just as well as others.

GILBEY expresses disbelief that they can live without being respectable. MRS GILBEY questions GILBEY's statement about their respectability. GILBEY mentions that having children in and out of gaol is not respectable. KNOX argues that they are not tramps due to an accident. GILBEY reveals that his father was a drinker and his uncle was a teetotaller. MRS KNOX defends her aunt against GILBEY's claim of kleptomania. MRS KNOX criticizes KNOX for his drinking habits and expresses concern about their daughter's behavior.

Lucius Septimius enters through the loggia and confronts Caesar. Lucius Septimius claims to have killed Pompey as he arrived in Egypt. Theodotus asserts that they provided Caesar with vengeance by presenting Pompey's head. Caesar expresses horror at the notion of vengeance and reflects on his relationship with Pompey. Lucius Septimius remains undaunted and compares Caesar's past actions to his own. Caesar offers Lucius Septimius a place in his service, but Lucius declines. Rufio identifies Lucius as a Republican, while Caesar clarifies his stance on being a Republican.

George Bernard Shaw wrote the playlet How He Lied To Her Husband in 1905 for Mr Arnold Daly. Mr Arnold Daly was performing in The Man of Destiny in New York when he needed a short play to accompany it. Shaw wrote the play during a holiday in the north of Scotland while it was raining continuously. Mr Daly also produced Mrs Warren's Profession in New York in 1905, which faced significant backlash from the press. The New York journalists condemned the play, leading to the arrest of Mr Daly and his company. A magistrate eventually acquitted Mr Daly, stating that the play was not immoral. Shaw expressed hope that Mrs Warren's Profession would be widely performed to raise public awareness about women's issues.

source.author: George Bernard Shaw
source.title: How He Lied to Her Husband

text: Fine artists should separate their studies of sex and crime from law enforcement perspectives. The stage cannot authentically present sex or murder, similar to how Macbeth does not actually kill Duncan. Artistic conventions can express the feelings of a murderer or the tragedy of love without literal representation. French actors often find the English stage indecent, despite the common perception of French licentiousness. French prudery differs from British prudery, leading to different standards for what is acceptable on stage. On the French stage, a kiss is a clear convention, while the English stage aims for realism in physical interactions.

Burgoyne states that he does not express his opinion and avoids profane language. Burgoyne informs Swindon that Springtown is in the hands of the rebels. Burgoyne mentions that the situation in Springtown has changed since two o'clock that morning. Swindon expresses confidence in the British soldier's ability to perform well. Burgoyne criticizes Swindon for relying too much on the soldiers and not enough on strategic thinking. Burgoyne suggests that the colonists could find a leader, which would worsen their situation. Several officers from various British and German regiments are present for a court proceeding.

Louis offers to give Ridgeon a cheque for two hundred pounds. Ridgeon refuses to lend Louis money, citing dishonor in the proposal. Louis suggests that Ridgeon could help his wife by getting patients to buy his art or commission portraits. Ridgeon expresses indignation at Louis's suggestion of blackmailing his patients. Sir Patrick, Sir Ralph, and Walpole enter the scene while Ridgeon is confronting Louis. Ridgeon accuses Louis of attempting to borrow money and suggesting blackmail.

MRS. HIGGINS asks Mr. Doolittle to step out on the balcony. Mr. Doolittle agrees to help Henry keep Eliza off his hands. The parlor-maid answers the bell and goes to fetch Miss Doolittle. Eliza enters and greets Professor Higgins and Colonel Pickering. Higgins expresses frustration about waiting for Eliza. Eliza begins to stitch at her needlework, ignoring Higgins' outburst. Eliza acknowledges the influence of Colonel Pickering on her manners.

Siegfried encounters Wotan, who is disguised as the Wanderer. Wotan reveals that he lost one of his eyes due to his marriage with Fricka. Siegfried dismisses Wotan as a lunatic and threatens him. Wotan reveals his divine power and the fires of Loki surround him. Siegfried destroys Wotan's spear with his sword, Nothung. Siegfried joyfully confronts the flames, which do not harm him. The narrative transitions to opera, featuring Siegfried and Brynhild in a duet.

The girl fell in love with Cashel at first sight. Cashel entered a room where two ladies, Lydia and Mrs. Byron, were present. Mrs. Byron recognized Cashel and embraced him. Cashel expressed discomfort with the affectionate display from Mrs. Byron. Lydia invited Cashel to meet Mrs. Byron based on their resemblance. Mrs. Byron inquired if Cashel resembled her. Cashel showed indifference to Mrs. Byron's affection and focused on Lydia.

Vivie expresses her shame about her mother's profession but cannot reveal it. Vivie drafts a prospectus listing Sir George Crofts as the chief shareholder and Mrs. Warren as the managing director. Frank and Praed read the two words that describe Vivie's mother, which Vivie refuses to say aloud. Vivie asserts her strength by stating she will not cry or faint. Vivie plans to tell her mother about their parting of ways. Frank feels he cannot marry Vivie due to the implications of her mother's money. Praed expresses disappointment in Sir George Crofts and urges Frank not to abandon Vivie.

The right to know is considered fundamental and unconditional. Ignorance can be argued to be blissful, but knowledge is still pursued as a right. Governments do not openly forbid the pursuit of knowledge on the grounds that it is a bad thing. The pursuit of knowledge is subject to social conditions and limitations. The exercise of the right to knowledge must respect other rights. Society does not permit harmful actions, such as torture, in the pursuit of knowledge. The right to knowledge is imperfectly recognized in practice.

source.author: George Bernard Shaw
source.title: The Doctor's Dilemma: Preface on Doctors

text: In England, a serious occasion is defined as one where nobody tells the truth. Doctors who conduct animal experiments may mislead the public to avoid punishment. Prizefighters benefit from exaggerating the dangers of their sport to maintain public interest. Vivisectors claim their animal subjects experience a painless death while producing cures for diseases. The public's beliefs are influenced by their interests and social class, particularly regarding vivisection and animal treatment. The term 'prostitute' can apply to anyone who engages in work for money that they would not do otherwise. Public opinion and market demand significantly influence individual moral decisions.

Irishmen in America planned to blow up Dublin Castle. Detectives persuaded young workmen to order bombs from local ironmongers. Military and naval commanders favored ultimatums backed by explosives. Historical events such as the wreck of Clerkenwell prison and the disestablishment of the Irish Church are questioned for their effectiveness. The guillotine was used in France on both Girondins and Jacobins, leading to significant political turmoil. America has no Star Chamber or feudal barons but has Trusts and millionaires with heavily defended factories. Civilizations can regress rapidly when the qualities that once drove their success become detrimental.

Benham arrived at Chexington and encountered Sir Philip Easton in the garden. Sir Philip Easton was engaged in fishing, reading, and playing cricket during the summer. Benham observed a familiarity between Sir Philip and Amanda, as well as Sir Philip's attentiveness to Lady Marayne. During lunch, Benham noted the expressiveness of Sir Philip's eyes and his concern for Amanda. Sir Philip expressed to Benham that Amanda misses him and mentioned bringing her books and flowers. Benham felt uncomfortable with Sir Philip's attentions towards Amanda and attempted to change the subject. Three days later, Benham informed Amanda that Sir Philip Easton had left.

Lady Harman observed that her husband had become restless and hostile towards her. Alice Burnet was identified as the leader of the malcontents in a conflict involving the matrons. Miss Babs Wheeler, an ardent Unionist, influenced Alice Burnet in her activities at the hostels. The Bloomsbury Hostel housed a hundred waitresses from Eustace and Mills, who looked down on the International girls. Mrs. Pembrose expelled Alice Burnet and her friends from their rooms under the pretext of redecoration. Miss Babs Wheeler addressed a meeting at the Bloomsbury Hostel despite prohibitions from Mrs. Pembrose. Lady Harman sought refuge in Saint Paul's Cathedral amidst the turmoil she faced in London.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Wife of Sir Isaac Harman

text: The text discusses the Socialist attitude towards the distribution of resources, specifically boots. It describes a scenario where people in Great Britain are in need of proper footwear. The text presents a hypothetical situation of acquiring leather from South America for boot production. It highlights the challenges faced in obtaining leather due to private property ownership. The narrative suggests that the owner of the leather would demand a high price for it. The text indicates that transportation of leather to England would also involve private property owners seeking profit. It concludes with the implication that profits from the boot production would benefit wealthy individuals rather than those in need.

The Vicar of Siddermorton has two rivals in scientific pursuits: Gully of Sidderton and Borland, a natural history dealer. Gully has seen a glare on Sidderford moor and sent a drawing to _Nature_. Borland operates a marine laboratory at Portburdock and collects rare sea birds. The Vicar is concerned that Gully may find a rare bird before him. The Vicar has previously secured the only known British specimen of a bird, recorded in Saunders' British Birds. Collectors are responsible for the decline of various rare species in England. The text suggests that the presence of collectors leads to a lack of biodiversity in the environment.

The narrator recalls seeing wax candles in the corridor and retrieves ten of them. The candles are arranged throughout the room to ensure that every area is illuminated. The narrator observes the steady burning of the candles as a way to occupy time while waiting. As the narrator watches the minute hand of the watch approach midnight, candles begin to extinguish unexpectedly. The narrator attempts to relight the candles but notices that more candles continue to go out on their own. An invisible force seems to extinguish the candles, causing the narrator to feel panic and urgency. The narrator uses a candlestick to relight candles more efficiently as they continue to go out.

Ostrog escaped in an aeropile while people attempted to shoot it down. The area became filled with smoke from the weapons being fired. Graham was elevated among the scaffolding and received shouts of congratulations. The people looked to Graham for leadership after Ostrog's escape. Graham felt a mix of nerves and determination as he prepared to act. The Master of the Earth experienced confusion and a lack of control over his own actions. Helen Wotton had warned the people about the approaching aeroplanes.

Mr. Wace learned that the crystal egg had already been sold to a tall, dark man in grey. The Great Portland Street dealer did not know the identity of the tall dark man in grey. Mr. Wace made a second call to the Great Portland Street dealer, which was also ineffective. Mr. Wace resorted to advertisements in periodicals likely to be seen by bric-a-brac collectors. Both _The Daily Chronicle_ and _Nature_ advised Mr. Wace to reconsider his action before they printed his story. After a month, Mr. Wace reluctantly abandoned the quest for the crystal egg, which remains undiscovered. The announcement regarding Neptune's erratic motion was made simultaneously from three observatories on the first day of the new year.

The town guard parades in honor of an event. Musicians ride on gray horses towards the town hall. The zoological gardens are protected by a bearded janitor. The gardens contain elephants, camels, a sitting bear, and goats. The keepers in the gardens wear uniforms similar to railway guards. A clockwork train arrives at the railway station. An elephant escapes from the zoo into the Blue Ward.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: Floor Games; a companion volume to "Little Wars"

text: A conflict occurred involving Jaffers and an unseen enemy at an inn. Jaffers fell to the ground after the struggle, remaining still at the foot of the steps. A stranger attempted to intervene but fell over Jaffers' body. A woman screamed as something passed by her, and a dog ran into Huxter's yard. Gibbons, an amateur naturalist, heard a man's voice swearing while alone on the downs. Mr. Thomas Marvel was sitting by the roadside near Adderdean, contemplating boots. Marvel disliked both roomy shoes and damp conditions, finding the boots he had unattractive.

Children often have a limited understanding of the doctrines they subscribe to, particularly regarding the nature of Christ and God. Many individuals exhibit beliefs that align with Arianism, despite its historical rejection by mainstream Christianity. Christianity has historically made significant efforts to articulate its beliefs clearly and unambiguously. The author identifies a growing modern religion that is distinct from traditional Christianity and is emerging in various cultural contexts. This modern religion is characterized by the worship of a finite God, differing fundamentally from traditional Christian views of God. Believers in this modern faith often describe their God as a loving and knowable personality, rather than an all-powerful deity. The modern religious perspective tends to embrace universalism, suggesting that all sincere calls to God, regardless of name, are responses from the True God.

Mr. Hoopdriver experienced discomfort while riding up a steep hill. He contemplated the Weald from the crest of the hill after a slow ascent. Mr. Hoopdriver fell asleep on the turf and woke up to find it was past two o'clock. He resumed his ride towards Chichester, enjoying the tracking of the road. The tracks he was following vanished at a stone cross under the shadow of the cathedral. Mr. Hoopdriver asked several people if they had seen a Young Lady in Grey on a bicycle. Feeling hot, tired, and hungry, he decided to get tea and meat at the Royal George.

Both Christendom and Islam created common schools to preserve their doctrines. Modern communication methods allow for the rapid dissemination of ideas globally. There is a need for an organized world state to replace nationalism and patriotism. The concept of a Federal World State is proposed as a common political idea. The movement for a World State aims to engage young minds and spread its ideas through various channels. The World State is envisioned as a fusion of all governments and empires. The discussion emphasizes the need for a concrete realization of what a World State would entail.

The narrator made journeys for Isabel in February. The narrator and Isabel experienced a sense of embarrassment during their meeting. They walked with old Fortescue, K. C., and another admirer of Isabel. Isabel expressed her intention to work with the narrator after her time at Oxford. The narrator felt a growing value in his relationship with Isabel. The narrator was concerned that Isabel might be transitory in his life. The narrator acknowledged the complexity of his feelings for Isabel due to their intellectual connection.

The battle took place near Hook's Farm. Red's forces included 1 gun, 5 cavalry, and 13 infantry on the left, and 2 guns, 20 cavalry, and 37 infantry on the right. Blue's cavalry charged Red's guns during the battle. Red's charge failed, resulting in Blue capturing several prisoners. Red's indecision led to a weak infantry attack that was easily repelled by Blue. Red retreated from his position with approximately 6 infantry-men, 4 cavalry, and 1 gun. Red won the toss for the choice of side and first move in the battle.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: Little Wars; a game for boys from twelve years of age to one hundred and fifty and for that more intelligent sort of girl who likes boys' games and books

text: The narrator realizes that they have fallen asleep and their fire has gone out. The narrator feels overwhelmed by creatures in the darkness and is physically attacked. The narrator finds an iron lever and uses it to fight off the attackers. The narrator observes that the Morlocks seem to be afraid and are fleeing. The narrator sees flames from a burning forest and understands the source of the smell of burning wood. The narrator encounters a group of Morlocks who are disoriented by the fire's light and heat. The narrator initially attacks the Morlocks but later refrains from striking them when realizing their helplessness.

Smithers demonstrated a medium's ability to hold an object in his teeth and blow it out. Miss Heydinger observed a moodiness in Lewisham after a demonstration of mediumship. Miss Heydinger expressed anger towards the medium for deceiving educated individuals. Lewisham was unfamiliar with the poem 'Sludge, the Medium' by Browning. Miss Heydinger believed that financial incentives for mediumship lead to immorality and cheating. Ethel Henderson appeared distressed and wished to escape her situation after Lagune left. Ethel Henderson reflected on her perceived punishment and expressed a desire for death.

Caddles expressed concern about a child's excessive appetite. Lady Wondershoot consulted the parish doctor regarding the child's milk consumption. The parish doctor stated that the proper milk allowance for a child of that age is one and a half to two pints per day. The doctor suggested that the child might be physiologically different, possibly a case of General Hypertrophy. Lady Wondershoot worried that the child's appetite was unfair to other parish children. The Vicar reacted skeptically to reports of giant wasps and other novelties in the news. The Vicar later observed abnormal growth in the grass and puff-balls near the Caddles' cottage.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Food of the Gods and How It Came to Earth

text: In Great Britain, the legal profession is characterized by the absence of discussions about 'the young,' focusing instead on 'smart juniors.' Reform and progressive criticism in the legal profession are primarily associated with retired individuals. Great Britain is experiencing the stresses of war a year later than France, Germany, and Russia. There is a possibility of significant criticism and resentment towards lawyer-politicians and the legal profession in Great Britain before 1918 or 1919. A potential outcome of the current discontent may involve attempts to replace lawyers with business men, soldiers, or scientists, followed by efforts to reform the legal profession. The Press is expected to play a significant role in any reform movement within the legal profession. The interaction between lawyer-politicians and the Press is seen as crucial for the future of democratic governance.

Mr. Direck and Mr. Britling discussed the nature of conservatism and its lack of racial basis. Mr. Direck mentioned a friend named Robinson, who he described as being of genuine English stock. Mr. Britling attracted the attention of two laboring men to assist with a car that had encountered a problem. The car sustained minor damage, including a slight crumpling of the mud-guard and a detached headlight wire. Mr. Britling returned home safely, where his family welcomed him with relief and admiration. Mr. Direck found Mr. Britling's household to be distinctly British and somewhat difficult to understand. Mrs. Britling was described as a tall, freckled woman with brown hair and preoccupied brown eyes.

The new government provided rations as a means of control over the population. The council had access to millions of workers and advanced machinery after the last wars. The government initially aimed to temporarily restore the pre-atomic economic system. The capitalist system was irreparably damaged by the introduction of unlimited resources. The absence of employment for a large population posed a social danger. The council began a complete reorganization of urban and industrial life. The council aimed to address economic disparities between different social classes.

The golden vase of Bias is inscribed with the words 'TO THE WISEST.' Atalanta's golden apple and one of the apples of discord were wrapped in a napkin of gold brought from Hades by Rampsinitus. The virtuoso claimed to have received the vase of Bias long ago because he had learned to despise all things. The collection includes Cinderella's glass slipper, Diana's sandal, and Fanny Elssler's shoe. The collection features the lyre of Orpheus, the trumpet of Anthony Van Corlear, and Dr. Franklin's famous whistle. A small vase of oracular gas from Delphos is included in the collection. The virtuoso referred to a bundle as 'Christian's burden of sin' and suggested looking into one's own consciousness for its contents.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: A Virtuoso's Collection (From "Mosses From An Old Manse")

text: The narrator expresses a longing for a maiden who has passed away. The maiden's spirit is described as pure and ethereal. The narrator visits the maiden's tomb regularly and feels a connection to her spirit. One night, the narrator finds the maiden's tomb empty, realizing she has moved on to a higher realm. The narrator reflects on their own earthly existence and desires to escape its burdens. The narrator also visits a living individual who is unaware of the spiritual presence around him. The narrator hopes to inspire pure thoughts and dreams in the living through their spiritual visits.

Beach birds seek food along the shore. The birds interact playfully with the waves. The narrator observes the birds and their tracks in the sand. The narrator recounts various activities along the beach, including collecting shells and examining sea creatures. The beach features a fresh-water brooklet that eventually sinks into the sand. The narrator reflects on the nature of their thoughts while tracking footprints in the sand. The beach provides space for writing in the sand, including verses and names.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Footprints on the Sea-Shore (From "Twice Told Tales")

text: Middleton looked out from his window into an old-fashioned garden and at a stone sun-dial. He reflected on the possible hiding place of a secret related to his mysterious ancestor. Middleton prepared to go down to dinner with his host, who was alone at the table. The dining room was dark but modernized with English comforts and a well-set table. Middleton and his host engaged in a friendly conversation during dinner. The Master discussed the decay of old families and the reluctance to part with them. A young lady at the table remained mostly silent and did not strongly attract Middleton's interest.

The text discusses the transition from summer to autumn, highlighting the changes in nature. It describes the heavy hoarfrost on grass and the falling leaves on an October morning. The Old Manse is portrayed as becoming lonelier after summer ends. Guests at the Old Manse experience a sense of tranquility and often fall asleep during their visits. The narrator believes that providing rest and peace is a valuable service to weary individuals. The text suggests that humanity suffers from a lack of sleep and excessive activity. The narrator advocates for a period of rest to help regenerate and clarify human perspectives.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: The Old Manse (From "Mosses From An Old Manse")

text: Governor Winthrop was made an angel. Hester Prynne was shocked at Mr. Dimmesdale's condition during their interview. Mr. Dimmesdale's moral force was reduced to weakness despite his intellectual faculties remaining strong. Hester felt a responsibility towards Mr. Dimmesdale due to their shared past. Pearl is now seven years old. Hester Prynne has become a familiar object to the townspeople over the years. Hester has shown self-devotion by helping those in need despite her own outcast status.

The narrator contemplates entering a turbulent stream and expresses a desire to avoid ending up in a mud-puddle. The narrator describes a corner of the street illuminated by a lamp, surrounded by tall edifices with closed blinds. The narrator observes strong winds causing mischief, particularly affecting a woman struggling with her umbrella and cloak. The narrator walks into the center of town, where shops are brightly lit against the dark night. The wet sidewalks reflect red light, and the rain-drops are described as glittering like rubies. A retired sea-captain is mentioned, heading towards the Marine Insurance Office to share stories with fellow sailors. An unhappy gentleman is seen rushing through the storm, seeking a doctor due to a domestic emergency.

Philemon inquired about a fountain of milk in an old earthen pitcher. Quicksilver attributed the mystery to his staff, which he claimed played odd tricks. Philemon and Baucis gave up their sleeping-room to guests and slept on the floor. In the morning, Philemon invited the guests to stay for breakfast, but they chose to leave early. Philemon and Baucis walked with the guests, growing familiar with the elder traveler. Quicksilver displayed quick wit and humor during their conversation. The elder traveler spoke about the importance of treating strangers as brothers.

The text discusses the complexities of vice and virtue in human nature. A grandfatherly figure enters an office seeking To-morrow, believing it holds vast benefits. The Man of Intelligence informs the grandfather that To-morrow is elusive and has scattered gifts among Yesterdays. A boy chases a butterfly, which symbolizes To-morrow, through the city. A man in rough attire seeks Truth and expresses his determination to find it. The Man of Intelligence tells the seeker that achieving Truth is a personal endeavor and cannot be assisted. The Man of Intelligence reveals that he is the Recording Spirit, not a minister of action.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: The Intelligence Office (From "Mosses From An Old Manse")

text: Adam Forrester and Lilias Fay planned to build a summer-house in the form of an antique temple. The summer-house was intended for refined and innocent enjoyments, including festivals and music. Adam Forrester referred to Lilias Fay as LILY due to her fragile form and pale cheek. Walter Gascoigne, a relative of Lilias Fay, followed the couple while displaying a melancholic demeanor. Lilias Fay identified a pleasant spot for the temple, which had a view of a distant lake and a church-spire. Adam Forrester agreed that the chosen spot was the loveliest for their Temple of Happiness. Walter Gascoigne expressed disapproval of the site by shaking his head and pointing to remnants of a former structure.

Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote a letter on August 28, 1860, regarding a story for the Essex Institute. Hawthorne reflects on a hill known as 'Brown's Folly' near Salem, which he remembers from his youth. The hill is described as a long ridge with a green lane and a brook that has since diminished. The hill offers views of the ocean and the surrounding rural landscape, allowing for a broad perspective on local estates. An old pleasure house was built on the hill by a pre-revolutionary magnate, which was later abandoned after an earthquake in 1755. The house was left under the care of Richard Derby during the owner's exile to England, and it became neglected over time. The site of the former mansion can still be traced, with remnants of its structure visible on the hill.

Mr. Smooth-it-away explained that the door of a cavern is used by shepherds as a smoke-house for mutton hams. The narrator experienced drowsiness while passing over the enchanted ground. The passengers awoke upon crossing into the pleasant land of Beulah. The engine emitted a loud and disturbing sound as they approached the final station-house. A multitude of shining ones welcomed two pilgrims emerging from the river. Mr. Smooth-it-away indicated he would not be going to the Celestial City and was only accompanying the narrator for company. The steam ferry boat was preparing for immediate departure as passengers expressed various concerns.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Mosses from an Old Manse and Other Stories

text: The narrator reflects on the relationship with Monsieur de Miroir. The narrator expresses concern about how their fate may affect their friend. The narrator recalls a time when they enjoyed the company of Monsieur de Miroir. The narrator notes changes in their appearance and mood over the years. The narrator contemplates the impact of their past on their present self. The narrator intends to seek wisdom from Monsieur de Miroir despite their fears. The narrator acknowledges the importance of their connection with Monsieur de Miroir.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Monsieur du Muroir (From "Mosses From An Old Manse")

text: The author expresses uncertainty about the origins and destinations of certain phenomena. The author believes it is dangerous to analyze these phenomena too closely. The author feels that words can obscure the truth between the soul and its expression. The author mentions feeling relieved from a heavy burden, comparing it to Christian's burden. The author observes a young boy from Malaga who is content and adaptable on a coal vessel. The boy speaks Spanish and English and enjoys fishing and swimming in the sea. The author appreciates the refreshing quality of the east wind during work hours.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the American Notebooks, Volume 1

text: Dr. Dolliver took a single drop from a silver stopple bottle and added it to a goblet of water. The drop turned the water a rosy hue and diffused a sweet odor throughout the chamber. Dr. Dolliver expressed skepticism about the efficacy of the concoction, attributing its creation to a madman. He noted that the medicine had been in his cupboard for seven years without any customers returning. Dr. Dolliver considered the silver-cased bottle to be worth something as an antiquarian item. He reflected on the labor he had invested in the medicine, which he believed was worth its weight in gold. Dr. Dolliver was motivated to try the medicine again due to his poor health and loneliness.

The text discusses the concept of a Master Genius who is expected to create an American literature. The Master Genius is described as unrecognized and unhonored by his contemporaries. Monsieur On-Dit is a character who spreads information about the Master Genius among other guests. Several characters express skepticism about the existence of an American genius. Davy Jones and Old Harry, later referred to as Venerable Henry, are among the notable guests mentioned. Seatsfield is introduced as a real person from Germany, initially mistaken for a fictional character. A guest representing Posterity arrives, prompting interest and attention from the other guests.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: A Select Party (From "Mosses From An Old Manse")

text: Edward Walcott observed that the ride was unusually long. Fanshawe appeared weary and dispirited after losing the excitement of intense thought. Edward suggested they stop at a nearby cottage for refreshment. The cottage appeared to be in a state of ruin and neglect. Inside the cottage, two elderly women were present, one looking ill and the other displaying sullen discontent. The sick woman approached Edward and expressed eager but ultimately disappointed emotions. The sick woman then returned to her chair and wept bitterly.

The Englishman made a remark about a spider above the Doctor's head before leaving. The Doctor claimed to have learned from the spider's web how to weave a plot and catch a victim. After the snow melted, Ned and Elsie visited a grave site that had a small hillock. They discovered fragments of bones and a key while exploring the grave site. The Doctor identified the key as silver and of antique workmanship, attaching it to a chain for Ned. Ned was about ten years old and Elsie was six or seven at the time of the discovery. Ned exhibited signs of a poetic and imaginative mind despite his pale appearance.

The obnoxious guest listened intently to the table-talk, seeking hidden meanings. The initiated guests shared profound insights about sorrow and spiritual depth. Moments of clarity emerged during the conversation, revealing the nature of mortal grief. Mr. Smith laughed at the conversation and died suddenly in his chair. The old woman expressed her fear and tremor at the sight of Mr. Smith's death. Gervayse Hastings observed the dead man and reflected on the transient nature of life. The festivals continued regularly, inviting individuals with notable misfortunes.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: The Christmas Banquet (From "Mosses From An Old Manse")

text: The narrator caught mackerel in the autumn. Mr. Bartlett's store served as a gathering place for the narrator and Uncle Parker. Uncle Parker was an old man with a history of numerous voyages and injuries. Uncle Parker had one eye blown out and the other glimmered in its socket. The fishermen in the village had varying levels of experience, with some having sailed to distant locations. A fish-dealer from the countryside listened to the fishermen's stories. The village featured a display of gingerbread men, picture-books, and fishing supplies.

CAPT. G. is nervous and visibly trembling during the wedding ceremony. The bride arrives at the church and is given away by her father. CAPT. G. struggles to remember his own name during the affirmation. CAPT. M. instructs CAPT. G. to kneel and participate in the ceremony. CAPT. G. is encouraged to kiss the bride by CAPT. M. CAPT. G. is expected to give a speech at the reception after the ceremony. CAPT. M. expresses concern about the legality of the marriage.

The drill was dismissed early for the corps members. McTurk expressed skepticism about the corps' activities. A sentry was stationed at the locked gymnasium door. Foxy reported to Keyte about the corps' secretive practices. Keyte attended a drill session to observe the corps. Perowne, Ansell, and Hogan led the drill and were obeyed by the corps. Stalky criticized the corps members during the drill.

Lizzie is described as a slender girl in a crinoline. Scott wakes up in an empty cart and begins his work in silence. William is in charge of managing tasks and has been since she arrived. Scott and William feed babies and manage goats together. William offers Scott stone-cold tea and toast that she had prepared for him. There are lamentations in the camp when the elder children see their nurse leave without them. Faiz Ullah jokes with the policemen while Scott feels ashamed.

The text references the Garden called Gethsemane in Picardy. The speaker expresses a sense of burden and a lack of forgiveness. The speaker mentions having a son who worked with guns in Flanders. The text discusses the sacrifices made by those who build foundations for future generations. The speaker reflects on the nature of peace and the sacrifices required to achieve it. The text includes a narrative about a character's experiences after revelry at The Mermaid. The character recalls various interactions and events involving notable figures and themes from literature.

Findlayson shared a bungalow with his assistant for the last three years. Peroo took a dinghy with a couple of nephews and was described as lolling in the stern. Hitchcock overheard Peroo discussing atheism with a guru and denying the efficacy of prayer. Muir sent a telegram warning of floods on the Ramgunga, predicting it would reach Melipur Ghaut in approximately fifteen hours. Findlayson received another telegram from Cockran about heavy rains at the Ganges Canal. Hitchcock and Findlayson planned to work the gangs all night to clean up the river-bed. Hitchcock mentioned specific equipment on the east bank that needed attention, including pontoons and overhead cranes.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: Kipling Stories and Poems Every Child Should Know, Book II

text: The characters in the text include Tim Kelly, Crook, and a little officer boy of the Tyrone. The Tyrone soldiers refer to a location as Silver's Theatre. A man from the Tyrone dies suddenly without any visible injuries. The little officer boy expresses distress and fear during the events described. The Tyrone soldiers are described as angry and eager for revenge after witnessing their dead. The narrative includes a warning about the dangers of approaching wounded enemies. The soldiers are depicted as disheveled and marked by battle after the conflict.

The conversation involves themes of morality and the perception of actions such as murder and suicide. The speaker expresses a belief that God's understanding of events may differ from human perception. The speaker plans to take a holiday at a hydro in the Midlands next week. The hydro features a nine-hole golf course, which the speaker's cousins frequent. The speaker invites another person to join him at the hydro, despite acknowledging it may be dull. The narrator suspects that the speaker has misappropriated funds from his cousins. The narrator spends a night at Holmescroft before joining the speaker at the hydro.

Harvey and Tom Platt interacted with a French crew while attempting to trade for tobacco. The French crew had American tobacco that had not paid duty to France. Harvey's French was not effective, while Tom Platt communicated successfully using gestures. The trade involved exchanging chocolate and crackers for tobacco. The captain of the French vessel offered Tom Platt a drink of gin. Disko owned the stores where Harvey arranged the trade. The narrative includes a confrontation with a cattle-boat that was poorly managed at sea.

The village of Sumtner Barton lies just across a railway line spanned by a red brick bridge. A Foresters' Fête is taking place in the village, which is associated with Mutual Benefit Societies. The characters plan to have lunch by the roadside instead of at the pub to enjoy local ales. A detachment of Regular troops is on maneuvers in the area. Mr. Lingnam discusses the need for the Empire's component parts to coordinate on war strategies. A boy on a bicycle nearly collides with a car as he attempts to navigate a narrow pavement.

St. Hubert's shrine features rustic work with reedings of peeled branches and panels of moss and thatch. Alan spent the afternoon inspecting gun positions on a mountain top and was shelled during this time. The town where Alan took tea has a mixture of French and German architectural influences. The cellar of the 'big house' where tea was served functions as a hospital for civil cases resulting from bombardments. Civil cases treated in the hospital include injuries from falling timber and flying stones. The bombardment is intended to terrify the civilian population to pressure politicians for peace. The Staff Officer described the location as the end of the line, situated among hills.

Dr. Lathrop is involved in a mission related to health in India. Lady Dufferin has drawn attention to the needs of women in India. The province of Punjab contributed about seven thousand rupees to civil dispensaries last year. Bradlaugh is perceived as a representative of the aspirations of two hundred and fifty million people in India. The death rate for the bureaucrats in India is five times higher than that of their counterparts elsewhere. Orde indicates that the actual daily work in India falls on the shoulders of local men. Orde demonstrates the presence of graves in the area by uncovering a skeleton while gardening.

An Almanac of twelve Sports was published by R. H. Russell in New York in 1898. The text includes a calendar for each month of the year 1898, listing Sundays through Saturdays. The author of the almanac is William Nicholson, with words by Rudyard Kipling. The almanac features various sports including hunting, coursing, racing, boating, fishing, cricket, archery, coaching, shooting, golf, boxing, and skating. Each sport is accompanied by a short poem or commentary related to it. The almanac concludes with a reflection on the cost of participation in these sports.

The narrator heard a faint call of 'Jack!' but did not verify it. The narrator met Kitty on horseback and forgot about the interview. Mrs. Wessington died a week later, which relieved the narrator. By January, the narrator burned the correspondence with Mrs. Wessington. In April 1885, the narrator was in Simla and decided to marry Kitty at the end of June. The narrator and Kitty went to Hamilton's on April 15, 1885, to measure for an engagement ring. The narrator saw four jhampanies in 'magpie' livery pulling a rickshaw, which reminded him of Mrs. Wessington.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Phantom Rickshaw and Other Ghost Stories

text: The crow demanded attention as it twirled before the fire. If a person dies at home and does not die at the ghât, they are taken to a specific place. The narrator recalls being told about a place in India for Hindus who recover from trance or catalepsy. Gunga Dass, a former Brahmin, described being taken to be burned during a cholera epidemic. Gunga Dass survived after being treated with medicines and was transported to Okara Station. Gunga Dass has been in his current location for two and a half years. Gunga Dass stated there is no way to escape from the place where he is.

The young mule questions the necessity of fighting. The troop-horse explains that they must obey orders. Billy the mule emphasizes the importance of following the man giving orders. Two Tails acknowledges the difficulty of obedience but agrees with Billy. The gun-bullocks prepare to return to their lines as morning approaches. Vixen, the dog, is under the gun tail with her man. The bullocks become stuck while trying to move and express their fear of white men.

The King questioned whether any baron would kneel to him if he were alone and without a crown. Rahere indicated that De Aquila, a Norman, might be the only one to kneel to the King under such circumstances. The King stated that Harold had lied to his father, William the Conqueror. Rahere mentioned that Robert, the King's brother, might claim that the King had not always told the truth about England. Henry asserted that England was promised to his father by Edward the Confessor. De Aquila noted that Harold nearly defeated the Normans at the Battle of Santlache. Harold claimed that he had been stoned for telling his tale of the battles.

Fleury's Ray is sensitive to oil and grease, requiring significant effort and expense to restore if disrupted. Captain Hodgson highlights the quality of thrust-collars, which are full-jewelled. The shaft-bearings are sourced from the Commercial Minerals Company and cost £37 each. The bearings were transferred from 'No. 97', which obtained them from the wreck of the 'Perseus' aëroplane. The rudder-gear and gas lift-shunt are the only moving machines in the engine room. Captain Purnall is in command and addresses a navigational issue with a nearby vessel. The nearby vessel is described as an outdated twin-screw tramp with an obsolete conning-tower.

The sergeant pushed and three soldiers danced along while one soldier shut his eyes in the sentry-box. The soldier was sent home on a bullock-cart after a night of drinking. There were two hundred and thirty sergeants and forty-one corporals present. The soldier needed affidavits to explain his behavior after being seen using his sword improperly. The narrative includes themes of love and betrayal, with the speaker expressing deep feelings for someone who has caused them pain. The speaker reflects on their experiences as a soldier and the passage of time. The speaker concludes with a sense of resignation about their life and the world around them.

The speaker expresses a return to military service after completing six years. The speaker mentions receiving back pay and a daily allowance for tobacco. The speaker reflects on the challenges of finding a trade outside the army. The speaker describes the sights and sounds of the barracks upon returning. The speaker interacts with a tailor regarding the fitting of military clothing. The speaker anticipates future adjustments to their military uniform and plans to buy a walking cane. The speaker comments on the difficulties faced by soldiers and the consequences of not supporting them.

A Song of the English is a work by Rudyard Kipling, illustrated by W. Heath Robinson. The edition of A Song of the English is published by Hodder & Stoughton in London. This edition is reprinted from The Seven Seas with permission from Messrs. Methuen & Co. The poem discusses themes of faith, obedience, and the heritage of the English people. The Coastwise Lights of England are described as guiding ships and providing safety at sea. The poem includes references to various locations and types of vessels, including warships and cargo ships. The Song of the Dead is mentioned as a separate section that reflects on those who have passed.

Hanrahan observes a procession of shadowy figures that resemble lovers. The figures possess heart-shaped mirrors instead of hearts and are gazing at their reflections. The procession includes women with beautiful heads but shadowy bodies, and their hair appears to move independently. A woman with sorrowful eyes, identified as Dervadilla, speaks to Hanrahan after seven hundred years of silence. Dervadilla explains that the first group of lovers includes figures like Blanad, Deirdre, and Grania, who sought lasting beauty. The second group of figures sought to prove their strength and beauty, while the shadowy women desired only to be loved. Dervadilla reveals that she and Dermot are punished for their past sins, which brought the Norman invasion to Ireland.

A man covered with dust informed the group that two messengers from the defeated Irish were raising the whole country against them near Manor Hamilton. The messengers were riding north-east between Ben Bulben and Cashel-na-Gael. Sir Frederick Hamilton ordered five troopers to mount quickly and intercept the messengers. The troopers crossed the river at Buckley's Ford and entered the woods following a beaten track. As they rode, the troopers discussed their lives and personal matters, including family and relationships. The group encountered a tall old woman in the river who was washing a dead body. The troopers recognized their own faces on the dead body as the woman asked about her son with a silver crown.

The text describes a conversation about the relationship between humans and immortal spirits. The characters mention various deities from mythology, including the Dagda, Lug, Aengus, and Bodb. The Sidhe are referenced as still being present and active in the world. Michael Robartes opens a door to a building and leads the narrator to a room filled with bookshelves. The narrator finds an extensive alchemical library with works by various historical figures, including Morienus, Avicenna, and Flamel. A woman enters the room and places fruit on the table, appearing to have been once handsome but now showing signs of wear. The narrator attempts to ask the woman about the ceremony but receives no verbal response.

Cuchullain and Concobar discuss the importance of Emain as a town. Concobar believes that only men can make towns great. Daire suggests that old men should keep company with one another. Daire offers ale to the older Kings, but most refuse. Cuchullain reflects on the nature of relationships and parenthood. Concobar calls the Kings together to discuss rebuilding Emain after the wars. Concobar expresses frustration over previous attempts to summon the Kings being interrupted by conflict.

William Pollexfen died and was buried by his wife Elizabeth in a grey stone tomb. George, the astrologer and son of William Pollexfen, was laid to rest in the same tomb after twenty years. The sailor John, who traveled many lands, never found rest ashore. The youngest son of William Pollexfen was buried near George after deciding to journey home at the age of fifty. A dying lady is described as having a lovely head amid dull red hair and a pallor on her face. Artists bring dolls and drawings to the dying lady, reflecting her beauty and features. The dying lady is portrayed as playful and courageous, with a strong will and a connection to her deceased brother.

Chapel of the Morning Star is preferred over Burns's beer house except at the end of the day. The machine shop of the realists is described as uncomfortable and lacking beer. Walter Pater is mentioned as saying music is the type of all the Arts. The text discusses the differences between music and oratory in terms of personal expression. A girl is described as playing the banjo, and her performance is noted for its personal expression. The text contrasts the nature of old instruments with modern ones, emphasizing the personal connection to music. A girl with a shrill voice is critiqued for her education and lack of personal expression in speech.

A young man questions a fool about his bag and the need for pennies. The fool expresses a desire to buy food and supplies with the pennies. The wise man asks the group if anyone believes in God, heaven, purgatory, or hell. The young men collectively deny their belief in these concepts. The wise man claims that teaching does not change the heart and encourages honesty. The wise man admits to his own ignorance and affirms the existence of God and heaven. The young men challenge the wise man to prove his claims about seeing an angel.

The text reflects on the feelings of dissatisfaction and longing experienced by an individual. The individual describes their background as poor, ailing, and ignorant, being the son of a livery stable keeper. The individual expresses a desire for artistic inspiration and self-discovery through the act of writing. The individual experiences disappointment after social interactions and reflects on their thoughts and emotions. The text references Dante and Boehme, indicating a connection to literary and philosophical themes. The individual observes contrasting judgments among friends, particularly in the context of artistic expression. The individual notes a friend's tendency to create a world free of judgment, reflecting on the nature of beauty and indulgence.

The speaker expresses feelings of loss and emptiness after a separation. The No King laments the lack of meaningful communication and the loss of romance. The speaker reflects on the coldness of heaven and the memories of lost love. The speaker desires to understand the nature of heroism and beauty as depicted in Homer's age. The speaker emphasizes the importance of inner peace over external praise. The speaker critiques the challenges of theatrical productions and the difficulties of life. The speaker concludes with a simple truth about love and aging.

source.author: William Butler Yeats
source.title: The Green Helmet and Other Poems

text: LITTLE BLUE BOOK NO. 335 is edited by E. Haldeman-Julius. The Land of Heart's Desire is written by W.B. Yeats. The scene is set in the Barony of Kilmacowen in the county of Sligo at the end of the Eighteenth Century. The characters in the play are Maurteen Bruin, Shawn Bruin, Father Hart, Bridget Bruin, Maire Bruin, and a Faery Child. The kitchen of Maurteen Bruin's house contains a turf fire, a table, and a window with a bowl of primroses. Maire Bruin is reading a yellow manuscript that has been in the thatch for fifty years. Father Hart and Maurteen Bruin discuss the impact of reading and writing on their lives.

The characters in the text include a Young Man and a Stranger. The Stranger mentions an old horse that has been wandering on the road all night. The Young Man expresses a sentiment about not wanting to fire at soldiers who are not of their race. The Stranger indicates that he will ensure the Young Man's safety from living men. The pathway mentioned leads to the ruined Abbey of Corcomroe. The First Musician describes the journey through various landscapes and the sounds of nature. The Stranger notes that they are almost at the summit where the abbey lies amid broken tombs.

The pupils are discussing a passage chosen for their lesson. The passage mentions two living countries, one visible and one invisible. The Wise Man expresses concern about the choice of the passage. The pupils consider changing their chosen subject. The Wise Man reflects on a dream he has had twice. The Fool asks for a penny multiple times throughout the text. The Wise Man describes the implications of the chosen passage as potentially altering everything.

Cuchulain expresses that while he is praised for his strength, his worth is not recognized. The Girl states that if Cuchulain's strength is equal to her beauty, she would prefer to live among holy men. Cuchulain has heard that men are revered for their holiness rather than their worth. The Fool by the Roadside reflects on the nature of life and the search for faithful love. The Youngest Pupil calls for the Seanchan to proclaim the right of poets. The Oldest Pupil notes that the man who dies has the chief part in the story. The King instructs to take up the body of the deceased and to lay it where they please.

The text includes a Latin phrase about the splendor of drunkenness. Charlie Ward expresses surprise at the existence of a hymn related to drunkenness. Paddy Cockfight discusses acquiring a fighting cock from a man in Mullingar. Paul Ruttledge inquires about the cost of a good fighting cock. Molly the Scold claims that an old cock owned by Andy Farrell could defeat other cocks. There is a loud commotion outside, attributed to free drinks causing chaos among the men. Mr. Green and Colonel Lawley, along with others, demand to enter the establishment.

The text discusses the challenges of achieving authenticity in literature. Synge is described as having little interest in political thoughts or mass movements. Synge preferred to judge individual people rather than engage with political abstractions. A scenario written by Synge involved two women of different religions quarreling in a cave during a time of conflict. Synge believed that creative art could only emerge from a focus on Ireland. Synge expressed disapproval of modern drama for its lack of expressive language. The text suggests that Synge's low vitality contributed to his observant and contemplative nature.

source.author: William Butler Yeats
source.title: Synge And The Ireland Of His Time

text: The narrator experienced a change of heart but did not believe it would come slowly. The narrator spent time at the British Museum and often delayed consulting necessary books due to physical discomfort. The narrator was compiling an anthology of Irish fairy stories and a two-volume selection from Irish novelists for American publishers. The narrator received twelve pounds for the first book and twenty pounds for the second book, which they did not consider bad pay. The narrator lived outside of Ireland for most of the year while maintaining focus on the subject matter of their poetry. The narrator reflected on the impact of setting stories in one's own landscape, comparing it to the works of Morris and Shelley. The narrator expressed a desire to create art that conceals the artist's handiwork, similar to ancient sculptures and old ballads.

Fionn has white hair, which may symbolize the troubles of those seeking wisdom. Bare is often referred to as an ugly old woman, but Dr. Joyce notes her old name Aebhin means beautiful. Aebhen was the goddess of the tribes of northern Leinster. Michael Robartes, Hanrahan, and Aedh are personages in 'The Secret Rose,' used as principles of the mind rather than actual characters. The Rose has been a symbol of spiritual love and beauty for many centuries. The lotus is represented in Assyrian bas-reliefs as blossoming upon the Tree of Life. The Rose appears in Irish poetry as a religious symbol, a symbol of beauty, and a symbol of Ireland.

The play was performed at the Abbey Theatre for the first time on December 14, 1911. Miss Maire O'Neill took the part of the Countess in the performance. The play was originally written before the author had stage experience. The author made a complete revision of the play to make it suitable for performance at the Abbey Theatre. The play lasts a little over an hour when performed without an interval. The new ending of the play was designed to suit the Abbey stage's specific features. The stalls at the theatre contained many distinguished individuals from Dublin.

The scene takes place in a dungeon of the Inquisition on the morning of the Auto-da-Fe. Ebremar enters the scene and expresses his intention to execute a Moorish girl for heresy. The First Inquisitor suggests that Ebremar should speak to the Moorish girl to persuade her to renounce her beliefs. Mosada reflects on her surroundings and the impending arrival of her brothers who will be working in the fields. Mosada possesses a poison ring that she plans to use to end her life. Mosada contemplates her death and the fading stars outside the barred window.

The man's wife took him to a healer in Rahasane after a few days of pain. The healer warned that if the man had fallen asleep on the grass, he would have been lost. Bristles may have been associated with fertility in various cultures. Professor Rhys interprets the bristleless boar as a symbol of darkness and cold. The text discusses battles involving the Sidhe, including one related to harvest and another concerning the dying. The battle between the Tribes of the goddess Danu and the Fomor is described as a struggle between light and darkness. Conchobar's death involved being struck by a ball made from the brain of a dead enemy, which was left in his head.

The narrator's father had a dark complexion, a large forehead, and dark hazel eyes. He was five feet seven inches tall and had a graceful and majestic deportment. The father excelled in bodily exercises, particularly fencing, and trained the narrator's sons in this skill. The narrator's mother maintained a youthful appearance and agility even at sixty years of age. The mother's health deteriorated after a siege by Indians, leading to her death shortly after the narrator became a widow. The narrator fulfilled her mother's dying wish to care for her father, who never complained about her love and fidelity. The narrator reflects on her mother's jealousy regarding her father's affection and understands it in hindsight.

source.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
source.title: Henry Esmond; The English Humourists; The Four Georges

text: The speaker expresses disbelief at the idea of fighting against a powerful nation and army. Hal acknowledges the likelihood of defeat but believes that it may be beneficial for them. The speaker has previously attempted to argue in favor of the British side without success. Hal respects the officers of the British army and believes in focusing on defeating them rather than insulting them. Hal is referred to as 'Chevaleer Baird' by some in the Continental army. Hal expresses confidence that his company can defeat the British army despite their training differences. Hal has been elected colonel of the county militia and invites the speaker to dinner at his home.

The narrator conducted operations on old Speck that resulted in an invitation to explore the town. The narrator and Speck visited various locations including the palace, church-tower, Museum, and Gymnasium. Speck introduced the narrator to his wife, Leocadia, and described him as a young world-observer and art-friend. Dorothea, Speck's daughter, was knowledgeable about British literature and inquired about famous writers. The narrator described several literary figures and promised to provide a signature of Mrs. Hemans. The narrator was captivated by Dorothea and did not miss a meal while engaged in conversation until six o'clock. Madame Speck served tea with cakes and tartines, and Dorothea chose not to play whist that evening.

A procession included two men in black holding a red canopy, a priest with the sacrament, and altar-boys with lamps. The clergyman entered a hospital for old women while the canopy and lamp-bearers remained outside. The Duke d'Arenberg has a picture-gallery that contains small, notable artworks rather than large pieces. Among the artworks in the Duke's gallery are a small Rembrandt, a Paul Potter, an Ostade, and a Dusart. The Duke's library features a marble head believed to be the original head of the Laocoon. Brussels churches are decorated with elaborate wooden pulpits, including one at St. Gudule supported by figures like Adam and Eve. In various churches, clergymen preach from uniquely designed pulpits, including one resembling a hermitage and another a palm tree.

The inhabitants of the city gathered to watch a performance in which Princess Rosalba was to be the heroine.
